57: provides higher accuracy than the retrieval-augmentation for downstream tasks with informative
58: queries. Moreover, it would be compelling if we could combine the strength of both methods and
59: achieve even higher accuracies. In this work, we attempt to answer the above questions through a
60: comprehensive study.
61: Specifically, we make the following contributions:
62: 1. We perform comprehensive study using two state-of-the-art LLMs, a proprietary 43B pre-
63: trained GPT and Llama2-70B (Touvron et al., 2023b) on 9 downstream long context tasks,
64: including single and multi document question answering (QA), query-based summarization,
65: and in context few-shot learning tasks.
66: 2. We demonstrate that retrieval-augmentation significantly improves the performance of 4K
67: context LLMs. Perhaps surprisingly, we find this simple retrieval-augmented baseline can
68: perform comparable to 16K long context LLMs, i.e., average score 29.32 vs. 29.45 by using
69: GPT-43B, and 36.02 vs. 36.78 by using Llama2-70B, while using much less computation.
70: 3. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of long context LLM (i.e., 16K or 32K)
71: can still be improved by retrieval, especially for the larger Llama2-70B. As a result, our best
72: model, retrieval augmented Llama2-70B-32k-ret with 32K context window (avg. score 43.6),
73: outperforms GPT-3.5-turbo-16k (avg. score 42.8) and Davinci-003 in terms of average score.
74: It also largely outperforms its non-retrieval Llama2-70B-32k baseline (avg. score 40.9), while
75: can be much faster at generation (e.g., 4× faster on NarrativeQA).
76: We organize the rest of the paper as follows. We discuss related work in Section 2, and present the
77: experimental setup in Section 3. We report results in Section 4 and conclude the paper in Section 5.

81: retrieval-augmented language models.

20: Abstract
21: Despite the recent progress in long-context large language models (LLMs), it re-
22: mains elusive how these transformer-based language models acquire the capability
23: to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context.
24: This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across 4
25: model families, 6 model scales, and 3 types of finetuning reveals that a special
26: type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving relevant information
27: from long context, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify important and
28: intriguing properties of retrieval heads: (1) universal: all the explored models
29: with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small
30: portion (less than 5%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval
31: heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending
32: the context length to 32-128K by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of
33: heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2
34: 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no
35: matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in
36: different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in
37: retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random
38: non-retrieval heads does not affect the model’s retrieval ability. We further show
39: that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the
40: model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context.
41: Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic
42: knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations
43: collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the
44: input tokens. We believe our insights on retrieval heads foster future research on
45: reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.

47: Introduction
48: This work studies the internal mechanism of how long-context language models can utilize infor-
49: mation at arbitrary locations within the input. Recent advances in long-context language model-
50: ing [1, 20, 6] show inspiring results, particularly on the Needle-in-a-Haystack test [14], which asks
51: the model to precisely retrieve the information of a short sentence (the needle) within a long context
52: (the haystack). Such capability is the basis of more advanced long-context tasks, which usually
53: interleaves retrieval and reasoning in a multi-step fashion [17]. Based on extensive experiments
54: across 4 model families, 6 model scales, and 3 types of finetuning, we show that across the models’
55: attention layers, there exist a small number of retrieval heads that search the information being asked,
56: and redirect the relevant tokens from the input to the output. Activation of retrieval heads explains

80: The discovery of the retrieval head is motivated by the question of what the attention mechanism
81: is doing when the model can or cannot find the given needle. We take important inspiration from
82: two existing works: the CopyNet [10] and the Induction Head [19]. The CopyNet is essentially a
83: single-layer, single-head attention mechanism in the age of RNNs that copy-paste tokens from the
84: input to the output. Induction Heads [19] are special heads within a multi-layer, multi-head attention
85: network that implements an implicit program induction algorithm. Combining the observation from

87: learning, there might exist special heads that are accountable for information retrieval and implement

100: required information; consequently these heads compensate each other’s functionality: removing a
101: subset of the heads, the model at least retrieve part of the required information; (4) the retrieval heads

157: Detecting Retrieval Head
158: To detect which head is implementing the retrieval algorithm, we introduct a retrieval score to
159: measures the frequency of a head’s copy-paste behavior during autoregressive decoding. An attention
160: head with high retrieval score suggests that statistically across various contexts, this head is frequently
161: copying the input tokens from the input to the output.
162: Needle-in-a-Haystack
163: Our retrieval head detection algorithm roots from the needle-in-a-
164: Haystack test, which asks the model to copy-paste the input tokens to the output. Given a question
165: q and its corresponding answer k (the needle), we insert k in a given context x (the haystack) at a
166: random position index range iq. The language model is then tasked with answering q based on the
167: haystack with the inserted needle. We set q and k unique and irrelevant with the given long context,
168: ensuring that if an answer is correctly generated, it is indeed copied from the context, not from the
169: model’s internal knowledge.

1: Title: Retrieval_augmented_generation
2: Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval_augmented_generation
3: License: CC BY SA 4.0
4: 
5: Retrieval-augmented generation Type of information retrieval using LLMs 
6: 
7:  Retrieval-augmented generation ( RAG ) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources. [ 1 ] [ 2 ] With RAG, LLMs first refer to a specified set of documents, then respond to user queries. These documents supplement information from the LLM's pre-existing training data . [ 3 ] This allows LLMs to use domain-specific and/or updated information that is not available in the training data. [ 3 ] For example, this enables LLM-based chatbots to access internal company data or generate responses based on authoritative sources. The technique was first proposed in 2020 and has since become a widely adopted approach in modern AI systems. 
8: 
9:  RAG improves LLMs by incorporating information retrieval before generating responses. [ 4 ] Unlike LLMs that rely on static training data, RAG pulls relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources. [ 1 ] According to Ars Technica , "RAG is a way of improving LLM performance, in essence by blending the LLM process with a web search or other document look-up process to help LLMs stick to the facts." This method helps reduce AI hallucinations , [ 4 ] which have caused chatbots to describe policies that don't exist, or recommend nonexistent legal cases to lawyers that are looking for citations to support their arguments. [ 5 ] 
10: 
11:  RAG also reduces the need to retrain LLMs with new data, saving on computational and financial costs. [ 1 ] Beyond efficiency gains, RAG also allows LLMs to include sources in their responses, so users can verify the cited sources. This provides greater transparency, as users can cross-check retrieved content to ensure accuracy and relevance. 
12: 
13:  The term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) was introduced in a 2020 paper that described combining a parametric language model with a non-parametric external memory accessed through retrieval at inference time. [ 4 ] 
14: 
15:  RAG and LLM limitations 
16:  LLMs can provide incorrect information. For example, when Google first demonstrated its LLM tool " Google Bard " (later re-branded to Gemini), the LLM provided incorrect information about the James Webb Space Telescope . This error contributed to a $100 billion decline in Google's stock value. [ 5 ] RAG is used to prevent these errors, but it does not solve all the problems. For example, LLMs can generate misinformation even when pulling from factually correct sources if they misinterpret the context. MIT Technology Review gives the example of an AI-generated response stating, "The United States has had one Muslim president, Barack Hussein Obama." The model retrieved this from the rhetorical chapter title "Barack Hussein Obama: America's First Muslim President?" in the book Faith in the New Millennium: The Future of Religion and American Politics . [ 6 ] The LLM did not "know" or "understand" the context of the title, generating a false statement. [ 3 ] 
17: 
18:  LLMs with RAG are programmed to prioritize new information. This technique has been called "prompt stuffing." Without prompt stuffing, the LLM's input is generated by a user; with prompt stuffing, additional relevant context is added to this input to guide the model's response. This approach provides the LLM with key information early in the prompt, encouraging it to prioritize the supplied data over pre-existing training knowledge. [ 7 ] 
19: 
20:  Process 
21:  Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an information-retrieval mechanism that allows models to access and utilize additional data beyond their original training set. Ars Technica notes that "when new information becomes available, rather than having to retrain the model, all that's needed is to augment the model's external knowledge base with the updated information ("augmentation"). [ 5 ] IBM states that "in the generative phase, the LLM draws from the augmented prompt and its internal representation of its training data to synthesize" an answer. [ 1 ] 
22: 
23:  RAG key stages 
24: 
25:  Typically, the data to be referenced is converted into LLM embeddings , numerical representations in the form of a large vector space. RAG can be used on unstructured (usually text), semi-structured, or structured data (for example knowledge graphs ). These embeddings are then stored in a vector database to allow for document retrieval . 
26: 
27:  Given a user query, a document retriever is first called to select the most relevant documents that will be used to augment the query. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] This comparison can be done using a variety of methods, which depend in part on the type of indexing used. [ 1 ] 
28: 
29:  The model feeds this relevant retrieved information into the LLM via prompt engineering of the user's original query. Newer implementations ( as of 2023 [ update ] ) can also incorporate specific augmentation modules with abilities such as expanding queries into multiple domains and using memory and self-improvement to learn from previous retrievals. [ citation needed ] 
30: 
31:  Finally, the LLM can generate output based on both the query and the retrieved documents. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] Some models incorporate extra steps to improve output, such as the re-ranking of retrieved information, context selection, and fine-tuning . 
32: 
33:  Applications 
34:  Retrieval-augmented generation is used in applications where generated responses need to be grounded in external or frequently updated information. [ citation needed ] 
35: 
36:  In healthcare, RAG has been studied as a way to ground large language model outputs in external medical knowledge sources, although reviews have noted continuing challenges around evaluation, ethics, and clinical reliability. [ 8 ] 
37: 
38:  Improvements 
39:  Improvements to the basic process above can be applied at different stages in the RAG flow. 
40: 
41:  Encoder 
42:  These methods focus on the encoding of text as either dense or sparse vectors. Sparse vectors , which encode the identity of a word, are typically dictionary -length and contain mostly zeros. Dense vectors , which encode meaning, are more compact and contain fewer zeros. Various enhancements can improve the way similarities are calculated in the vector stores (databases). [ 9 ] 
43: 
44:  Performance improves by optimizing how vector similarities are calculated. Dot products enhance similarity scoring, while approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) searches improve retrieval efficiency over K-nearest neighbors (KNN) searches. [ 10 ] 
45:  Accuracy may be improved with Late Interactions, which allow the system to compare words more precisely after retrieval. This helps refine document ranking and improve search relevance. [ 11 ] 
46:  Hybrid vector approaches may be used to combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors, taking advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations. [ 9 ] 
47:  Other retrieval techniques focus on improving accuracy by refining how documents are selected. Some retrieval methods combine sparse representations, such as SPLADE, with query expansion strategies to improve search accuracy and recall. [ 12 ] 
48: 
49:  Retriever-centric methods 
50:  These methods aim to enhance the quality of document retrieval in vector databases: 
51: 
52:  Pre-training the retriever using the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), a technique that helps the model learn retrieval patterns by predicting masked text within documents. [ 13 ] 
53:  Supervised retriever optimization aligns retrieval probabilities with the generator model's likelihood distribution. This involves retrieving the top-k vectors for a given prompt, scoring the generated response's perplexity , and minimizing KL divergence between the retriever's selections and the model's likelihoods to refine retrieval. [ 14 ] 
54:  Reranking techniques can refine retriever performance by prioritizing the most relevant retrieved documents during training. [ 15 ] 
55:  Language model 
56: 
57:  Retro language model for RAG. Each Retro block consists of Attention, Chunked Cross Attention, and Feed Forward layers. Black-lettered boxes show data being changed, and blue lettering shows the algorithm performing the changes. 
58: 
59:  By redesigning the language model with the retriever in mind, a 25-time smaller network can get comparable perplexity as its much larger counterparts. [ 16 ] Because it is trained from scratch, this method (Retro) incurs the high cost of training runs that the original RAG scheme avoided. The hypothesis is that by giving domain knowledge during training, Retro needs less focus on the domain and can devote its smaller weight resources only to language semantics. The redesigned language model is shown here. 
60: 
61:  It has been reported that Retro is not reproducible, so modifications were made to make it so. The more reproducible version is called Retro++ and includes in-context RAG. [ 17 ] 
62: 
63:  Chunking 
64:  See also: Chunking (computing) 
65:  Chunking involves various strategies for breaking up the data into vectors so the retriever can find details in it. 
66: 
67:  Different data styles have patterns that correct chunking can take advantage of. 
68: 
69:  Hybrid search 
70:  Sometimes vector database searches ( aka semantic search technique) can miss key facts needed to answer a user's question. One way to mitigate this is to do a traditional text search ( aka full text search ), combine those results to the text chunks linked to the retrieved vectors from the vector search, and feed the combined hybrid text (using effective scoring or reranking scoring) into the language model for generation. [ 18 ] 
71: 
72:  Challenges 
73:  RAG does not prevent hallucinations in LLMs. According to Ars Technica , "It is not a direct solution because the LLM can still hallucinate around the source material in its response." [ 5 ] 
74: 
75:  While RAG improves the accuracy of large language models (LLMs), it does not eliminate all challenges. One limitation is that while RAG reduces the need for frequent model retraining, it does not remove it entirely. Additionally, LLMs may struggle to recognize when they lack sufficient information to provide a reliable response. Without specific training, models may generate answers even when they should indicate uncertainty. According to IBM , this issue can arise when the model lacks the ability to assess its own knowledge limitations. [ 1 ] 
76: 
77:  RAG poisoning 
78:  RAG systems may retrieve factually correct but misleading sources, leading to errors in interpretation. In some cases, an LLM may extract statements from a source without considering its context, resulting in an incorrect conclusion. Additionally, when faced with conflicting information, RAG models may struggle to determine which source is accurate. The worst case outcome of this limitation is that the model may combine details from multiple sources producing responses that merge outdated and updated information in a misleading manner. According to the MIT Technology Review , these issues occur because RAG systems may misinterpret the data they retrieve. [ 3 ]

1: Title: Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models
2: arXiv ID: 2310.03025
3: 
4: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024
5: RETRIEVAL MEETS LONG CONTEXT LARGE LANGUAGE
6: MODELS
7: Peng Xu†, Wei Ping†, Xianchao Wu, Lawrence McAfee
8: Chen Zhu, Zihan Liu, Sandeep Subramanian, Evelina Bakhturina
9: Mohammad Shoeybi, Bryan Catanzaro
10: NVIDIA
11: †{pengx, wping}@nvidia.com
12: ABSTRACT
13: Extending the context window of large language models (LLMs) is getting popular
14: recently, while the solution of augmenting LLMs with retrieval has existed for years.
15: The natural questions are: i) Retrieval-augmentation versus long context window,
16: which one is better for downstream tasks? ii) Can both methods be combined to
17: get the best of both worlds? In this work, we answer these questions by studying
18: both solutions using two state-of-the-art pretrained LLMs, i.e., a proprietary 43B
19: GPT and Llama2-70B. Perhaps surprisingly, we find that LLM with 4K context
20: window using simple retrieval-augmentation at generation can achieve compa-
21: rable performance to finetuned LLM with 16K context window via positional
22: interpolation on long context tasks, while taking much less computation. More
23: importantly, we demonstrate that retrieval can significantly improve the perfor-
24: mance of LLMs regardless of their extended context window sizes. Our best model,
25: retrieval-augmented Llama2-70B with 32K context window, outperforms GPT-3.5-
26: turbo-16k and Davinci003 in terms of average score on nine long context tasks
27: including question answering, query-based summarization, and in-context few-shot
28: learning tasks. It also outperforms its non-retrieval Llama2-70B-32k baseline by a
29: margin, while being much faster at generation. Our study provides general insights
30: on the choice of retrieval-augmentation versus long context extension of LLM for
31: practitioners.
32: 1
33: INTRODUCTION
34: The long context large language models (LLM) have recently received a lot of attention in produc-
35: tion (e.g., Anthropic, 2023; OpenAI, 2023b), research community (e.g., Chen et al., 2023; Liu et al.,
36: 2023; Tworkowski et al., 2023), and open source community (e.g., Kaiokendev, 2023). Although
37: the approximate attention methods have been studied for years (e.g., Tay et al., 2022a) (due to the
38: quadratic time and memory complexities of self-attention mechanism in sequence length), the recent
39: advance for long context LLMs with exact attention is mainly driven by the development of faster
40: GPU with more memory and memory-efficient exact attention (Dao et al., 2022; Dao, 2023).
41: An alternative and long-standing solution for handling long context is retrieval. Specifically, the
42: LLMs only read relevant context retrieved from a standalone retriever (e.g., Karpukhin et al., 2020;
43: Wang et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023), which is much easier to scale 1 and runs orders of magnitudes
44: faster than LLMs for selecting relevant context. Conceptually, the retrieval-augmented decoder-only
45: LLM can be viewed as applying the sparse attention over its long context window, where the sparsity
46: pattern is not predefined as Child et al. (2019) but determined by the standalone retriever. In other
47: words, unretrieved context is treated as irrelevant and has zero-valued attention weights.
48: Given the surge of interest in long context LLM research and much more required computation
49: at inference 2, it is still unclear for practitioners whether extending the context window of LLM
50: 1The dense embedding retriever can easily retrieve context from billions of tokens using the fast similarity
51: search library (Johnson et al., 2019).
52: 2For example, the price of GPT-4 with 32k context length is twice the 8k context model.
53: 1
54: arXiv:2310.03025v2  [cs.CL]  23 Jan 2024
55: 
56: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2024
57: provides higher accuracy than the retrieval-augmentation for downstream tasks with informative
58: queries. Moreover, it would be compelling if we could combine the strength of both methods and
59: achieve even higher accuracies. In this work, we attempt to answer the above questions through a
60: comprehensive study.
61: Specifically, we make the following contributions:
62: 1. We perform comprehensive study using two state-of-the-art LLMs, a proprietary 43B pre-
63: trained GPT and Llama2-70B (Touvron et al., 2023b) on 9 downstream long context tasks,
64: including single and multi document question answering (QA), query-based summarization,
65: and in context few-shot learning tasks.
66: 2. We demonstrate that retrieval-augmentation significantly improves the performance of 4K
67: context LLMs. Perhaps surprisingly, we find this simple retrieval-augmented baseline can
68: perform comparable to 16K long context LLMs, i.e., average score 29.32 vs. 29.45 by using
69: GPT-43B, and 36.02 vs. 36.78 by using Llama2-70B, while using much less computation.
70: 3. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the performance of long context LLM (i.e., 16K or 32K)
71: can still be improved by retrieval, especially for the larger Llama2-70B. As a result, our best
72: model, retrieval augmented Llama2-70B-32k-ret with 32K context window (avg. score 43.6),
73: outperforms GPT-3.5-turbo-16k (avg. score 42.8) and Davinci-003 in terms of average score.
74: It also largely outperforms its non-retrieval Llama2-70B-32k baseline (avg. score 40.9), while
75: can be much faster at generation (e.g., 4× faster on NarrativeQA).
76: We organize the rest of the paper as follows. We discuss related work in Section 2, and present the
77: experimental setup in Section 3. We report results in Section 4 and conclude the paper in Section 5.
78: 2
79: RELATED WORK
80: In this section, we discuss the related work in long context LLM, efficient attention methods, and
81: retrieval-augmented language models.
82: 2.1
83: PARALLEL WORK
84: When we are preparing this manuscript, we notice that a concurrent work (Bai et al., 2023) (arXived
85: on 28 Aug 2023) also studies the impact of retrieval on long context LLM, including black-box model
86: GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k (OpenAI, 2022), white-box model Llama2-7B-chat-4k (Touvron et al., 2023b),
87: and ChatGLM2-6B-32k (Zeng et al., 2022). Different from our findings, they find that retrieval is
88: only helpful for Llama2-7B-chat-4k with 4K context window, but not helpful for long context model,
89: i.e., GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k and ChatGLM2-6B-32k. We hypothesize the major reasons are: i) it is
90: challenging to do controlled experiments using black-box APIs, ii) the white-box LLMs used in their
91: study are relatively small, thus they have limited zero-shot capability of incorporating context through
92: retrieval. Our conclusions are drawn from much larger LLMs. In particular, our best long context
93: model Llama2-70B-32k performs as well as Davinci003 and GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, while it can still be
94: further enhanced by retrieval (see Table 3).
95: 2.2
96: LONG CONTEXT LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS
97: Over the past few years, pretraining large language models (LLMs) with long context window
98: becomes a viable solution thanks to faster GPU with more memory and memory-efficient exact
99: attention (e.g., Dao et al., 2022). For example, the context window for pretrained LLM have been
100: increased from 1024 of GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019), 2048 of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), 4096 of
101: Llama 2 (Touvron et al., 2023b), to 8192 of GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023a). However, further extending the
102: context window in pretraining can be challenging, because, i) pretraining LLM from scratch with long
103: context (e.g., >16K tokens) is very expensive due to the quadratic time and memory complexities of
104: exact attention, and ii) most of documents in pretraining corpus (e.g., Common Crawl) are relatively
105: short.
106: Most recently, researchers start to extend the context window of LLMs with continued training or
107: fine-tuning (e.g., Kaiokendev, 2023; Nijkamp et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Tworkowski et al., 2023;
108: Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023). Tworkowski et al. (2023) introduced LongLLaMA by fine-tuning the

113: attention (Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023) extends the context length of LLaMA 7B from 4K to 32K
114: by introducing “landmark tokens” to represent blocks of the context and fine-tuning the attention

119: et al., 2021) extrapolates context window length by removing the positional embeddings while simply
120: biasing the key-query attention scores with a linear penalty that is proportional to their distance, so
121: one does not need finetuning for context window extrapolation. Ratner et al. (2023) chunks long
122: context into multiple sub-windows and re-use the positional embeddings across these windows,
123: thus can handle longer context without any further finetuning. In this work, we apply positional

126: pretraining. In terms of evaluation, we focus on downstream task performance (e.g., Shaham et al.,
127: 2023; Bai et al., 2023) after instruction tuning (Wei et al., 2021).
128: There are other studies showing the interplay between retrieval-augmentation and long context LLM.
129: Liu et al. (2023) performs the black-box evaluation for the long context capability of existing LLM
130: products, including ChatGPT 3.5 (OpenAI, 2022), GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023a), Claude (Anthropic,
131: 2023), in retrieval-augmented setting, and identify the “lost in the middle” phenomenon in these
132: models.
133: 2.3
134: EFFICIENT ATTENTION METHODS
135: In previous study, many approximate attention methods (Tay et al., 2022a) have been introduced for
136: dealing with the quadratic complexity of self-attention that becomes a computational bottleneck for
137: long context. They can be grouped into the following categories: i) Sparse attention mechanisms
138: with predefined sparsity patterns (e.g., Child et al., 2019; Parmar et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2019; Beltagy
139: et al., 2020; Zaheer et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2021), ii) recurrence-based method (Dai et al., 2019;
140: Bulatov et al., 2022), iii) low-rank projection attention (e.g., Wang et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2021;
141: Tay et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2021), iv) memory-based mechanisms (e.g., Rae et al., 2020; Liu et al.,
142: 2018), v) similarity and clustering based methods (e.g., Kitaev et al., 2020; Tay et al., 2020; Roy
143: et al., 2021). These approximate methods introduce inductive bias (e.g., predefined sparsity) that can
144: fit well for specific domain, but may reduce model quality in general LLM training.

472: 3.5
473: INSTRUCTION TUNING
474: To train the pretrained LLMs to follow instructions for question answering or text summarization, we
475: also performed instruction tuning. We first construct a blend of instruction tuning datasets consisting
476: of 102K training samples from the Soda dataset (Kim et al., 2022), ELI5 dataset (Fan et al., 2019),
477: FLAN dataset (Wei et al., 2021) , Open Assistatant dataset (Köpf et al., 2023), Dolly (Conover et al.,
478: 2023) and a proprietary sourced conversational dataset, to adapt all foundation models to follow
479: instructions. In terms of the template, we use "System: {System}\n\nUser: {Question}\n\nAssistant:
480: {Answer}" as the format to support multi-turn dialogue training. As all of the tasks contain the
481: context information for reasoning over at inference time, we add the context before the dialogue, i.e.
482: "System: {System}\n\n{Context}\n\nUser: {Question}\n\nAssistant: {Answer}".
483: We finetune the LLM by taking the loss only on the {Answer} part with batch size 128 and learning
484: rate of 5e-6 for 1000 steps. For the rest of the paper, results are all reported using the instruction
485: tuned chat model on top of the foundational GPT-43B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-70B.
486: 4
487: RESULTS
488: In this section, we report the results and provide detailed analysis.
489: 4.1
490: MAIN RESULTS
491: In Table 2, we compare different model variants with context lengths ranging from 4K to as long
492: as 32K using GPT-43B and Llama2-70B. First, we find that baseline models without retrieval of
493: 4k sequence length achieve the worst results for both GPT-43B and Llama2-70B. This is because
494: the minimum average sequence length of all seven tasks exceeds 4096, the context window of
495: the foundation models and therefore valuable texts get truncated randomly. As a result, retrieval
496: is especially helpful for 4K LLMs e.g., Llama2-70B-4K is improved from 31.61 to 35.73 while
497: GPT-43B-4K is improved from 26.44 to 29.32. Second, we observe that HotpotQA (HQA) especially
498: favors long sequence models as the score improves from 34.64 to 43.97 for Llama2-70B and from
499: 28.91 to 37.48 for GPT-43B when the sequence length increases from 4k to 16k. This is because
500: Hotpot QA is a multi-hop dataset where the questions are not hard to answer but all intermediate
501: hops are necessary to get correct answer. Therefore, long context are beneficial to increase the recall
502: of incorporating all intermediate hops.

598: It is quite interesting that the retrieval-augmented long context LLM (e.g., 16K and 32K) can obtain
599: better results than retrieval-augmented 4K context LLM, even they are feed with the same top 5
600: chunks of evidence. We hypothesize this interesting observation is related to the “lost in the middle”
601: phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023), where the LLMs has such “U-shaped” performance curve. Specifically,
602: LLMs are better at utilizing relevant information that occurs at the beginning or end of its input
603: context window. To further verify the hypothesis, we conduct the “lost-in-the-middle” study following
604: Liu et al. (2023) for Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k. As show in Figure 1, we confirm that the
605: phenomenon also exists in Llama2-70B with different context lengths. In particular, the comparison
606: of the curves from Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k suggests that the long context model has
607: better accuracy for incorporating top-5 retrieved context.
608: Note that, we have very different observation from the conclusion drawn from LongBench work (Bai
609: et al., 2023): “Retrieval brings improvement for model with weak ability on long contexts, but the
610: performance still lags behind models that have strong long context understanding capability”. Here,
611: we demonstrate retrieval can significantly improve the performance of both GPT-43B and Llama2-70B
612: regardless their context window size. For example, our best retrieval-augmented Llama2-70B-32k-ret
613: outperforms its baseline w/o retrieval by a margin, i.e., 39.60 vs. 37.36. We think the major reason for
614: such different conclusion is that Bai et al. (2023) uses much smaller LLM with 6B and 7B parameters,
615: which usually has relatively worse zero-shot capability to incorporate the retrieved chunked context.
616: To further validate the hypothesis, we also report the results using Llama2-7B in Table 5. One can
617: actually draw similar conclusions to Bai et al. (2023) . We think the underlying reasons are: i) For
618: Llama2-7B-chat-4k, its short context length is the bottleneck for long context tasks. Thus, retrieval-
619: augmentation largely improves the results. ii) For Llama2-7B-chat-32 and ChatGLM2-6B-32k, the
620: context length bottleneck has been mostly removed. However, their retrieval-augmented models have
621: limited zero-shot capability of incorporating retrieved chunks of context, due to the smaller size. As
622: a result, retrieval is not helpful for both Llama2-7B-32k and ChatGLM2-6B-32k, which is different
623: from large LLMs like Llama2-70B-32k in our case.

874: 4.3
875: ABLATION ON DIFFERENT RETRIEVERS
876: To investigate the impacts of different retrievers on top of Llama2-70B, we compare Dragon, Con-
877: triever, and OpenAI embeddings on top of Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k. The results in
878: Table 4 confirms that our finding, i.e., retrieval can boost the performance of both short context and
879: long context LLMs, is consistent across different retrievers.
880: 4.4
881: INCREASING THE NUMBER OF RETRIEVED CHUNKS
882: To study the impact of adding more retrieved chunks to the context, we increase the number of
883: retrieved chunks from 5 to 20 using Dragon retriever and the results can be found in Table 5. We
884: observe that for different sequence lengths, the best averaged results are obtained either from top 5 or
885: top 10. Even if 20 chunks can still fit into the 16K and 32K context window (as shown in Figure 2),
886: adding more chunks up to 20 is not helpful and will sometime hurt the performance. We believe this
887: is related to the “lost in the middle” phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023) or the model is getting distracted
888: by irrelevant information and therefore needs further research.
889: 4.5
890: RETRIEVAL FOR FEW-SHOT TASKS
891: In addition to the zero-shot tasks of query-based summarization tasks and question answering tasks
892: mentioned above, we further investigate the benefits of long context models for few-shot tasks using
893: two additional datasets (Trec and SAMSum) from LongBench. We take the question from each
894: dataset as the query and use it to search relevant QA pairs provided in the given few-shot examples.
895: Table 6 shows that our best model Llama2-70B-32k-ret outperforms its non-retrieval Llama2-70B-32k
896: baseline as well as GPT-3.5-turbo-16k by a large margin. It again confirms the benefits on using
897: retrieval together with long context models.
898: 5
899: CONCLUSION
900: In this work, we systematically study the retrieval-augmentation versus long context extension
901: using the state-of-the-art LLMs after instruction tuning for various long context QA and query-
902: based summarization tasks. After study, we have the following interesting findings: i) Retrieval
903: largely boosts the performance of both 4K short context LLM and 16K/32K long context LLMs.
904: ii) The 4K context LLMs with simple retrieval-augmentation can perform comparable to 16K long
905: context LLMs, while being more efficient at inference. iii) After context window extension and
906: retrieval-augmentation, the best model Llama2-70B-32k-ret can outperform GPT-3.5-turbo-16k and
907: Davinci003 in terms of average score on a suit of downstream tasks with informative queries. Our
908: study shed light on the promising direction of combining retrieval and long context techniques
909: together to build better LLM.
910: 6
911: FUTURE DIRECTIONS
912: There are many potential research directions that can be extended from this work. One direction is
913: to develop advanced methods (e.g. memory or hierarchical attention) for existing pretrained large
914: language models e.g. Llama2-70B, which is itself non-trivial. Also, further extending the context
915: window to 64k and even longer would be a very interesting study for large 70B parameter models
916: even though pre-training longer sequence requires much more computation. Lastly, how to mitigate
917: the “lost-in-the-middle” phenomenon is an open research topic and continue pretraining with UL2
918: loss (Tay et al., 2022b) could be one potential solution.

20: Abstract
21: Despite the recent progress in long-context large language models (LLMs), it re-
22: mains elusive how these transformer-based language models acquire the capability
23: to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context.
24: This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across 4
25: model families, 6 model scales, and 3 types of finetuning reveals that a special
26: type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving relevant information
27: from long context, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify important and
28: intriguing properties of retrieval heads: (1) universal: all the explored models
29: with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small
30: portion (less than 5%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval
31: heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending
32: the context length to 32-128K by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of
33: heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2
34: 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no
35: matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in
36: different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in
37: retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random
38: non-retrieval heads does not affect the model’s retrieval ability. We further show
39: that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the
40: model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context.
41: Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic
42: knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations
43: collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the
44: input tokens. We believe our insights on retrieval heads foster future research on
45: reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
46: 1
47: Introduction
48: This work studies the internal mechanism of how long-context language models can utilize infor-
49: mation at arbitrary locations within the input. Recent advances in long-context language model-
50: ing [1, 20, 6] show inspiring results, particularly on the Needle-in-a-Haystack test [14], which asks
51: the model to precisely retrieve the information of a short sentence (the needle) within a long context
52: (the haystack). Such capability is the basis of more advanced long-context tasks, which usually
53: interleaves retrieval and reasoning in a multi-step fashion [17]. Based on extensive experiments
54: across 4 model families, 6 model scales, and 3 types of finetuning, we show that across the models’
55: attention layers, there exist a small number of retrieval heads that search the information being asked,
56: and redirect the relevant tokens from the input to the output. Activation of retrieval heads explains

80: The discovery of the retrieval head is motivated by the question of what the attention mechanism
81: is doing when the model can or cannot find the given needle. We take important inspiration from
82: two existing works: the CopyNet [10] and the Induction Head [19]. The CopyNet is essentially a
83: single-layer, single-head attention mechanism in the age of RNNs that copy-paste tokens from the
84: input to the output. Induction Heads [19] are special heads within a multi-layer, multi-head attention
85: network that implements an implicit program induction algorithm. Combining the observation from
86: the two works, we natually hypothesize that, just like induction heads are accountable for in-context
87: learning, there might exist special heads that are accountable for information retrieval and implement
88: a conditional copy-paste algorithm.
89: We design algorithms to detect retrieval heads within the transformer architecture (Sec. 2), and conduct
90: large-scale experiments to demonstrate important properties of them (Sec. 3): (1) retrieval heads are
91: universal and sparse: for any model family (LLaMA [21], Yi [25], QWen [2] and Mistral [12]), at
92: any scale (6B, 14B, and 34B and 8×7B), either base or chat, either dense or MoE, as long as the
93: model can precisely recite the input information, they have a small number of retrieval heads (Fig. 1);
94: (2) they are intrinsic: the base model (e.g., LLaMA2 base) already contains retrieval heads (as a
95: consequence of large-scale pretraining). Subsequent derivations, such as the long-context continue
96: pretraining (LLaMA2 7B 80K), chat fine-tuning (Qwen Chat), or even sparse upcycling [16, 13] uses
97: the same retrieval heads as the base model (Fig. 5); (3) they are dynamically activated according to
98: the context: the strongest retrieval heads (e.g., 13 for LLaMA 2 7B) are always activated no matter
99: what the required information is, while weaker retrieval heads are activated on different parts of the
100: required information; consequently these heads compensate each other’s functionality: removing a
101: subset of the heads, the model at least retrieve part of the required information; (4) the retrieval heads
102: are causal: say we put a needle "the best thing to do in San Francisco is to eat a sandwich in Dolores
103: Park on a sunny day", completely masking out retrieval heads, the model hallucinates (by saying the
104: best thing is to visit Golden Gate bridge); partially masking out the heads, the model retrieves part of
105: the needle (e.g., it gets the sandwich but forget the Dolores Park); masking out random non-retrieval
106: heads, the model still find full needle; when we do not mask the head yet the model still hallucinate
107: in some cases, the retrieval heads are not activated. We further note that chain-of-thought reasoning
108: also heavily relies on retrieval heads because the model needs to refer back the input information,
109: indicating a complex relationship between the model’s retrieval and reasoning capability.
110: The discovery of retrieval head has profound implications on long-context modeling: (1) it marks a
111: significant step forward in the field of mechanistic interpretability [3, 19] because for the first time
112: we pin point a particular subnet implementing the conditional retrieval algorithm; (2) it explains why
113: certain context-compression methods fail to keep factuality (because they removes the retrieval head,
114: e.g., in Xiao et al. 24), and suggests future research on KV cache compression [7, 15], a key problem
115: for deploying long-context models, should consider the influence of retrieval heads.

157: Detecting Retrieval Head
158: To detect which head is implementing the retrieval algorithm, we introduct a retrieval score to
159: measures the frequency of a head’s copy-paste behavior during autoregressive decoding. An attention
160: head with high retrieval score suggests that statistically across various contexts, this head is frequently
161: copying the input tokens from the input to the output.
162: Needle-in-a-Haystack
163: Our retrieval head detection algorithm roots from the needle-in-a-
164: Haystack test, which asks the model to copy-paste the input tokens to the output. Given a question
165: q and its corresponding answer k (the needle), we insert k in a given context x (the haystack) at a
166: random position index range iq. The language model is then tasked with answering q based on the
167: haystack with the inserted needle. We set q and k unique and irrelevant with the given long context,
168: ensuring that if an answer is correctly generated, it is indeed copied from the context, not from the
169: model’s internal knowledge.

172: copy-paste operations. Specifically, during auto-regressive decoding (we use greedy decoding by
173: default), denote the current token being generated as w and the attention scores of a head as a ∈R|x|.

176: (2) xj = w, j = arg max(a), j ∈iq, i.e., the input token that receives the most attention probability
177: mass by this head is a token within the needle and is the same token as the currently generated token.

473: INSTRUCTION TUNING
474: To train the pretrained LLMs to follow instructions for question answering or text summarization, we
475: also performed instruction tuning. We first construct a blend of instruction tuning datasets consisting
476: of 102K training samples from the Soda dataset (Kim et al., 2022), ELI5 dataset (Fan et al., 2019),
477: FLAN dataset (Wei et al., 2021) , Open Assistatant dataset (Köpf et al., 2023), Dolly (Conover et al.,
478: 2023) and a proprietary sourced conversational dataset, to adapt all foundation models to follow
479: instructions. In terms of the template, we use "System: {System}\n\nUser: {Question}\n\nAssistant:
480: {Answer}" as the format to support multi-turn dialogue training. As all of the tasks contain the
481: context information for reasoning over at inference time, we add the context before the dialogue, i.e.
482: "System: {System}\n\n{Context}\n\nUser: {Question}\n\nAssistant: {Answer}".
483: We finetune the LLM by taking the loss only on the {Answer} part with batch size 128 and learning
484: rate of 5e-6 for 1000 steps. For the rest of the paper, results are all reported using the instruction
485: tuned chat model on top of the foundational GPT-43B, Llama2-7B, and Llama2-70B.
486: 4
487: RESULTS
488: In this section, we report the results and provide detailed analysis.
489: 4.1
490: MAIN RESULTS
491: In Table 2, we compare different model variants with context lengths ranging from 4K to as long
492: as 32K using GPT-43B and Llama2-70B. First, we find that baseline models without retrieval of
493: 4k sequence length achieve the worst results for both GPT-43B and Llama2-70B. This is because
494: the minimum average sequence length of all seven tasks exceeds 4096, the context window of
495: the foundation models and therefore valuable texts get truncated randomly. As a result, retrieval
496: is especially helpful for 4K LLMs e.g., Llama2-70B-4K is improved from 31.61 to 35.73 while
497: GPT-43B-4K is improved from 26.44 to 29.32. Second, we observe that HotpotQA (HQA) especially
498: favors long sequence models as the score improves from 34.64 to 43.97 for Llama2-70B and from
499: 28.91 to 37.48 for GPT-43B when the sequence length increases from 4k to 16k. This is because
500: Hotpot QA is a multi-hop dataset where the questions are not hard to answer but all intermediate
501: hops are necessary to get correct answer. Therefore, long context are beneficial to increase the recall
502: of incorporating all intermediate hops.

598: It is quite interesting that the retrieval-augmented long context LLM (e.g., 16K and 32K) can obtain
599: better results than retrieval-augmented 4K context LLM, even they are feed with the same top 5
600: chunks of evidence. We hypothesize this interesting observation is related to the “lost in the middle”
601: phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023), where the LLMs has such “U-shaped” performance curve. Specifically,
602: LLMs are better at utilizing relevant information that occurs at the beginning or end of its input
603: context window. To further verify the hypothesis, we conduct the “lost-in-the-middle” study following
604: Liu et al. (2023) for Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k. As show in Figure 1, we confirm that the
605: phenomenon also exists in Llama2-70B with different context lengths. In particular, the comparison
606: of the curves from Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k suggests that the long context model has
607: better accuracy for incorporating top-5 retrieved context.
608: Note that, we have very different observation from the conclusion drawn from LongBench work (Bai
609: et al., 2023): “Retrieval brings improvement for model with weak ability on long contexts, but the
610: performance still lags behind models that have strong long context understanding capability”. Here,
611: we demonstrate retrieval can significantly improve the performance of both GPT-43B and Llama2-70B
612: regardless their context window size. For example, our best retrieval-augmented Llama2-70B-32k-ret
613: outperforms its baseline w/o retrieval by a margin, i.e., 39.60 vs. 37.36. We think the major reason for
614: such different conclusion is that Bai et al. (2023) uses much smaller LLM with 6B and 7B parameters,
615: which usually has relatively worse zero-shot capability to incorporate the retrieved chunked context.
616: To further validate the hypothesis, we also report the results using Llama2-7B in Table 5. One can
617: actually draw similar conclusions to Bai et al. (2023) . We think the underlying reasons are: i) For
618: Llama2-7B-chat-4k, its short context length is the bottleneck for long context tasks. Thus, retrieval-
619: augmentation largely improves the results. ii) For Llama2-7B-chat-32 and ChatGLM2-6B-32k, the
620: context length bottleneck has been mostly removed. However, their retrieval-augmented models have
621: limited zero-shot capability of incorporating retrieved chunks of context, due to the smaller size. As
622: a result, retrieval is not helpful for both Llama2-7B-32k and ChatGLM2-6B-32k, which is different
623: from large LLMs like Llama2-70B-32k in our case.

875: ABLATION ON DIFFERENT RETRIEVERS
876: To investigate the impacts of different retrievers on top of Llama2-70B, we compare Dragon, Con-
877: triever, and OpenAI embeddings on top of Llama2-70B-4k and Llama2-70B-32k. The results in
878: Table 4 confirms that our finding, i.e., retrieval can boost the performance of both short context and
879: long context LLMs, is consistent across different retrievers.
880: 4.4
881: INCREASING THE NUMBER OF RETRIEVED CHUNKS
882: To study the impact of adding more retrieved chunks to the context, we increase the number of
883: retrieved chunks from 5 to 20 using Dragon retriever and the results can be found in Table 5. We
884: observe that for different sequence lengths, the best averaged results are obtained either from top 5 or
885: top 10. Even if 20 chunks can still fit into the 16K and 32K context window (as shown in Figure 2),
886: adding more chunks up to 20 is not helpful and will sometime hurt the performance. We believe this
887: is related to the “lost in the middle” phenomenon (Liu et al., 2023) or the model is getting distracted
888: by irrelevant information and therefore needs further research.
889: 4.5
890: RETRIEVAL FOR FEW-SHOT TASKS
891: In addition to the zero-shot tasks of query-based summarization tasks and question answering tasks
892: mentioned above, we further investigate the benefits of long context models for few-shot tasks using
893: two additional datasets (Trec and SAMSum) from LongBench. We take the question from each
894: dataset as the query and use it to search relevant QA pairs provided in the given few-shot examples.
895: Table 6 shows that our best model Llama2-70B-32k-ret outperforms its non-retrieval Llama2-70B-32k
896: baseline as well as GPT-3.5-turbo-16k by a large margin. It again confirms the benefits on using
897: retrieval together with long context models.
898: 5
899: CONCLUSION
900: In this work, we systematically study the retrieval-augmentation versus long context extension
901: using the state-of-the-art LLMs after instruction tuning for various long context QA and query-
902: based summarization tasks. After study, we have the following interesting findings: i) Retrieval
903: largely boosts the performance of both 4K short context LLM and 16K/32K long context LLMs.
904: ii) The 4K context LLMs with simple retrieval-augmentation can perform comparable to 16K long
905: context LLMs, while being more efficient at inference. iii) After context window extension and
906: retrieval-augmentation, the best model Llama2-70B-32k-ret can outperform GPT-3.5-turbo-16k and
907: Davinci003 in terms of average score on a suit of downstream tasks with informative queries. Our
908: study shed light on the promising direction of combining retrieval and long context techniques
909: together to build better LLM.
910: 6
911: FUTURE DIRECTIONS
912: There are many potential research directions that can be extended from this work. One direction is
913: to develop advanced methods (e.g. memory or hierarchical attention) for existing pretrained large
914: language models e.g. Llama2-70B, which is itself non-trivial. Also, further extending the context
915: window to 64k and even longer would be a very interesting study for large 70B parameter models
916: even though pre-training longer sequence requires much more computation. Lastly, how to mitigate
917: the “lost-in-the-middle” phenomenon is an open research topic and continue pretraining with UL2
918: loss (Tay et al., 2022b) could be one potential solution.

588: Now we study how retrieval heads influence more realistic tasks beyond Needle-in-a-Haystack. We
589: use extractive QA as a test bed, as common usecase of long-context model where the user typically
590: upload a pdf (research papers, finantial reports, legal documents, .etc) and ask questions about
591: specific information within the document. To make sure the knowledge being asked does not exist
592: in the model’s internal knowledge, we synthesize an extractive QA dataset by selecting a set of
593: up-to-date news articles, extract a paragraph from it, and asking GPT-4 to produce a question-answer
594: pair based on the extracted paragraph, similar to the evaluation conducted in Anthropic [1]. As
595: illustrated in Figure 8, randomly masking out non-retrieval heads demonstrated no significant impact
596: on performance. Masking out retrieval heads led to a substantial decrease in F1 scores, with reductions
597: of 9.2% and 23.1%. These observations demonstrate that real-world document QA tasks heavily rely
598: on the functionality of retrieval heads.

## 1. Wikipedia RAG Overview

**Definition & Purpose**: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables LLMs to retrieve and incorporate external knowledge at inference time, reducing hallucinations, avoiding retraining costs, and providing source attribution.

**Process**: Embed documents → store in vector DB → retrieve relevant chunks for query → augment prompt → generate response.

**Key Improvements**:
- **Encoder**: Dense/sparse vectors, hybrid approaches, late interaction (ColBERT), ANN search
- **Retriever-centric**: ICT pre-training, supervised optimization (KL divergence), reranking
- **Language model redesign**: Retro (chunked cross-attention) achieves comparable perplexity with 25× smaller model
- **Chunking**: Strategy matters for retrieval granularity
- **Hybrid search**: Combine semantic + lexical search

**Challenges**: Hallucination not eliminated (LLM can misinterpret retrieved context), RAG poisoning (misleading sources), context misinterpretation, uncertainty calibration.

---

## 2. Paper 2310.03025's View on RAG (Empirical Comparison)

**Setup**: Two SOTA LLMs (proprietary 43B GPT, Llama2-70B), 9 long-context tasks (QA, summarization, few-shot), context windows 4K–32K via positional interpolation.

**RAG Implementation**: Simple retrieval-augmentation at generation (not training). 300-word chunks, top-N retrieval. Retrievers: Dragon, Contriever, OpenAI embeddings.

**Key Findings**:
- **4K + RAG ≈ 16K without RAG**: Llama2-70B-4K+RAG (36.02) vs Llama2-70B-16K (36.78); GPT-43B-4K+RAG (29.32) vs GPT-43B-16K (29.45) — with much less compute
- **RAG helps long-context models too**: Llama2-70B-32K-ret (43.6) outperforms Llama2-70B-32K (40.9) and GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (42.8)
- **Compute efficiency**: 4× faster generation on NarrativeQA with RAG+32K vs 32K alone
- **Model size matters**: Llama2-7B-32K does NOT benefit from RAG (limited zero-shot incorporation ability), but Llama2-70B-32K does
- **Lost-in-the-middle**: Long-context models better utilize retrieved chunks at beginning/end of context; retrieval + long context mitigates this
- **Top-5 chunks optimal**: More chunks (10, 20) sometimes hurt performance (distraction / lost-in-the-middle)

---

## 3. Paper 2404.15574's Mechanistic View (Retrieval Heads)

**Core Discovery**: A sparse set of attention heads ("retrieval heads", <5% of heads) implement conditional copy-paste from context to output.

**Properties**:
1. **Universal**: All 4 model families (Llama, Yi, Qwen, Mistral), 6 scales (6B–34B, MoE), base/chat/long-context variants have retrieval heads
2. **Sparse**: ~12–36 strongest heads per model (Llama-2-7B: 12 always-active heads)
3. **Intrinsic**: Exist in base models from pretraining; same heads used after length extension, chat fine-tuning, sparse upcycling (Pearson r > 0.8 within family)
4. **Dynamically activated**: Strongest heads always attend to required info; weaker heads activate context-dependently; they compensate for each other
5. **Causal**: Masking retrieval heads → hallucination/incomplete retrieval; masking random heads → no effect

**Downstream Impact**:
- **Needle-in-haystack**: Retrieval heads explain factuality; masking top 20 heads drops accuracy from 94.7% → 63.6%
- **Extractive QA**: Masking retrieval heads reduces F1 by 9–23%
- **Chain-of-Thought**: CoT reasoning heavily depends on retrieval heads (model must refer back to question/previous steps); answer-only prompting unaffected

**Implications**: KV cache compression must preserve retrieval heads; explains why some context compression fails factuality.

---

## 4. Synthesis: Connecting Empirical and Mechanistic Findings

| Empirical Finding (2310.03025) | Mechanistic Explanation (2404.15574) |
|---|---|
| **RAG helps 4K models match 16K** | Retrieval heads can attend to relevant chunks in shorter context; external retrieval pre-filters noise, reducing "lost in middle" burden |
| **RAG helps 32K models further** | Long context provides more capacity for retrieval heads to operate; retrieved chunks placed at context edges (where retrieval heads attend best) |
| **Model size matters (70B yes, 7B no)** | Larger models have stronger/more retrieval heads and better zero-shot ability to incorporate retrieved context via these heads |
| **Lost-in-the-middle mitigated by RAG** | Retrieved chunks are shorter and more focused; retrieval heads attend better to beginning/end of shorter retrieved context vs. full long context |
| **Top-5 chunks optimal; more hurts** | Retrieval heads have limited capacity; excess chunks dilute attention, activate "attention sink" (initial tokens) → hallucination |
| **CoT reasoning benefits from RAG** | CoT requires frequent reference to question/previous steps — exactly what retrieval heads do; RAG provides cleaner context for heads to attend to |

**Unified Picture**: Retrieval heads are the internal mechanism that "reads" context. RAG improves the *input* to these heads (cleaner, shorter, more relevant chunks), while long context expands the *workspace* where heads can operate. The two are complementary: RAG pre-filters, long context provides capacity. Larger models have stronger retrieval heads, explaining why they benefit from both. Hallucination occurs when retrieval heads fail to activate or attend to wrong tokens (attention sink) — RAG reduces this failure mode by providing higher-signal context."})

## Overview
This synthesis connects the mechanistic interpretability findings from Paper 2 (2404.15574) — the discovery of **retrieval heads** — to the empirical results from Paper 1 (2310.03025) on retrieval vs. long context for QA. The retrieval head mechanism provides a causal explanation for *why* the empirical patterns observed in Paper 1 occur.

---

## 1. Why Retrieval Helps 4K Models Reach 16K Performance

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** Llama2-70B-4K + retrieval achieves comparable average scores to Llama2-70B-16K without retrieval (36.02 vs 36.78 with Contriever; Table 2).

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- Retrieval heads implement a **conditional copy-paste algorithm**: they attend to relevant tokens in the input and copy them to the output (Fig. 2, Sec. 2).
- Only ~5% of heads are retrieval heads (Table 1), but they are **intrinsic** — present in the base model from pretraining (Sec. 3.3, Fig. 5-6).
- The 4K context window can hold the top-5 retrieved chunks (Paper 1 Table 1: avg ~2K tokens). Retrieval heads don't need the full document — they only need to attend to the *relevant* chunks placed in context.
- By retrieving only the most relevant chunks, retrieval effectively **pre-filters** the context for the retrieval heads, giving them a high signal-to-noise ratio within the 4K window.

---

## 2. Why Retrieval STILL Helps 16K/32K Models

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** Retrieval improves Llama2-70B-32K from 37.36 to 39.60 (avg +2.24; Table 2). The retrieval-augmented 32K model outperforms its non-retrieval baseline by a margin while being 4× faster on NarrativeQA.

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- **"Lost in the middle" is a retrieval head phenomenon**: Paper 1 Fig. 1 shows Llama2-70B has a U-shaped performance curve across context positions. Paper 2 explains this: retrieval heads are **dynamically activated** (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 4). The strongest retrieval heads (e.g., 12 for Llama-2-7B) are *always* activated regardless of context; weaker heads activate only for specific tokens/contexts.
- In long context, retrieved chunks are positioned at the **beginning** of the context window (Paper 1 Sec. 4.1). Retrieval heads are better at using information at the beginning/end of context — the "U-shape" reflects retrieval head activation patterns.
- Longer context gives retrieval heads **more room** to operate: retrieved chunks don't compete with as much irrelevant haystack. Paper 2 Fig. 4 shows strong retrieval heads always activated; longer context means fewer distractors between the query and retrieved evidence.

---

## 3. Why Model Size Matters (70B vs 7B)

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** Llama2-7B-32K does *not* benefit from retrieval (Table 5: 4k base 31.61 → +ret 35.73; 32k base 37.36 → +ret 39.60 for 70B, but 7B-32k +ret *hurts*: 28.20 → 27.63). Paper 1 explicitly attributes this to "limited zero-shot capability of incorporating retrieved chunks" for smaller models (Sec. 4.1, lines 617-623).

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- Retrieval heads are **intrinsic from pretraining** (Sec. 3.3): "the base model (e.g., LLaMA2 base) already contains retrieval heads as a consequence of large-scale pretraining."
- **Larger models → more/stronger retrieval heads**: Paper 2 tests across 6 model scales (6B to 34B + MoE). Table 1 shows retrieval head counts scale with model size. Llama-2-70B (not directly tested but same family) would have substantially more retrieval heads than 7B.
- Paper 2 Sec. 4.3: "smaller size... limited zero-shot capability of incorporating retrieved chunks" — this is *exactly* a retrieval head capacity issue. Smaller models have fewer/weaker retrieval heads, so they cannot effectively utilize the retrieved chunks even when placed in context.
- The **causal** nature of retrieval heads (Sec. 3.4, Fig. 7): masking them causes hallucination. If 7B has too few retrieval heads to begin with, adding retrieved chunks doesn't help — the mechanism to use them is insufficient.

---

## 4. Why Top-5 Chunks Optimal, More Hurts

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** Table 5 shows top-5 or top-10 chunks optimal; top-20 hurts performance even when they fit in 16K/32K context. "More context does not always give better results" (Sec. 4.4).

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- Retrieval heads have **limited capacity**: only ~5% of heads are retrieval heads (Table 1). Each retrieval head can only attend to a limited number of tokens effectively.
- **Dynamically activated heads compensate** (Sec. 3.2): "weaker heads only activate on certain tokens and contexts... these heads compensate each other's functionality." But this compensation has limits.
- **Too many chunks = "lost in middle" for retrieval heads**: Paper 2 Fig. 9 shows that when retrieval fails, heads either attend to wrong sections (wrong extraction) or the attention sink (hallucination). More chunks = more distractors between relevant tokens, causing weaker retrieval heads to attend to irrelevant chunks.
- The **sparse** nature of retrieval heads (less than 5%) means they create a bottleneck: they can only "copy-paste" from a limited number of source positions per forward pass.

---

## 5. Why HotpotQA (Multi-Hop) Favors Long Context

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** HotpotQA especially favors long context: score improves from 34.64 to 43.97 for Llama2-70B when context increases from 4K to 16K (Table 2). "Long context are beneficial to increase the recall of incorporating all intermediate hops" (Sec. 4.1).

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- **CoT reasoning depends on retrieval heads** (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 10-11): "chain-of-thought reasoning also heavily relies on retrieval heads because the model needs to refer back the input information."
- Multi-hop QA requires **chaining retrievals**: retrieve hop 1 → reason → retrieve hop 2 → reason. This is exactly what retrieval heads do: they "redirect the relevant tokens from the input to the output" (Abstract).
- In 4K context with retrieval: only top-5 chunks fit. If the multi-hop answer requires information spread across >5 chunks, retrieval heads cannot access all hops simultaneously.
- In 16K/32K context: **all hops can be in context simultaneously**, allowing retrieval heads to attend to each hop in sequence during CoT generation. Paper 2 Fig. 11 shows that when retrieval heads are masked during CoT, the model becomes "blind to important input information and hallucinate instead."

---

## 6. Compute/KV Cache Implications

**Empirical finding (Paper 1):** Retrieval-augmented 32K is 4× faster on NarrativeQA (Abstract, Sec. 4.5).

**Mechanistic explanation (Paper 2):**
- **Only ~5% of heads need full KV cache** (Sec. 5, Discussion): "only 5% heads need full KV cache → compression opportunity."
- Retrieval heads are the ones that **actually attend to distant tokens**. Non-retrieval heads attend locally or to special tokens (attention sinks).
- This suggests **selective KV caching**: keep full KV cache only for retrieval heads; compress/evict for other heads. This directly explains the 4× speedup: retrieval-augmented 32K only needs to process retrieved chunks (~2K tokens) through the retrieval heads, while the non-retrieval 32K processes the full 32K through all heads.

---

## Summary: Mechanism → Behavior Mapping

| Empirical Pattern (Paper 1) | Mechanistic Cause (Paper 2) |
|----------------------------|----------------------------|
| 4K + ret ≈ 16K no-ret | Retrieval heads copy from pre-filtered relevant chunks; don't need full doc |
| Ret helps 16K/32K too | Retrieved chunks positioned at context start (where retrieval heads work best); less distractor competition |
| 70B benefits, 7B doesn't | Retrieval heads intrinsic from pretraining; scale with model size; 7B has insufficient retrieval head capacity |
| Top-5 optimal, top-20 hurts | Retrieval heads sparse (~5%); limited copy-paste capacity; more chunks = more distractors for weak heads |
| HotpotQA favors long context | CoT requires chained retrievals; retrieval heads implement this; long context holds all hops |
| Ret-aug 32K 4× faster | Only retrieval heads (~5%) need full KV cache; retrieval reduces effective context for those heads |

---

## Conclusion
The retrieval head mechanism provides a **unified causal explanation** for all major empirical findings in Paper 1. Retrieval heads are the *functional substrate* that:
1. **Copy relevant information** from context to output (explaining why retrieval works at all)
2. **Are sparse and capacity-limited** (explaining top-5 optimum, 7B failure)
3. **Are position-sensitive** (explaining lost-in-the-middle, why retrieved-chunk position matters)
4. **Enable CoT reasoning** (explaining HotpotQA long-context advantage)
5. **Are the only heads needing full context** (explaining compute/KV cache savings)

This synthesis demonstrates that retrieval augmentation and long context extension are not competing approaches — they operate on the *same mechanism* (retrieval heads) at different stages: retrieval pre-filters for the heads; long context gives them room to operate."})

2: 
3: ## 1. Wikipedia RAG Overview
4: 
5: **Definition & Purpose**: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables LLMs to retrieve and incorporate external knowledge at inference time, reducing hallucinations, avoiding retraining costs, and providing source attribution.
6: 
7: **Process**: Embed documents → store in vector DB → retrieve relevant chunks for query → augment prompt → generate response.
8: 
9: **Key Improvements**:
10: - **Encoder**: Dense/sparse vectors, hybrid approaches, late interaction (ColBERT), ANN search
11: - **Retriever-centric**: ICT pre-training, supervised optimization (KL divergence), reranking
12: - **Language model redesign**: Retro (chunked cross-attention) achieves comparable perplexity with 25× smaller model
13: - **Chunking**: Strategy matters for retrieval granularity
14: - **Hybrid search**: Combine semantic + lexical search
15: 
16: **Challenges**: Hallucination not eliminated (LLM can misinterpret retrieved context), RAG poisoning (misleading sources), context misinterpretation, uncertainty calibration.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 2. Paper 2310.03025's View on RAG (Empirical Comparison)
21: 
22: **Setup**: Two SOTA LLMs (proprietary 43B GPT, Llama2-70B), 9 long-context tasks (QA, summarization, few-shot), context windows 4K–32K via positional interpolation.
23: 
24: **RAG Implementation**: Simple retrieval-augmentation at generation (not training). 300-word chunks, top-N retrieval. Retrievers: Dragon, Contriever, OpenAI embeddings.
25: 
26: **Key Findings**:
27: - **4K + RAG ≈ 16K without RAG**: Llama2-70B-4K+RAG (36.02) vs Llama2-70B-16K (36.78); GPT-43B-4K+RAG (29.32) vs GPT-43B-16K (29.45) — with much less compute
28: - **RAG helps long-context models too**: Llama2-70B-32K-ret (43.6) outperforms Llama2-70B-32K (40.9) and GPT-3.5-turbo-16K (42.8)
29: - **Compute efficiency**: 4× faster generation on NarrativeQA with RAG+32K vs 32K alone
30: - **Model size matters**: Llama2-7B-32K does NOT benefit from RAG (limited zero-shot incorporation ability), but Llama2-70B-32K does
31: - **Lost-in-the-middle**: Long-context models better utilize retrieved chunks at beginning/end of context; retrieval + long context mitigates this
32: - **Top-5 chunks optimal**: More chunks (10, 20) sometimes hurt performance (distraction / lost-in-the-middle)
33: 
34: ---
35: 
36: ## 3. Paper 2404.15574's Mechanistic View (Retrieval Heads)
37: 
38: **Core Discovery**: A sparse set of attention heads ("retrieval heads", <5% of heads) implement conditional copy-paste from context to output.
39: 
40: **Properties**:
41: 1. **Universal**: All 4 model families (Llama, Yi, Qwen, Mistral), 6 scales (6B–34B, MoE), base/chat/long-context variants have retrieval heads
42: 2. **Sparse**: ~12–36 strongest heads per model (Llama-2-7B: 12 always-active heads)
43: 3. **Intrinsic**: Exist in base models from pretraining; same heads used after length extension, chat fine-tuning, sparse upcycling (Pearson r > 0.8 within family)
44: 4. **Dynamically activated**: Strongest heads always attend to required info; weaker heads activate context-dependently; they compensate for each other
45: 5. **Causal**: Masking retrieval heads → hallucination/incomplete retrieval; masking random heads → no effect
46: 
47: **Downstream Impact**:
48: - **Needle-in-haystack**: Retrieval heads explain factuality; masking top 20 heads drops accuracy from 94.7% → 63.6%
49: - **Extractive QA**: Masking retrieval heads reduces F1 by 9–23%
50: - **Chain-of-Thought**: CoT reasoning heavily depends on retrieval heads (model must refer back to question/previous steps); answer-only prompting unaffected
51: 
52: **Implications**: KV cache compression must preserve retrieval heads; explains why some context compression fails factuality.
53: 
54: ---
55: 
56: ## 4. Synthesis: Connecting Empirical and Mechanistic Findings
57: 
58: | Empirical Finding (2310.03025) | Mechanistic Explanation (2404.15574) |
59: |---|---|
60: | **RAG helps 4K models match 16K** | Retrieval heads can attend to relevant chunks in shorter context; external retrieval pre-filters noise, reducing "lost in middle" burden |
61: | **RAG helps 32K models further** | Long context provides more capacity for retrieval heads to operate; retrieved chunks placed at context edges (where retrieval heads attend best) |
62: | **Model size matters (70B yes, 7B no)** | Larger models have stronger/more retrieval heads and better zero-shot ability to incorporate retrieved context via these heads |
63: | **Lost-in-the-middle mitigated by RAG** | Retrieved chunks are shorter and more focused; retrieval heads attend better to beginning/end of shorter retrieved context vs. full long context |
64: | **Top-5 chunks optimal; more hurts** | Retrieval heads have limited capacity; excess chunks dilute attention, activate "attention sink" (initial tokens) → hallucination |
65: | **CoT reasoning benefits from RAG** | CoT requires frequent reference to question/previous steps — exactly what retrieval heads do; RAG provides cleaner context for heads to attend to |
66: 
67: **Unified Picture**: Retrieval heads are the internal mechanism that "reads" context. RAG improves the *input* to these heads (cleaner, shorter, more relevant chunks), while long context expands the *workspace* where heads can operate. The two are complementary: RAG pre-filters, long context provides capacity. Larger models have stronger retrieval heads, explaining why they benefit from both. Hallucination occurs when retrieval heads fail to activate or attend to wrong tokens (attention sink) — RAG reduces this failure mode by providing higher-signal context.
