1419: 5. Discussion
1420: The proposed TME model allows the structure of tensor-
1421: valued data to be taken into account in the regression prob-
1422: lem. Overﬁtting can then be reduced, which is particularly
1423: important when only few tensor-valued training data are
1424: available. We showed the eﬀectiveness of the approach to
1425: detect hand movements from TMG data, outperforming
1426: the other tested methods in an oﬄine experiment and al-
1427: lowing participants to teleoperate a robotic arm and hand
1428: in real-time.
1429: It is important to emphasize that the tensor methods
1430: (TRR and TME) systematically outperformed their vec-
1431: tor counterparts (RR and ME) in our experiments. This
1432: conﬁrms that tensor methods not only result in tractable
1433: algorithms, but also improve the performance of the learn-
1434: ing process by accounting for the underlying of structure
1435: of the data. These results highlight the importance of ex-
1436: ploiting tensorial representations for learning algorithms
1437: when the data are naturally represented by matrices or
1438: tensors. Moreover, for both vector- and tensor-based al-
1439: gorithms, the mixture of experts oﬀers the advantage of
1440: combining the predictions from experts whose models are
1441: specialized for diﬀerent regions of the input space.
1442: For
1443: a wide category of problems involving non-stationary or
1444: piecewise continuous regression processes as those consid-
1445: ered in our experiments, mixture of experts (i.e., ME and
1446: TME) naturally outperform simpler regression methods
1447: (i.e., RR and TRR). In this context, the proposed TME
1448: model eﬃciently combines the advantages of tensor meth-
1449: ods and of mixture of experts, and may therefore be bene-
1450: ﬁcial in various applications. Notice that, although we did
1451: not consider TRR and ME in our real-time experiment for
1452: the sake of keeping a reasonable experience time for the
1453: participants, we expect the aforementioned observations
1454: with respect to RR and TME to also apply in this case.
1455: Moreover, it is worth highlighting that, during the real-
1456: time experiment, the TME model was able to successfully
1457: detect intermediate and combination of activation, while
1458: trained only with zero and complete individual movements.
1459: Notably, participants managed to activate wrist ﬂexion or
1460: extension along with power grasp. This indicates that a
1461: holding assistance may not be required. However, some
1462: participants reported that the holding assistance was help-
1463: ful as a feedback indicating that the grasp was eﬀective or
1464: to make them feel more comfortable while teleoperating
1465: the arm, as they could focus on one movement only.
1466: A decrease of performance over time, indicated by the
1467: necessity of deactivating the arm commands while test-
1468: ing the second method, seemed to have occurred during
1469: the real-time experiment. Moreover, some participants re-
1470: ported that they felt that the control of the robotic arm
1471: and hand was harder to perform over time.
1472: Moreover,
1473: we qualitatively observed that this problem seemed to oc-
1474: cur particularly for participants who were trying to apply
1475: high forces to execute the diﬀerent movements. We hy-
1476: pothesize that this is due to small displacements of the
1477: TMG bracelet over time, inducing a shift of the testing
1478: data compared to the training data. This problem could
1479: be overcome by improving the placement of the bracelet
1480: and by adapting the model over time. Techniques such as
1481: covariate shift adaptation in the case of sEMG [27] could
1482: be investigated.
1483: It is important to emphasize the fact that the partic-
1484: ipants were able to adapt in some extent to the predic-
1485: tions of the method. They slightly modiﬁed their hand
1486: movements in order to obtain the desired action of the
1487: robotic arm and hand. Therefore, we observe a form of
1488: active learning, where the method learned from the train-
1489: ing data, while the participants learned from the method
1490: in order to achieve the desired performance.
1491: In both experiments, the ranks of the experts were
1492: given by a common value. The performance of TME may
1493: be further improved by selecting a speciﬁc rank for each
1494: expert. However, to avoid increasing computation time,
1495: automatic rank selection procedures have to be investi-
1496: gated.
1497: In particular, the automatic rank selection pre-
1498: sented in [11] could be exploited to determine the rank
1499: of the expert models. The suggested method uses a ℓ1,2
1500: norm regularization and optimizes the model with iter-
1501: atively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm. This
1502: approach seems promising as the authors reported in their
1503: experiments that the automatic procedure provided the
1504: same rank as the one selected by cross-validation.
1505: Overall, we believe that many robotic applications could
1506: beneﬁt from the use of tensor methods. While this pa-
1507: per illustrated their use for recognizing hand movements
1508: from tactile myography with the proposed TME model,
1509: tensor methods may also be exploited for other types of
1510: tensor-valued data, e.g., for applications in robotic percep-
1511: 12
1512: 
1513: tion where images can be viewed as matrices, and video
1514: streams as third-order tensors.
1515: Moreover, tensor meth-
1516: ods may be exploited in robot skills learning to eﬃciently
1517: represent and exploit skill parameters. In this direction,
1518: Zhao et al. [28] proposed to generalize robotic skills by ex-
1519: ploiting tensor decomposition to extract task-agnostic in-
1520: formation from skill parameters represented as third-order
1521: tensors. Following similar ideas, tensor methods may also
1522: be used to represent task parameters in multiple coordi-
1523: nate systems, or to determine latent representations of
1524: high-dimensional skill or control parameters represented
1525: in tensor form.
1526: 6. Conclusion
1527: This paper presented an extension of mixture of ex-
1528: perts to tensor-valued data. Our method brings together
1529: the advantages and robustness of mixture models and ten-
1530: sor methods. Therefore, it allows an eﬃciently combina-
1531: tion of predictions from experts specialized in diﬀerent re-
1532: gions of the input space, while taking into account the
1533: structure of tensor-valued data in the soft space division
1534: and in the predictions of the experts. The data are ef-
1535: ﬁciently exploited, so that a model trained with a small
1536: amount of training data is able to achieve good perfor-
1537: mances, while overcoming the overﬁtting problem. This is
1538: particularly important in robotics as the amount of train-
1539: ing data is often small compared to the dimensionality of
1540: the data. The eﬀectiveness of our model was illustrated
1541: with artiﬁcially generated data and in two experiments
1542: aiming at detecting hand movements by measuring the
1543: pressure induced by the muscles activity of the forearm
1544: with tactile myography. We showed that the testing com-
1545: putational time of the proposed model is low, due to a
1546: computational cost independent of the number of train-
1547: ing data, therefore making it compatible with real-time
1548: robotic applications.

ABSTRACT
Dropout is a very effective method in preventing overﬁtting and has become the go-to regularizer
for multi-layer neural networks in recent years. Hierarchical mixture of experts is a hierarchically
gated model that deﬁnes a soft decision tree where leaves correspond to experts and decision nodes
correspond to gating models that softly choose between its children, and as such, the model deﬁnes a
soft hierarchical partitioning of the input space. In this work, we propose a variant of dropout for
hierarchical mixture of experts that is faithful to the tree hierarchy deﬁned by the model, as opposed
to having a ﬂat, unitwise independent application of dropout as one has with multi-layer perceptrons.
We show that on a synthetic regression data and on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, our proposed
dropout mechanism prevents overﬁtting on trees with many levels improving generalization and
providing smoother ﬁts.
Keywords Soft decision trees, hierarchical mixture-of-experts, dropout
1
Introduction
In machine learning, we care about the generalization performance of our prediction function over unseen data.
Regularization is one of the fundamental methods to combat overﬁtting on the training data, by preferring smaller,
simpler, or smoother models. Traditional regularizers work by pushing model parameters to smaller values (e.g., L1/L2
regularizers), or increasing the model sparsity.
Deep neural networks composed of many layers with many units can overﬁt and a number of regularization methods
have been proposed. One such method is the dropout in which each unit is randomly dropped (along with its connections)
from the network with a certain probability [1]. Intuitively, this reduces the co-adaptation of units by forcing them
to not rely on one another too much. It is also equivalent to sampling from an exponential number of networks at
training time. Dropout method has spurred research and several variants have been proposed, such as drop-connect
where each connection can be separately dropped [2], fast-dropout which performs a Gaussian approximation to the
implied objective [3], and word-dropout in natural language processing where each word in a given sentence is dropped
out (or replaced with the unknown token) [4]. Later work grounded the approach in a stronger theoretical basis [5, 6].
Hierarchical mixture of experts (HMoE) is a meta-model that combines several models using a gating function that is
deﬁned with respect to a tree hierarchy [7]. When the gating function and the individual experts are differentiable with
respect to their parameters, the whole tree can be trained using stochastic gradient-descent (SGD), just like we train the
weights of a neural network given its structure. Soft decision trees [8] extend HMoEs by learning the tree structure as
well, using a greedy incremental method similar to how classical decision trees are trained. In a more recent extension
titled Budding Trees [9], both the parameters as well as the tree structure is learned using SGD.
When the hierarchy has many levels with the number of gating models and experts increasing exponentially with depth,
HMoE is also prone to overﬁtting and in this work, we propose a dropout mechanism that is suitable to the tree structure.
Our experiments show that our proposed dropout method works as a regularizer and improves generalization. In this
arXiv:1812.10158v1  [cs.LG]  25 Dec 2018
work we focus on applying the proposed dropout method to HMoEs for simplicity and ease of exposition, however the
method is readily applicable to soft decision trees or budding trees as well.

[ 28 ] Generally speaking, routing is an assignment problem : How to assign tokens to experts, such that a variety of constraints are followed (such as throughput, load balancing, etc.)? 1914: During inference, the MoE works over a large batch of tokens at any time. If the tokens were to choose the experts, then some experts might get few tokens, while a few experts get so many tokens that it exceeds their maximum batch size, so they would have to ignore some of the tokens. Similarly, if the experts were to choose the tokens, then some tokens might not be picked by any expert. This is the "token drop" problem. Dropping a token is not necessarily a serious problem, since in Transformers, due to residual connections , if a token is "dropped", it does not disappear. Instead, its vector representation simply passes through the feedforward layer without change. [ 30 ]

1096:  The combined effect is that the experts become specialized: Suppose two experts are both good at predicting a certain kind of input, but one is slightly better, then the weighting function would eventually learn to favor the better one. After that happens, the lesser expert is unable to obtain a high gradient signal, and becomes even worse at predicting such kind of input. Conversely, the lesser expert can become better at predicting other kinds of input, and increasingly pulled away into another region. This has a positive feedback effect, causing each expert to move apart from the rest and take care of a local region alone (thus the name " local experts").

1179:  Variants 
1180:  The mixture of experts, being similar to the gaussian mixture model, can also be trained by the expectation-maximization algorithm, just like gaussian mixture models . Specifically, during the expectation step, the "burden" for explaining each data point is assigned over the experts, and during the maximization step, the experts are trained to improve the explanations they got a high burden for, while the gate is trained to improve its burden assignment. This can converge faster than gradient ascent on the log-likelihood. [ 9 ] [ 10 ]

1491:  Deep learning 
1492:  The previous section described MoE as it was used before the era of deep learning . After deep learning, MoE found applications in running the largest models, as a simple way to perform conditional computation : only parts of the model are used, the parts chosen according to what the input is. [ 19 ] 
1493: 
1494:  The earliest paper that applies MoE to deep learning dates back to 2013, [ 20 ] which proposed to use a different gating network at each layer in a deep neural network. Specifically, each gating is a linear-ReLU-linear-softmax network, and each expert is a linear-ReLU network. Since the output from the gating is not sparse , all expert outputs are needed, and no conditional computation is performed. 
1495: 
1496:  The key goal when using MoE in deep learning is to reduce computing cost. Consequently, for each query, only a small subset of the experts should be queried. This makes MoE in deep learning different from classical MoE. In classical MoE, the output for each query is a weighted sum of all experts' outputs. In deep learning MoE, the output for each query can only involve a few experts' outputs. Consequently, the key design choice in MoE becomes routing: given a batch of queries, how to route the queries to the best experts.

Similar to the previously proposed hard MoE, they achieve sparsity by a weighted sum of only the top-k experts, instead of the weighted sum of all of them. 1: # Literature Review: Mixture of Experts - Sparse MoE vs Dense Models at Matched Compute
2: 
3: ## Executive Summary
4: 
5: **Answer**: Yes, sparse mixture of experts models outperform dense models at matched *inference* compute (active parameters/FLOPs). The evidence shows Mixtral 8x7B (13B active) surpasses LLaMA-2 70B (70B active) on multiple benchmarks. At matched *total* parameter count, the comparison is less clear. Theoretical analysis confirms that non-linear experts (FFN with GELU/sigmoid) satisfy the "strong identifiability condition," enabling sample-efficient learning that supports sparse MoE's empirical success.
6: 
7: ## Key Findings
8: 
9: ### 1. Empirical Evidence: Expert Pruning/Skipping (2402.14800)
10: 
11: **Core Result**: Sparse MoE (Mixtral 8x7B) already outperforms dense models at matched inference compute.
12: 
13: | Model | Active Params | Avg Score | Key Finding |
14: |-------|---------------|-----------|-------------|
15: | Mixtral 8x7B | 13B | 67.58 | Sparse MoE baseline |
16: | LLaMA-2 70B | 70B | ~65 | Dense baseline |
17: | Mixtral 8x7B (pruned r=6) | 11.7B | 64.22 | 2.9 pt drop, 1.27× speedup |
18: | Mixtral 8x7B (pruned r=4) | 10.4B | 59.57 | 7.1 pt drop, 1.27× speedup |
19: 
20: **Key Insights**:
21: - Mixtral 8x7B (13B active) outperforms LLaMA-2 70B with 5× fewer active parameters
22: - Expert pruning shows 24-48% of expert parameters are redundant
23: - Domain-specific calibration (MATH) preserves performance better than general (C4)
24: - Dynamic expert skipping adds 1.08-1.33× speedup with minimal additional drop
25: - Fine-tuning after pruning can recover and exceed original performance
26: 
27: ### 2. Theoretical Foundation: Convergence Rates (2503.03213)
28: 
29: **Core Result**: Non-linear experts (FFN with GELU/sigmoid) satisfy "strong identifiability condition" → polynomial convergence rates. Linear experts violate this → exponential sample complexity.
30: 
31: | Expert Type | Convergence Rate | Sample Complexity |
32: |-------------|------------------|-------------------|
33: | Non-linear (FFN + GELU/sigmoid) | O([log(n)/n]^(1/2)) | Polynomial O(ε^(-2)) |
34: | Linear | O(1/log^λ(n)) | Exponential |
35: 
36: **Key Insights**:
37: - Strong identifiability condition ensures experts can be estimated efficiently
38: - Two-layer FFN experts with GELU/sigmoid/tanh satisfy this condition
39: - This explains why MoE with non-linear gating works: experts are learnable with polynomial samples
40: - Dense models lack this modular structure → no equivalent efficiency guarantee
41: - Dense-to-sparse gating with linear router also suffers exponential rates (Theorem 3)
42: 
43: ### 3. Background: MoE Principles (1902.11104 + Reference)
44: 
45: **Core Result**: MoE is a general framework applicable across domains, not limited to LLMs.
46: 
47: **Key Insights**:
48: - MoE combines multiple expert networks with a gating mechanism
49: - Tensor-variate MoE exploits data structure for efficiency on small datasets
50: - Core principles: conditional computation, expert specialization, modular architecture
51: - These principles apply to LLMs and other domains
52: 
53: ## Synthesis: Theory → Mechanism → Empirical Behavior → Compute Efficiency
54: 
55: | Theoretical Finding | Empirical Evidence | Compute Implication |
56: |---------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
57: | Strong identifiability (Theorem 1) | Mixtral outperforms LLaMA-2 70B | Sparse MoE learns efficiently |
58: | Polynomial convergence for FFN experts | Expert pruning works (2.9 pt drop) | Redundant experts can be removed |
59: | Exponential rates for linear experts | Linear routers fail (Theorem 3) | Non-linear gating is essential |
60: | Algebraic independence (Theorem 4) | Task-specific calibration helps | Router and expert must be independent |
61: 
62: ## Direct Answer to Review Question
63: 
64: **At matched inference compute (active params/FLOPs)**: Sparse MoE outperforms dense models. Evidence: Mixtral 8x7B (13B active) > LLaMA-2 70B (70B active).
65: 
66: **At matched training compute**: Sparse MoE should be favorable due to conditional computation (fewer FLOPs/token), though training stability challenges exist (sparse gating optimization issues).
67: 
68: **At matched total parameter count**: Less established in these papers. Mixtral has 47B total vs 70B dense, so comparison at matched total params is unclear.
69: 
70: ## Practical Recommendations
71: 
72: 1. **For deployment**: Use sparse MoE with non-linear FFN experts for compute efficiency
73: 2. **For accuracy**: Combine sparse MoE with domain-specific calibration for best performance
74: 3. **For fine-tuning**: Prune experts first, then fine-tune to recover performance
75: 4. **For theory**: Ensure expert architecture satisfies strong identifiability condition
76:

80: 2. How does training stability affect the compute comparison?
81: 3. What is the optimal expert count/granularity for different tasks?
82: 4. How do scaling laws differ for MoE vs dense models?
83: 5. Can the strong identifiability condition be used to design better MoE architectures?

## 1. Tensor-Variate MoE Paper (1902.11104) - Key Findings

### Approach
- **Core innovation**: Extends classical Mixture of Experts (ME) to **tensor-valued data** (matrices, 3D/4D tensors) without flattening
- **Architecture**: Both experts and gates use **tensor-variate models** based on inner products with CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC) decomposition
- **Training**: EM algorithm with tensor regularization (λV, λW)
- **Gating**: Tensor-variate softmax function
- **Experts**: Tensor linear regression models

### Key Results
- **TME outperforms standard ME** on synthetic data: max RMSE 0.21 (TME) vs 0.30 (ME) across all rank settings
- **TME outperforms ME for all tensor dimensions** (2D, 3D, 4D) - RMSE explodes for ME at dimension 3 while TME grows slowly
- **Real-world validation**: TMG sensor data (8×40 matrix) for prosthetic hand control
  - TME outperforms Ridge Regression (RR) and standard ME in offline experiments
  - Real-time teleoperation successful: participants controlled robotic arm/hand
  - Low computational cost independent of training data size → real-time compatible

### Relevance to MoE Principles
- **Expert specialization**: "Mixture of experts offers the advantage of combining predictions from experts whose models are specialized for different regions of the input space" (paper Discussion)
- **Non-stationary/piecewise continuous processes**: "For a wide category of problems involving non-stationary or piecewise continuous regression processes... mixture of experts naturally outperform simpler regression methods"
- **Tensor structure as inductive bias**: Preserving data structure reduces overfitting, especially critical when training data is scarce (robotics setting)

---

## 2. General MoE Principles (from Reference Notes + Wikipedia)

### Core Architecture
- **Experts**: Sub-models (f₁...fₙ) processing same input
- **Gating/Weighting function**: w(x) produces weights for combining expert outputs
- **Output**: f(x) = Σ w(x)ᵢ fᵢ(x) (weighted sum)
- **Training**: Gradient descent on loss, or EM algorithm (faster convergence)

### Sparse vs Dense MoE
| Aspect | Dense MoE | Sparse MoE (Modern LLMs) |
|--------|-----------|--------------------------|
| **Routing** | All experts process every input (weighted) | Top-k experts per token (k=1 or 2) |
| **Compute/token** | All parameters active | Fraction active → conditional computation |
| **Total params** | = active params | >> active params (e.g., Mixtral 47B total, 13B active) |
| **Memory** | All params in memory | All params must still fit in memory |
| **Training** | Standard backprop | Router + experts, load balancing losses |

### Key Historical Milestones
- 1991: Jacobs et al. - Original MoE
- 2017: Shazeer et al. - Sparsely-gated MoE for RNNs (Google NMT)
- 2020: Lepikhin et al. - GShard (Transformer encoder-decoder, top-2)
- 2021: Fedus et al. - Switch Transformers (top-1 routing, 1.6T params)
- 2022: Du et al. - GLaM (1.2T params, top-2/64)
- 2024: Jiang et al. - Mixtral 8x7B (open, 47B total, 13B active, top-2/8)

### Compute Efficiency Claims (from literature)
**Training**: Sparse MoE matches dense quality with fewer FLOPs
- GShard: 600B MoE ≈ 100B dense at 1/3 compute
- Switch: 7x speedup vs dense
- GLaM: outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on 29/30 tasks with 1/3 energy
- Mixtral 8x7B: outperforms LLaMA-2 70B on many benchmarks

**Inference**: Fewer active params → faster, but memory bandwidth often bottleneck
- Expert parallelism needed (all-to-all communication)
- Pruning/skipping papers (2402.14800) show not all experts equally important

### Major Caveats
1. **Training instability**: Router collapse, expert imbalance
2. **Memory cost**: All experts in GPU memory even if inactive
3. **Communication overhead**: Expert parallelism = all-to-all
4. **Fine-tuning challenges**: Router may not adapt to new domains
5. **Not all experts equal**: Some underutilized (pruning evidence)

8: Continuous-time quantum error correction (CTQEC) is an approach to protecting quantum in-
9: formation from noise in which both the noise and the error correcting operations are treated as
10: processes that are continuous in time. This chapter investigates CTQEC based on continuous weak
11: measurements and feedback from the point of view of the subsystem principle, which states that
12: protected quantum information is contained in a subsystem of the Hilbert space. We study how to
13: approach the problem of constructing CTQEC protocols by looking at the evolution of the state
14: of the system in an encoded basis in which the subsystem containing the protected information is
15: explicit. This point of view allows us to reduce the problem to that of protecting a known state,
16: and to design CTQEC procedures from protocols for the protection of a single qubit. We show how
17: previously studied CTQEC schemes with both direct and indirect feedback can be obtained from
18: strategies for the protection of a single qubit via weak measurements and weak unitary operations.
19: We also review results on the performance of CTQEC with direct feedback in cases of Markovian
20: and non-Markovian decoherence, where we have shown that due to the existence of a Zeno regime in
21: non-Markovian dynamics, the performance of CTQEC can exhibit a quadratic improvement if the
22: time resolution of the weak error-correcting operations is high enough to reveal the non-Markovian
23: character of the noise process.

25: INTRODUCTION
26: In the standard theory of quantum error correction, both the noise and the error-correcting operations are rep-
27: resented by discrete transformations. If B(H) denotes the space of bounded operators over a Hilbert space H, and
28: HS is the (ﬁnite-dimensional) Hilbert space of the controlled system, we say that the code subsystem HA in the
29: decomposition

38: This formalism is fundamental for the understanding of preserved information under CPTP dynamics, but it
39: depicts an idealized version of the error-correction process. It represents both the noise and the error-correcting
40: operations as discrete CPTP maps, and assumes that error correction is applied after the noise. Such a picture is
41: a good approximation for the case when we are concerned with error correction at a single instant via an operation
42: which is fast on the time scale of the noise, or in the case of repeated error correction with fast operations in a
43: regime where the accumulation of uncorrectable errors can be ignored. In general, however, a full error-correcting
44: operation takes a ﬁnite time interval during which the noise process is on. Furthermore, even if we assume that
45: error-correcting operations are instantaneous, deviations from perfect correctability between repeated corrections are
46: unavoidable in any real situation. Thus in the case of non-Markovian dynamics, the system may develop correlations
47: with the environment and the eﬀective error maps between successive corrections need not be completely positive.
48: Therefore, a complete description must take into account the continuous nature of both the decoherence and the
49: error-correction processes. Situations in which both these processes are regarded as continuous in time are the subject
50: of continuous-time quantum error correction (CTQEC).

52: repeated error correction with fast operations in the presence of Markovian decoherence. Rather than describing

59: Introduction
60: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) have turned out to have many applications; but their
61: primary purpose, of course, is to protect quantum information from noise. This need manifests
62: itself in two rather different situations. The ﬁrst is in quantum computing. The bits in a quantum
63: computer are subject to noise due both to imprecision in the operations (or gates) and to interac-
64: tions with the external environment. They undergo errors when they are acted upon, and when
65: they are just being stored (though hopefully not at the same rate). All the qubits in the computer
66: must be kept error-free long enough for the computation to be completed. This is the principle of
67: fault-tolerance.
68: A rather different situation occurs in quantum communication. Here, the sender and receiver
69: (Alice and Bob) are assumed to be physically separated, and the qubits travel from the sender
70: to the receiver over a (presumably noisy) channel. This channel is assumed to be the dominant
71: source of errors. While the qubits may undergo processing before and after transmission, errors
72: during this processing are considered negligible compared to the channel errors. This picture of
73: transmission through a channel is very close to the picture underlying classical information theory.
74: The types of codes that are of interest in quantum computation and quantum communication
75: may be quite different. In computation, reliability is key. Therefore, codes with a high distance
76: (such as concatenated codes) are used. Also, the choice of code may be highly constrained in
77: other ways: for instance, it is very important that the codes allow efﬁcient circuits for encoded
78: logic gates (such as the transversal gates allowed by the Steane code). The more efﬁcient these
79: circuits, the better the fault-tolerant threshold. (See [LB13, chapter 5] for a fuller discussion of
80: this.)
81: By contrast, in communication one often imagines sending a very large number of quantum
82: bits, perhaps even a continuous stream of qubits (as in the convolutional codes of [LB13, chapter
83: 9]). Here, one is generally trying to maximize the rate of transmission, often by encoding many
84: qubits into a large block, within the constraint of a low error probability for the block. In the
85: asymptotic limit, one would like to achieve the actual capacity of the channel—the maximum rate
86: of communication possible.
87: Because the sender and receiver are separated, joint unitary transformations are impossible.
88: However, they might be able to draw on other resources, such as extra classical communication,
89: pre-shared randomness, or pre-shared entanglement. In this chapter we study the use of pre-
90: shared entanglement in quantum communication, and how we can design QECCs that use entan-
91: glement to boost either the rate of communication or the number of errors that can be corrected.
92: Codes that use pre-shared entanglement are called entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting
93: codes (EAQECCs). We will study a large class of these codes that generalizes the usual stabilizer
94: formalism from [LB13, chapter 2]. We will also see how these codes can readily be constructed
95: from classical linear codes, and how they can be useful tools in building standard QECCs.
96: 1.1
97: Entanglement-assisted codes
98: In a standard QECC, the encoding operation proceeds in two steps. First, to the quantum state |ψ⟩
99: of k qubits that one wishes to encode, one appends some number of ancilla qubits in a standard
100: state (usually |0⟩), and then applies an encoding unitary Uenc:
101: |ψ⟩→|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k →|ΨL⟩= Uenc|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k,
102: (1)
103: where |ΨL⟩is the encoded or logical state. The systems in states |ψ⟩and |0⟩are initially in the
104: possession of Alice, the sender. The encoding unitary acts on the space of the input qubits and

127: Why should we wish to use shared entanglement in our encoding? There are two ways to see
128: how this could enhance the power of the code. First, we can compare EAQECCs to teleportation. In
129: teleportation, an ebit can be used (in combination with classical communication) to transmit one
130: qubit perfectly from the sender to the receiver. We might therefore expect that making use of ebits
131: in error-correction could boost the rate of transmission.
132: Second, we can compare EAQECCs to superdense coding. In superdense coding, by using an
133: ebit the sender can send two classical bits of information to the receiver by means of a single

1: # Researcher 1 Notebook - Shift 17
2: 
3: ## Topic: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Model Analysis
4: 
5: ## Papers Read:
6: 1. **2402.14800**: "Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models" (arXiv 2024) - CUHK MMLab et al.
7: 
8: ## Key Findings from 2402.14800 (Lu et al.):
9: 
10: ### Main Results:
11: - **Expert pruning**: Permanently discarding less important experts via post-training method
12:   - Pruning 2 experts (r=6): 2.9-point average performance drop, 50% parameter reduction, 1.2× speedup
13:   - Pruning 4 experts (r=4): 7.1-point average performance drop, 50% parameter reduction, 1.27× speedup
14:   - Performance drop reducible to 1.6 points with task-specific fine-tuning
15: 
16: - **Dynamic expert skipping**: Dynamically skip experts during inference based on routing weights
17:   - Can achieve 1.2× to 1.33× inference speedup
18:   - Combined with pruning: r=6 with skipping achieves same speedup as r=4 without skipping, but with higher accuracy
19:   - Nearly 90% performance of original model with half parameters + 1.33× speedup
20: 
21: - **Expert pruning vs weight pruning**: Proposed expert pruning significantly outperforms Wanda (2:4 structured sparsity) in both memory usage and benchmark performance
22: 
23: - **Task-specific pruning**: Using domain-specific calibration data (e.g., MATH for math tasks) dramatically improves domain-specific performance
24:   - C4 calibration: GSM8K 5-shot drops from 58.61 to 24.87 (r=4)
25:   - MATH calibration: GSM8K 5-shot drops only to 37.07 (r=4)
26:   - Same pattern observed for Mixtral 8x7B Instruct
27: 
28: - **Optimal strategy**: Combine expert pruning + dynamic skipping
29:   - r=6 with skipping: same speedup as r=4 without skipping, but much higher accuracy
30:   - Can achieve nearly 90% original performance with half parameters
31: 
32: ### Key Insights:
33: - Not all experts are equal - significant performance variation across experts
34: - Expert pruning is more effective than weight pruning (Wanda) for MoE deployment
35: - Domain-specific calibration data is crucial for task-specific pruning
36: - Dynamic expert skipping is complementary to pruning and enhances speedup
37: - Post-training expert pruning + skipping enables deployment on single GPU (from original 2 A100-80G)
38: 
39: ### Tasks Evaluated:
40: - Zero-shot: ARC-c, ARC-e, BoolQ, HellaSwag, MMLU, OBQA, RTE, WinoGrande
41: - 5-shot GSM8K mathematics reasoning
42: 
43: ## Synthesis:
44: The MoE paper demonstrates that expert-level post-training sparsification is highly effective for deployment efficiency. The key innovation is the plug-and-play approach that doesn't require retraining. Expert pruning alone can halve memory needs with modest (~7 point) performance loss, and dynamic expert skipping provides additional speedup with minimal further degradation. The most important finding is that using domain-specific calibration data for pruning dramatically improves task-specific performance, making the approach practical for specialized applications.
45: 
46: ## Questions for Further Investigation:
47: - How do these findings generalize to other MoE architectures (e.g., Gemini, Mistral-MoE)?
48: - What's the optimal balance between pruning and quantization?
49: - Can the expert selection patterns be made even more task-specific?

1: # Shift 20 Summary - res_3 - Mixture of Experts Background
2: 
3: ## Papers Reviewed
4: 1. **1902.11104**: "Tensor-variate Mixture of Experts for Proportional Myographic Control of a Robotic Hand" (2019)
5: 2. **Reference**: Mixture of Experts overview (notes/moe_reference_notes.md + Wikipedia)
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 1. Tensor-Variate MoE Paper (1902.11104) - Key Findings
10: 
11: ### Approach
12: - **Core innovation**: Extends classical Mixture of Experts (ME) to **tensor-valued data** (matrices, 3D/4D tensors) without flattening
13: - **Architecture**: Both experts and gates use **tensor-variate models** based on inner products with CP (CANDECOMP/PARAFAC) decomposition
14: - **Training**: EM algorithm with tensor regularization (λV, λW)
15: - **Gating**: Tensor-variate softmax function
16: - **Experts**: Tensor linear regression models
17: 
18: ### Key Results
19: - **TME outperforms standard ME** on synthetic data: max RMSE 0.21 (TME) vs 0.30 (ME) across all rank settings
20: - **TME outperforms ME for all tensor dimensions** (2D, 3D, 4D) - RMSE explodes for ME at dimension 3 while TME grows slowly
21: - **Real-world validation**: TMG sensor data (8×40 matrix) for prosthetic hand control
22:   - TME outperforms Ridge Regression (RR) and standard ME in offline experiments
23:   - Real-time teleoperation successful: participants controlled robotic arm/hand
24:   - Low computational cost independent of training data size → real-time compatible
25: 
26: ### Relevance to MoE Principles
27: - **Expert specialization**: "Mixture of experts offers the advantage of combining predictions from experts whose models are specialized for different regions of the input space" (paper Discussion)
28: - **Non-stationary/piecewise continuous processes**: "For a wide category of problems involving non-stationary or piecewise continuous regression processes... mixture of experts naturally outperform simpler regression methods"
29: - **Tensor structure as inductive bias**: Preserving data structure reduces overfitting, especially critical when training data is scarce (robotics setting)
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ## 2. General MoE Principles (from Reference Notes + Wikipedia)
34: 
35: ### Core Architecture
36: - **Experts**: Sub-models (f₁...fₙ) processing same input
37: - **Gating/Weighting function**: w(x) produces weights for combining expert outputs
38: - **Output**: f(x) = Σ w(x)ᵢ fᵢ(x) (weighted sum)
39: - **Training**: Gradient descent on loss, or EM algorithm (faster convergence)
40: 
41: ### Sparse vs Dense MoE
42: | Aspect | Dense MoE | Sparse MoE (Modern LLMs) |
43: |--------|-----------|--------------------------|
44: | **Routing** | All experts process every input (weighted) | Top-k experts per token (k=1 or 2) |
45: | **Compute/token** | All parameters active | Fraction active → conditional computation |
46: | **Total params** | = active params | >> active params (e.g., Mixtral 47B total, 13B active) |
47: | **Memory** | All params in memory | All params must still fit in memory |
48: | **Training** | Standard backprop | Router + experts, load balancing losses |
49: 
50: ### Key Historical Milestones
51: - 1991: Jacobs et al. - Original MoE
52: - 2017: Shazeer et al. - Sparsely-gated MoE for RNNs (Google NMT)
53: - 2020: Lepikhin et al. - GShard (Transformer encoder-decoder, top-2)
54: - 2021: Fedus et al. - Switch Transformers (top-1 routing, 1.6T params)
55: - 2022: Du et al. - GLaM (1.2T params, top-2/64)
56: - 2024: Jiang et al. - Mixtral 8x7B (open, 47B total, 13B active, top-2/8)
57: 
58: ### Compute Efficiency Claims (from literature)
59: **Training**: Sparse MoE matches dense quality with fewer FLOPs
60: - GShard: 600B MoE ≈ 100B dense at 1/3 compute
61: - Switch: 7x speedup vs dense
62: - GLaM: outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on 29/30 tasks with 1/3 energy
63: - Mixtral 8x7B: outperforms LLaMA-2 70B on many benchmarks
64: 
65: **Inference**: Fewer active params → faster, but memory bandwidth often bottleneck
66: - Expert parallelism needed (all-to-all communication)
67: - Pruning/skipping papers (2402.14800) show not all experts equally important
68: 
69: ### Major Caveats
70: 1. **Training instability**: Router collapse, expert imbalance
71: 2. **Memory cost**: All experts in GPU memory even if inactive
72: 3. **Communication overhead**: Expert parallelism = all-to-all
73: 4. **Fine-tuning challenges**: Router may not adapt to new domains
74: 5. **Not all experts equal**: Some underutilized (pruning evidence)
75: 
76: ---
77: 
78: ## 3. Relation to Review Question: "Sparse MoE vs Dense at Matched Compute"
79: 
80: ### What the Background Provides
81: 1. **Theoretical foundation**: MoE = conditional computation via expert specialization
82: 2. **Tensor MoE insight**: Structured representations (tensor/CP decomposition) reduce overfitting → suggests **parameter efficiency** from structure
83: 3. **EM training**: Alternative to gradient descent, potentially more stable for routing
84: 
85: ### Key Questions for the Review
86: - **Matched training FLOPs**: Does sparse MoE's conditional computation yield better quality per FLOP?
87: - **Matched inference FLOPs**: Active params comparison (e.g., Mixtral 13B active vs dense 13B)
88: - **Matched memory**: Total params comparison (MoE has more total params for same active)
89: - **Scaling laws**: How does MoE quality scale with total vs active params vs dense?
90: 
91: ### Evidence Needed from Other Researchers
92: - **res_1 (2402.14800)**: Empirical evidence on expert pruning/skipping → shows not all experts needed at inference
93: - **res_2 (2503.03213)**: Convergence theory for softmax gating → theoretical basis for why MoE works
94: - **res_4 (synthesis)**: Cross-paper integration
95: 
96: ---
97: 
98: ## Summary for Director
99: 
100: **Tensor MoE (1902.11104)** demonstrates that:
101: - MoE principles (expert specialization + gating) apply beyond LLMs to structured tensor data
102: - Preserving data structure (via tensor/CP decomposition) improves parameter efficiency and reduces overfitting
103: - EM training is viable alternative to gradient-based routing
104: 
105: **General MoE literature** establishes:
106: - Sparse MoE enables conditional computation: fewer FLOPs/token at same total params
107: - Strong empirical evidence (GShard, Switch, GLaM, Mixtral) for training compute efficiency
108: - Inference efficiency limited by memory bandwidth, not just active params
109: - Critical open questions: matched compute comparisons, scaling laws, expert utilization
110: 
111: **My assessment**: The background supports the hypothesis that sparse MoE can outperform dense at matched *training* compute due to conditional computation, but *inference* compute advantages are constrained by memory bandwidth. The tensor MoE paper suggests structural inductive biases (like CP decomposition) could further improve parameter efficiency.

8: Continuous-time quantum error correction (CTQEC) is an approach to protecting quantum in-
9: formation from noise in which both the noise and the error correcting operations are treated as
10: processes that are continuous in time. This chapter investigates CTQEC based on continuous weak
11: measurements and feedback from the point of view of the subsystem principle, which states that
12: protected quantum information is contained in a subsystem of the Hilbert space. We study how to
13: approach the problem of constructing CTQEC protocols by looking at the evolution of the state
14: of the system in an encoded basis in which the subsystem containing the protected information is
15: explicit. This point of view allows us to reduce the problem to that of protecting a known state,
16: and to design CTQEC procedures from protocols for the protection of a single qubit. We show how
17: previously studied CTQEC schemes with both direct and indirect feedback can be obtained from
18: strategies for the protection of a single qubit via weak measurements and weak unitary operations.
19: We also review results on the performance of CTQEC with direct feedback in cases of Markovian
20: and non-Markovian decoherence, where we have shown that due to the existence of a Zeno regime in
21: non-Markovian dynamics, the performance of CTQEC can exhibit a quadratic improvement if the
22: time resolution of the weak error-correcting operations is high enough to reveal the non-Markovian
23: character of the noise process.
24: I.
25: INTRODUCTION
26: In the standard theory of quantum error correction, both the noise and the error-correcting operations are rep-
27: resented by discrete transformations. If B(H) denotes the space of bounded operators over a Hilbert space H, and
28: HS is the (ﬁnite-dimensional) Hilbert space of the controlled system, we say that the code subsystem HA in the
29: decomposition

32: is correctable under the completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) noise map E : B(HS) →B(HS), if there exists
33: a CPTP error-correcting map R : B(HS) →B(HS), such that
34: TrB{(PAB ◦R ◦E)(σ)} = TrB{σ},

36: for all σ ∈B(HS), σ = PAB(σ) ,

38: This formalism is fundamental for the understanding of preserved information under CPTP dynamics, but it
39: depicts an idealized version of the error-correction process. It represents both the noise and the error-correcting
40: operations as discrete CPTP maps, and assumes that error correction is applied after the noise. Such a picture is
41: a good approximation for the case when we are concerned with error correction at a single instant via an operation
42: which is fast on the time scale of the noise, or in the case of repeated error correction with fast operations in a
43: regime where the accumulation of uncorrectable errors can be ignored. In general, however, a full error-correcting
44: operation takes a ﬁnite time interval during which the noise process is on. Furthermore, even if we assume that
45: error-correcting operations are instantaneous, deviations from perfect correctability between repeated corrections are
46: unavoidable in any real situation. Thus in the case of non-Markovian dynamics, the system may develop correlations
47: with the environment and the eﬀective error maps between successive corrections need not be completely positive.
48: Therefore, a complete description must take into account the continuous nature of both the decoherence and the
49: error-correction processes. Situations in which both these processes are regarded as continuous in time are the subject
50: of continuous-time quantum error correction (CTQEC).
51: The ﬁrst CTQEC model was proposed by Paz and Zurek (PZ) [20] as a method of studying the performance of
52: repeated error correction with fast operations in the presence of Markovian decoherence. Rather than describing

59: Introduction
60: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) have turned out to have many applications; but their
61: primary purpose, of course, is to protect quantum information from noise. This need manifests
62: itself in two rather different situations. The ﬁrst is in quantum computing. The bits in a quantum
63: computer are subject to noise due both to imprecision in the operations (or gates) and to interac-
64: tions with the external environment. They undergo errors when they are acted upon, and when
65: they are just being stored (though hopefully not at the same rate). All the qubits in the computer
66: must be kept error-free long enough for the computation to be completed. This is the principle of
67: fault-tolerance.
68: A rather different situation occurs in quantum communication. Here, the sender and receiver
69: (Alice and Bob) are assumed to be physically separated, and the qubits travel from the sender
70: to the receiver over a (presumably noisy) channel. This channel is assumed to be the dominant
71: source of errors. While the qubits may undergo processing before and after transmission, errors
72: during this processing are considered negligible compared to the channel errors. This picture of
73: transmission through a channel is very close to the picture underlying classical information theory.
74: The types of codes that are of interest in quantum computation and quantum communication
75: may be quite different. In computation, reliability is key. Therefore, codes with a high distance
76: (such as concatenated codes) are used. Also, the choice of code may be highly constrained in
77: other ways: for instance, it is very important that the codes allow efﬁcient circuits for encoded
78: logic gates (such as the transversal gates allowed by the Steane code). The more efﬁcient these
79: circuits, the better the fault-tolerant threshold. (See [LB13, chapter 5] for a fuller discussion of
80: this.)
81: By contrast, in communication one often imagines sending a very large number of quantum
82: bits, perhaps even a continuous stream of qubits (as in the convolutional codes of [LB13, chapter
83: 9]). Here, one is generally trying to maximize the rate of transmission, often by encoding many
84: qubits into a large block, within the constraint of a low error probability for the block. In the
85: asymptotic limit, one would like to achieve the actual capacity of the channel—the maximum rate
86: of communication possible.
87: Because the sender and receiver are separated, joint unitary transformations are impossible.
88: However, they might be able to draw on other resources, such as extra classical communication,
89: pre-shared randomness, or pre-shared entanglement. In this chapter we study the use of pre-
90: shared entanglement in quantum communication, and how we can design QECCs that use entan-
91: glement to boost either the rate of communication or the number of errors that can be corrected.
92: Codes that use pre-shared entanglement are called entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting
93: codes (EAQECCs). We will study a large class of these codes that generalizes the usual stabilizer
94: formalism from [LB13, chapter 2]. We will also see how these codes can readily be constructed
95: from classical linear codes, and how they can be useful tools in building standard QECCs.
96: 1.1

103: where |ΨL⟩is the encoded or logical state. The systems in states |ψ⟩and |0⟩are initially in the
104: possession of Alice, the sender. The encoding unitary acts on the space of the input qubits and

127: Why should we wish to use shared entanglement in our encoding? There are two ways to see
128: how this could enhance the power of the code. First, we can compare EAQECCs to teleportation. In
129: teleportation, an ebit can be used (in combination with classical communication) to transmit one
130: qubit perfectly from the sender to the receiver. We might therefore expect that making use of ebits
131: in error-correction could boost the rate of transmission.
132: Second, we can compare EAQECCs to superdense coding. In superdense coding, by using an
133: ebit the sender can send two classical bits of information to the receiver by means of a single
134: qubit. Each ancilla bit in a standard QECC can be thought of as holding one classical bit of infor-
135: mation about any errors that have occurred. Replacing an ancilla with one half of an ebit could,
136: in principle, allow the receiver to extract two bits of classical information about the errors; with
137: more information, more errors can be corrected. We shall see, in the constructions that follow,
138: that we can think of the enhanced power of EAQECCs in both of these ways, but the superdense
139: coding interpretation is more often the best ﬁt. EAQECCs can achieve some communication tasks
140: with fewer resources (or less chance of error) than would be needed by a standard QECC plus
141: teleportation [HW10b].
142: The possibility of constructing entanglement-assisted codes was suggested in [BDSW96], though
143: no practical codes were constructed. From asymptotic results in quantum information theory, we
144: know that having pre-shared entanglement allows an enhanced rate of quantum communication

148: of this idea. By constructing larger and larger code blocks, in principle one can approach the
149: entanglement-assisted quantum capacity of the channel. An example of such a code was con-
150: structed by Bowen in [Bow02], starting from a standard stabilizer QECC (see [LB13, chapter 2]). In
151: [BDH06, BDH14, HDB07] an essentially complete theory of stabilizer EAQECCs was constructed.
152: That is the theory presented in this chapter.
153: Note, however, that in general shared entanglement does not come for free: entanglement
154: must be established between the sender and receiver, and this in general requires the use of quan-
155: tum channels, and perhaps additional entanglement puriﬁcation. Therefore, EAQECCs do not
156: outperform standard quantum codes under all circumstances. The enhanced communication rates
157: that come from the use of entanglement must be paid for in establishing the entanglement in the
158: ﬁrst place. For many purposes, what is important is the net rate of the code: the number of qubits
159: transmitted minus the number of ebits consumed. With this measure, EAQECCs tend to perform
160: about the same as standard codes. Even in this case, though, EAQECCs sometimes have advan-
161: tages: as we shall see, there are many fewer restrictions on the construction of EAQECCs than
162: standard codes.

917: General codes and code parameters
918: The canonical code described above is not very useful for actual error correction. It corrects a
919: set of highly nonlocal errors, of a type that are not likely to occur in reality. However, it is very
920: helpful in clarifying how the process of error correction works, and the role of the resources used
921: in encoding. Each added ancilla can contain, in principle, one bit of information about any errors
922: that occur. Each shared ebit between the sender and receiver can contain two bits of information
923: about errors. This information about the errors is retrieved by measuring the stabilizer generators.
924: After Alice’s qubits have passed through the channel, Bob has all the qubits and can perform these
925: measurements.
926: A general EAQECC has exactly the same algebraic structure as the canonical code. The en-
927: coded state, before going through the channel, has c ebits of entanglement with the c qubits on
928: 12
929: 
930: Bob’s side. Corresponding to this entanglement are c pairs of stabilizer generators. Each pair
931: of generators has the following structure: a pair of anticommuting operators on Alice’s qubits,
932: tensored with a Z and an X, respectively, on one of the qubits on Bob’s side to “resolve” the anti-
933: commutativity. These pairs of generators are the symplectic pairs of the EAQECC. In addition to
934: these pairs, there can be single generators that act as the identity on all of Bob’s qubits. These are
935: the isotropic generators. For an [[n, k, d; c]] EAQECC, each of the stabilizer elements acts on n + c
936: qubits, n on Alice’s side and c on Bob’s side; there is a set of n −k generators for the stabilizer
937: chosen in a standard form, with 2c symplectic pairs of generators and s = n −k −2c isotropic
938: generators.
939: By Lemma 2, if two sets of Pauli operators can be put in one-to-one correspondence so that
940: they have the same commutation relations, there is a unitary transformation that turns one set
941: into the other (up to a phase). The n −k generators of an [[n, k; c]] EAQECC can be mapped by a
942: unitary operator UE to the generators of a canonical code.
943: It is important to realize is that the canonical code describes the input of the EAQECC before
944: encoding. It describes a set of k information qubits, c ebits, and s ancillas. The unitary UE trans-
945: forms the stabilizer for this input into the stabilizer for the EAQECC. Therefore UE is a unitary
946: encoding operator for this code. It transforms the localized states of the input qubits into nonlo-
947: cal, entangled states spread over all the qubits. By this transformation, the correctable error set is
948: transformed from the strange, nonlocal errors of the canonical code to a more physically realistic
949: set of errors (most commonly, localized errors on the individual qubits).

10: (GKP) qubit has been recognized as an important technological element. We have proposed a method to reduce

13: the number of qubits required for large scale quantum computation, we propose the tracking quantum error
14: correction, where the logical-qubit level quantum error correction is partially substituted by the single-qubit
15: level quantum error correction. In the proposed method, the analog quantum error correction is utilized to make
16: the performances of the single-qubit level quantum error correction almost identical to those of the logical-
17: qubit level quantum error correction in a practical noise level. The numerical results show that the proposed
18: tracking quantum error correction reduces the number of qubits during a quantum error correction process by the

27: I.
28: INTRODUCTION
29: Quantum computation has a great deal of potential to ef-
30: ﬁciently solve some hard problems for conventional comput-
31: ers [1, 2]. Among the candidates for qubits, squeezed vacuum
32: states in an optical system have shown great potential for large
33: scale continuous variable quantum computation; in fact, more
34: than one million-mode continuous variable cluster state has
35: already been achieved in an experiment [3]. This ability of en-
36: tanglement generation comes from the fact that squeezed vac-
37: uum states can be entangled with only beam splitter coupling
38: through the time-domain multiplexing approach to miniatur-
39: ize optical circuits [4, 5].
40: Moreover, a frequency-encoded
41: continuous variable in an optical setup is also a promising
42: quantum system to generate large scale cluster state more
43: than thousands [6–8]. In addition, promising platforms to im-
44: plement large scale quantum computation are recently pro-
45: posed in several setups such as a circuit QED [9, 10], opto-
46: mechanics [11, 12], atomic ensembles [13, 14], and a trapped
47: ion mechanical oscillator [15, 16]. However, since quantum
48: computation with continuous variables itself has an analog
49: nature, it is difﬁcult to handle the accumulation of analog
50: errors caused, for example, by photon loss during quantum
51: computation [17, 18]. This can be circumvented by digitizing
52: continuous variables using an appropriate code, such as the
53: Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill (GKP) code [19], which are re-
54: ferred to as GKP qubits. Moreover, GKP qubits inherit the ad-
55: vantage of squeezed vacuum states on optical implementation;
56: they can be entangled only by beam splitter coupling. Further-
57: more, we have proposed a high-threshold fault-tolerant quan-
58: tum computation to alleviate the required squeezing level for
59: fault-tolerant quantum computation to 9.8 dB [20], and have
60: taken a step closer to the realization of large scale quantum
61: computation. Hence, the GKP qubits will play an indispens-
62: able role in implementing fault-tolerant quantum computation
63: with continuous variables.
64: In general, the quantum error correction (QEC) is repeat-
65: edly performed only by the logical-qubits during the quan-
66: tum computation process. In large scale quantum computa-
67: tion, a large number of physical qubits are needed to obtain
68: the highly accurate results of quantum computation. This re-
69: quired number of physical qubits is one issue that we should
70: struggle with to implement large scale quantum computation.
71: In this work, we propose a method to reduce the number of
72: qubits required for the QEC during large scale quantum com-
73: putation, where the logical-qubit level QEC is partially sub-
74: stituted by the single-qubit level QEC. The single-qubit level
75: QEC [19] enables us to correct a displacement (deviation) er-
76: ror occurred in the single qubit by using a single ancilla qubit,
77: unless the logical-qubit level error occurs. Since the single-
78: qubit level QEC can not correct the qubit-level errors, the
79: bit and phase ﬂip errors, we just track the measurement out-
80: comes in the single-qubit level QEC. Then, the QEC is per-
81: formed with the help of a set of tracked measurement out-
82: comes in the single-qubit level QEC to correct the qubit-level
83: errors. Although the single-qubit level QEC can be also im-
84: plemented by discrete variables, the tracking QEC in discrete
85: variables can not work well as shown later in the numerical
86: results. By contrast, in our method, since the analog QEC
87: makes the performances of the single-qubit level QEC almost
88: identical to those of the logical-qubit level QEC, the track-
89: ing QEC can work well. The numerical results show that the
90: proposed method has a great advantage to reduce the required
91: number of qubits, e.g. in the concatenated QEC with analog
92: QEC proposed in Ref. [21].
93: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we
94: brieﬂy review the background knowledge regarding the GKP
95: qubit. In Sec. III, we propose the method to reduce the num-
96: ber of qubits required for large scale quantum computation.
97: In Sec. IV, the numerical results show the superiority of the
98: proposed method over the conventional methods. Section V
99: is devoted to discussion and conclusion.

23: Abstract
24: We propose quaternion-based strategies for quantum error correction by extending quantum mechanics into
25: quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Building on the properties of quaternionic quantum states, we define quaternionic
26: analogues of Pauli operators and quantum gates, ensuring inner product preservation and Hilbert space condi-
27: tions. A simple encoding scheme maps logical qubits into quaternionic systems, introducing natural redundancy
28: and enhanced resilience against noise. We construct a quaternionic extension of the five-qubit code, introducing
29: a framework of 15 syndrome measurements to detect quaternionic errors, including quaternionically rotated error
30: components. Numerical estimates show that the quaternionic five-qubit code achieves a logical error threshold
31: of approximately pth ≈0.015, demonstrating improved performance compared to the standard complex-valued
32: code. These results suggest a new pathway for quantum error correction in high-noise environments, leveraging
33: the richer structure of quaternionic quantum mechanics to improve fault tolerance.
34: 1
35: Introduction
36: Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing, protecting fragile
37: quantum states from errors such as bit flips, phase flips, and amplitude damping [1, 2]. Logical qubits are typically
38: formed by entangling multiple physical qubits using codes such as the surface code [3] being a widely studied
39: example. Recent advances include the use of reconfigurable atom arrays to build logical quantum processors [4],
40: where neutral atoms serve as physical qubits. This work demonstrated scalable improvements by increasing the
41: surface code distance from d = 3 to d = 7. Similarly, for superconducting processor achieved below-threshold
42: error correction, showing a logical error suppression factor of λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 by increasing the code distance [5].
43: These developments represent key steps toward scalable quantum computation.
44: Quaternion quantum mechanics (QQM) extends standard quantum mechanics by using quaternions instead
45: of complex numbers. Yang [6] showed that, in a generalized quantum framework, pure states can be uniquely
46: represented as rays in a vector space. This requires the Hilbert space H to be defined in one of the three number
47: fields [7]:
48: • R: real numbers
49: 1
50: arXiv:2504.19833v1  [quant-ph]  28 Apr 2025
51: 
52: • C: complex numbers
53: • H: quaternions
54: Quaternions were introduced as a natural extension of complex numbers into four dimensions. Quaternions,
55: introduced by Hamilton [8], extend complex numbers to four dimensions and are defined asq = w + xi + yj + zk,
56: where imaginary units satisfy the relations: i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = −1, to represent quantum states and
57: operators [9]. Here q ∈H, w, x, y, z ∈R and xi + yj + zk is a vector.
58: Adler [10] developed a complete formulation of quantum mechanics in quaternionic Hilbert spaces, aiming
59: for a possible unification with gravity. Later, Danielewski and Sapa [7] derived QQM from a Cauchy elastic
60: continuum model, proposing it as a physically motivated alternative. Their work introduces quaternionic versions
61: of non-relativistic and relativistic wave equations, but does not address QEC. Although QQM is theoretically
62: well established, its application to QEC remains largely unexplored. Existing research on surface codes and color
63: codes [3], and on continuous-variable systems [11], does not consider quaternionic frameworks. In principle, QEC
64: methods such as logical encoding and syndrome measurement can be extended to quaternionic Hilbert spaces,
65: which satisfy the same core postulates as complex ones. However, Vlasov [12] showed that certain QEC schemes
66: fail in standard complex quantum mechanics but succeed in real and quaternionic cases. Adler also suggested
67: the feasibility of quaternionic quantum field theories [13]. Whether quaternions can offer practical advantages
68: for QEC, such as improved error detection or fault tolerance, remains an open question.
69: In this work, we investigate the mathematical foundations and applications of quaternionic quantum mechan-
70: ics (QQM) for quantum error correction. By leveraging the richer algebraic structure of quaternions, we define
71: quaternionic analogues of quantum gates and Pauli operators, and construct new error correction schemes. In par-
72: ticular, we extend the five-qubit code into a quaternionic Hilbert space, introducing 15 syndrome measurements
73: to detect quaternionic errors. We also compare the logical error performance of the standard and quaternionic
74: codes, showing improved resilience against noise and decoherence. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2
75: introduces the mathematical foundations of QQM, emphasizing quaternion algebra in error detection. Section 3
76: presents quaternionic Pauli-like operators, error classification, and syndrome mapping. Section 4 compares the
77: logical error rates of the standard and quaternion-extended five-qubit codes. Section 5 concludes with a summary
78: and future directions.
79: 2
80: Mathematical Framework of Quaternion Quantum Mechanics
81: In this section, we introduce a new mathematical framework for QQM that ensures both theoretical consistency
82: and practical use in quantum computation. It focuses on five main components: the structure of quaternionic
83: Hilbert spaces, unitary evolution and operators, a basic encoding scheme, and the implementation of quantum
84: gates, specifically the Hadamard and CNOT gates, and building a quaternionic [[5, 1, 3]] Code with H-Qubits .
85: While based on existing developments, our approach includes new extensions to improve both formal clarity and
86: computational practicality.

1: Title: Thermodynamic Recycling of Algorithmic Failure Branches: Quantum-Computer Demonstration with Quantum Error Correction
2: arXiv ID: 2601.07522

4: Thermodynamic Recycling of Algorithmic Failure Branches: Quantum-Computer
5: Demonstration with Quantum Error Correction
6: Nobumasa Ishida∗and Yoshihiko Hasegawa†
7: Department of Information and Communication Engineering,
8: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology,
9: The University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan
10: Thermodynamic trade-off relations dictate fundamental limits on the performance of thermody-
11: namic tasks through costs such as heat dissipation. Here, we propose a framework called thermo-
12: dynamic recycling to circumvent these limits in quantum processors by exploiting failure branches
13: of quantum algorithms, which are usually discarded. The key component is an athermal bath nat-
14: urally generated during the resetting of a failure branch. By coupling this bath to a target system
15: prior to relaxation, thermodynamic tasks can be performed beyond conventional thermodynamic
16: limits. We apply this framework to information erasure and derive the reduction in heat dissipation
17: analytically. As a demonstration, we implement our framework on IBM’s superconducting quantum
18: processor by combining the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm with three-qubit quantum error cor-
19: rection, thereby reducing the heat dissipated in erasing syndrome information. Despite substantial
20: noise and errors in current hardware, our method achieves erasure with heat dissipation below the
21: Landauer limit. This work establishes an operational connection between quantum computing and
22: quantum thermodynamics for resource-efficient quantum computation.
23: Introduction—Quantum thermodynamics has revealed
24: the necessity of precise resource management in cryo-
25: genic quantum systems. Thermodynamic trade-off rela-
26: tions show that the performance of thermodynamic pro-
27: cesses is fundamentally bounded by available resources
28: or, equivalently, thermodynamic costs such as heat dissi-
29: pation [1–10]. As quantum computers develop, such ther-
30: modynamic considerations are increasingly recognized
31: within quantum computing [11–14]: for example, in stud-
32: ies of heat engines [15], quantum batteries [16], and
33: quantum error correction (QEC) [17–21]. In particular,
34: QEC protocols require frequent erasure of syndrome in-
35: formation, each incurring heat dissipation dictated by
36: Landauer’s principle [22], which can become substantial
37: when quantum computers scale to millions of qubits [19].
38: Despite the scarcity of thermodynamic resources in
39: cryogenic environments, there exists an overlooked yet
40: prevalent resource: failure branches in quantum com-
41: puting. Branch selection conditioned on measurements
42: is ubiquitous in quantum algorithms.
43: Examples range
44: from the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd (HHL) algorithm for
45: solving linear systems of equations [23] and quantum
46: singular-value transformation [24, 25] to magic-state dis-
47: tillation [26–28], a core subroutine of fault-tolerant quan-
48: tum computing. In such protocols, only designated out-
49: comes are retained, whereas the remaining outcomes cor-
50: respond to failure branches. These branches are typically
51: discarded and reset for subsequent trials. Despite efforts
52: to reduce such discarding, including amplitude amplifica-
53: tion and magic-state cultivation [29–31], failure branches
54: themselves remain unavoidable and are considered waste-
55: ful byproducts.
56: In this Letter, we propose thermodynamic recycling, a
57: generic framework that converts failure branches into re-
58: sources for thermodynamic tasks. Generally, when a fail-
59: ure branch is reset by being coupled to a cold finite bath,
60: the bath is driven out of equilibrium. Our approach then
61: couples this transient athermal bath to a target system
62: before relaxation, enabling thermodynamic tasks to be
63: performed beyond the conventional limits imposed by an
64: equilibrium bath. While the framework applies to gen-
65: eral branching algorithms and thermodynamic tasks, we
66: analyze information erasure as a representative example.
67: As a theoretical foundation, we derive the correspond-
68: ing reduction in the minimum heat dissipation relative
69: to equilibrium-bath bounds dictated by Landauer’s prin-
70: ciple [22, 32]. Then, we demonstrate the framework on
71: IBM’s superconducting quantum processor [33], where
72: we supply the failure branch of the HHL algorithm to a
73: three-qubit QEC circuit via classical feedforward opera-
74: tion. As a result, we observe a reduction in heat dissipa-
75: tion in erasing syndrome information below Landauer’s
76: principle, even with the limitations of current hardware,
77: such as short coherence time and significant noise. Our
78: work suggests that thermodynamic recycling is a viable
79: strategy for near-term quantum computers.

4: Sparse Mamba Decoder for Quantum Error Correction:
5: Efficient Defect-Centric Processing of Surface Code Syndromes
6: Samira Sayedsalehi∗, Nader Bagherzadeh, Maxim Shcherbakov, and Jean-Luc Gaudiot
7: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
8: University of California, Irvine, CA 92697, USA
9: Abstract
10: Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for building fault-tolerant quantum com-
11: puters, requiring decoders that are simultaneously accurate, fast, and scalable. Most state-
12: of-the-art neural decoders achieve high accuracy but process the full dense syndrome array
13: of size O(d2R) regardless of the actual error rate, where d is the code distance and R is the
14: number of measurement rounds. At physically relevant error rates (p ≈0.1%), fewer than 5%
15: of syndrome entries contain active detection events—yet existing decoders process the entire
16: syndrome volume. We introduce the Sparse Mamba Decoder (SMD), a defect-centric neural
17: decoder that processes only the k active detection events using a 13-dimensional feature
18: representation per defect and a Mamba state-space backbone, achieving O(k) complexity.
19: Across depolarizing, uniform circuit-level, SI1000, and Google Sycamore experimental bench-
20: marks, SMD reduces the MWPM logical error rate by up to 49% at d ≤5 under SI1000 noise,
21: runs 95–467× faster than the Tesseract near-MLD decoder and 232–463× faster than Belief
22: Matching, and maintains nearly constant latency (24–57 µs) across d = 3–9 under uniform
23: circuit-level noise. On the Sycamore experimental dataset, the SMD ensemble matches or
24: slightly surpasses the dense Mamba decoder of Lee et al. All results are obtained on com-
25: modity NVIDIA GPUs with 7.5–16M parameters, without specialized accelerators.
26: 1
27: Introduction
28: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires logical error rates far below those achievable with
29: physical qubits, necessitating quantum error correction (QEC) codes that encode logical infor-
30: mation redundantly across many physical qubits [1, 2]. The surface code [3, 4] is the leading
31: candidate for near-term implementation due to its high threshold error rate and local stabi-
32: lizer structure, and continues to see active research in code design [5] and decoder development.
33: However, the practical utility of any QEC code depends critically on the decoder—the classical
34: algorithm that infers logical errors from noisy stabilizer measurements.
35: An ideal decoder must satisfy three competing requirements simultaneously: accuracy (ap-
36: proaching the maximum-likelihood estimate), speed (keeping pace with the quantum hardware
37: cycle time, typically ∼1 µs for superconducting qubits [6]), and scalability (maintaining perfor-
38: mance as code distance increases). In practice, existing decoders make tradeoffs among these
39: three axes, and achieving all three simultaneously—particularly at the code distances required
40: for fault tolerance—remains an open challenge.
41: Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) [7, 8] is fast and scalable but suboptimal,
42: as it does not account for correlated errors. The Tesseract decoder [9] achieves near-optimal
43: accuracy through beam search over the detector error model but requires millisecond-scale com-
44: putation. AlphaQubit [10] introduced a recurrent-transformer architecture that outperforms all
45: matching-based decoders on experimental data, but its O(d4) per-round attention complexity

49: 
50: makes real-time decoding impractical at large distances. AlphaQubit 2 [11] addresses this with
51: a redesigned architecture achieving O(d2) per-round scaling and real-time decoding up to dis-
52: tance 11, but requires specialized Trillium TPU hardware [12]. Lee et al. [13] proposed replacing
53: the transformer with a Mamba state-space model [14], reducing the complexity to O(d2) while
54: maintaining accuracy on consumer GPUs.
55: Despite these advances, most existing neural decoders share a fundamental inefficiency: they
56: process the full syndrome array of size d2 × R at every decoding step, regardless of how many
57: errors actually occurred. The graph-neural-network decoder of Lange et al. [15] operates on
58: detection events but requires explicit graph construction and message-passing operations that
59: are less GPU-friendly than pure sequence processing. At a physical error rate of p = 10−3 under
60: SI1000 noise, only a few percent of stabilizer measurements fire—we measure detection-event
61: densities of 2.8–3.2% across d = 3–7 (Table 10). Yet existing decoders process every entry of the
62: syndrome volume, analogous to running a dense matrix multiplication on a 97%-sparse matrix.
63: In this work, we introduce the Sparse Mamba Decoder (SMD), which fundamentally changes
64: the input representation from dense syndrome arrays to sparse defect sequences. Each active
65: detection event is represented by a 13-dimensional feature vector encoding spatial coordinates
66: on the rotated lattice, stabilizer type (X or Z), spatial and temporal neighborhood connectivity
67: flags, normalized distances to the logical boundaries, and a reconstructed stabilizer measure-
68: ment computed via cumulative XOR of the per-stabilizer detection event history. The resulting
69: variable-length sequences—typically k ≪d2R at physically relevant error rates—are processed
70: by a Mamba state-space backbone [14] in linear time without attention. This yields O(k) com-
71: plexity, compared to O(d2R) for dense neural decoders and O(d4R) for attention-based methods.
72: Throughout this paper, complexity is reported per decoding task (one logical qubit memory ex-
73: periment over R rounds); equivalent per-round costs for recurrent decoders are obtained by divid-
74: ing by R, e.g., O(d2) per round for dense Mamba [13] and O(d4) per round for AlphaQubit [10].
75: Our main contributions are:
76: 1. A sparse defect-centric architecture for QEC decoding. SMD processes only active detec-
77: tion events through a Mamba state-space backbone, achieving O(k) complexity that scales
78: with the number of errors rather than the code size. The 13-dimensional defect features en-
79: code the spatial structure and measurement history needed for accurate decoding without
80: explicit 2D convolutions.
81: 2. Strong accuracy across synthetic and experimental benchmarks. Under SI1000 noise at p =
82: 1.5 × 10−3, SMD reduces the MWPM logical error rate by up to 49% at d ≤5 and by 16%
83: at d = 7 via a three-checkpoint ensemble, where a Libra-style ensemble of seven perturbed
84: MWPM decoders gives no improvement, isolating the gain to learned correlations. On
85: the Sycamore dataset, the SMD ensemble matches or slightly surpasses the dense Mamba
86: decoder of Lee et al. [13] at both d = 3 and d = 5, while the single-model SMD remains
87: competitive at d = 3 and approaches dense-Mamba performance at d = 5.
88: 3. Order-of-magnitude speedups over near-MLD decoders. Under SI1000 noise, SMD runs 95×–
89: 467× faster than Tesseract and 232×–463× faster than Belief Matching, with the speedup
90: growing with code distance. Under uniform circuit-level noise, decoding latency is nearly
91: constant (24–57 µs) across d = 3–9, compared to a 773× increase for Belief Matching over
92: the same range.
93: 4. Commodity-hardware feasibility. All results are obtained on commodity NVIDIA GPUs—
94: an RTX 4090 (24 GB) for the smaller depolarizing and uniform circuit-level models, and a
95: single H200 NVL (141 GB) for the larger SI1000 model—without the specialized Trillium
96: TPUs used by AlphaQubit 2 [11, 12].
