100: Background
101: 2.1
102: Surface Codes and Stabilizer Measurements
103: The rotated surface code of distance d encodes one logical qubit into d2 data qubits using a CSS
104: (Calderbank-Shor-Steane) structure of (d2 −1) stabilizer measurements arranged in a checker-
105: board pattern on a two-dimensional lattice [4] (Figure 1). These stabilizers form two independent
106: families: Z-type checks detect X-errors (bit flips) by measuring the Z-parity of adjacent data
107: qubits, while X-type checks detect Z-errors (phase flips) by measuring the X-parity of their
108: neighbors; a Y -error triggers both check types simultaneously, enabling its identification. In a
109: memory experiment, stabilizer measurements are repeated for R rounds, producing a syndrome
110: array of shape (d2 −1) × R, with X and Z corrections handled independently.
111: A detection event at stabilizer i and round t is defined as the temporal difference of consecutive
112: measurements:
113: di,t = si,t ⊕si,t−1,
114: (1)
115: where si,t ∈{0, 1} is the raw measurement outcome and ⊕denotes XOR. In the absence of
116: errors, all detection events are zero; physical errors on data qubits trigger clusters of nearby
117: detection events in space-time.
118: Figure 1: a) Planar layout of a rotated surface code with code distance d = 3. White circles
119: represent data qubits, while blue circles • and pink circles • represent Z-type and X-type stabi-
120: lizer measurement qubits, respectively. b) Circuit representation of the X-type (top) and Z-type
121: (bottom) stabilizer measurements. Open circles (◦) denote the four data qubits coupled to each
122: measurement qubit.
123: The decoder’s task is to predict the logical observable λ ∈{0, 1} from the set of detection
124: events {di,t}i,t, determining whether a logical error has occurred.
125: 2.2
126: The Decoding Problem
127: Given a syndrome σ = {di,t}, the optimal decoder predicts the most likely logical observable:
128: ˆλ = arg max
129: λ∈{0,1} P(λ | σ),
130: (2)
131: which requires marginalizing over all physical error configurations consistent with the observed
132: syndrome. This decoding problem is NP-hard in general [16]. Practical decoders approximate
133: this inference using matching-based methods (MWPM [7]), tensor-network contraction [17], or
134: learned neural networks [10, 13].

138: Related Work
139: Matching-based decoders reduce the decoding problem to a minimum-weight perfect matching
140: on a graph derived from the detector error model. MWPM [8] and its correlated variants achieve
141: a circuit-level threshold of approximately 0.5–1%, with Sparse Blossom [7] achieving O(n1.32)
142: observed complexity. Union-Find [18] offers near-linear O(nα(n)) complexity at slightly reduced
143: accuracy. Belief Matching [19] combines belief propagation with matching-based decoding and
144: improves accuracy under circuit-level noise, although belief propagation alone can perform poorly
145: on surface codes due to short cycles in the Tanner graph. The Tesseract decoder [9] reaches
146: near-optimal accuracy through beam search over the detector error model, but at millisecond-
147: scale per-shot cost. Recently, ensemble approaches such as Libra [20] have explored combining
148: multiple perturbed matching decoders to close the residual gap to maximum-likelihood decoding.

150: a near-optimal but exponentially expensive baseline [17], which we use as a reference on the
151: Sycamore experimental dataset.

13: The theory of quantum error correction was established more than a decade ago as the primary
14: tool for ﬁghting decoherence in quantum information processing [1, 2, 3, 4]. Although great progress
15: has already been made in this ﬁeld, limited methods are available in constructing new quantum error
16: correction codes from old codes. Here we exhibit a simple and general method to construct new
17: quantum error correction codes by nesting certain quantum codes together. The problem of ﬁnding
18: long quantum error correction codes is reduced to that of searching several short length quantum
19: codes with certain properties. Our method works for all length and all distance codes, and is quite
20: eﬃcient to construct optimal or near optimal codes. Two main known methods in constructing new
21: codes from old codes in quantum error-correction theory, the concatenating and pasting, can be
22: understood in the framework of nested quantum error correction codes.
23: PACS numbers: 03.67.Pp, 03.67.-a, 89.70.Kn, 03.67.Lx
24: Quantum computers oﬀer a means of solving certain
25: problems, including prime factorization, exponentially
26: faster than classical computers [5].
27: One of the main
28: diﬃculties in building the quantum computers is that
29: the quantum information are fragile to decoherence. To
30: solve this problem, the quantum error correction codes
31: (QECC) are designed which provide us an active way
32: of protecting our precious quantum data from quantum
33: noises.
34: Since the initial discovery of quantum error-
35: correcting coeds (QECC), researchers have made great
36: progress in codes construction. But for large number of
37: qubits there has been less progress, and only a few gen-
38: eral code constructions are know.
39: The main diﬃculty
40: in constructing long codes is that we need to choose the
41: suitable QECC from a large quantity of quantum states
42: whose number in general grows exponentially with the
43: length. This random search method will be intractable
44: for long codes. However, long QECC is indeed necessary
45: when we can control more and more qubits to realize
46: the scalable quantum computation. If we can divide the
47: searching of QECC into several easier steps, then the dif-
48: ﬁculty in constructing long QECC will be reduced dra-
49: matically. In this work, we propose a general and easy
50: method to construct the nested QECC.

10: Operator quantum error correction provides a unified framework for the known techniques of 
11: quantum error correction such as the standard error correction model, the method of 
12: decoherence-free subspaces, and the noiseless subsystem method. We first show an example of a 
13: new quantum error correction scheme which can not be described by operation quantum error 
14: correction. Then we introduce a different notion of noiseless subsystems according to the example. 
15: Base on this notion, we present a more unified approach which incorporates operator quantum 
16: error correction as a special case. Moreover, we also give a sufficient and necessary condition of 
17: quantum error correction using this approach. We show that this approach provides more recovery 
18: operations than operator quantum error correction, which possibly leads to simpler decoding 
19: procedures. 
20: PACS number(s): 03.67.Pp, 03.67.Hk, 03.67.Lx

8: Continuous-time quantum error correction (CTQEC) is an approach to protecting quantum in-
9: formation from noise in which both the noise and the error correcting operations are treated as
10: processes that are continuous in time. This chapter investigates CTQEC based on continuous weak
11: measurements and feedback from the point of view of the subsystem principle, which states that
12: protected quantum information is contained in a subsystem of the Hilbert space. We study how to
13: approach the problem of constructing CTQEC protocols by looking at the evolution of the state
14: of the system in an encoded basis in which the subsystem containing the protected information is
15: explicit. This point of view allows us to reduce the problem to that of protecting a known state,
16: and to design CTQEC procedures from protocols for the protection of a single qubit. We show how
17: previously studied CTQEC schemes with both direct and indirect feedback can be obtained from
18: strategies for the protection of a single qubit via weak measurements and weak unitary operations.
19: We also review results on the performance of CTQEC with direct feedback in cases of Markovian
20: and non-Markovian decoherence, where we have shown that due to the existence of a Zeno regime in
21: non-Markovian dynamics, the performance of CTQEC can exhibit a quadratic improvement if the
22: time resolution of the weak error-correcting operations is high enough to reveal the non-Markovian
23: character of the noise process.

38: This formalism is fundamental for the understanding of preserved information under CPTP dynamics, but it
39: depicts an idealized version of the error-correction process. It represents both the noise and the error-correcting
40: operations as discrete CPTP maps, and assumes that error correction is applied after the noise. Such a picture is

Introduction
Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing, protecting fragile
quantum states from errors such as bit flips, phase flips, and amplitude damping [1, 2]. Logical qubits are typically
formed by entangling multiple physical qubits using codes such as the surface code [3] being a widely studied
example. Recent advances include the use of reconfigurable atom arrays to build logical quantum processors [4],
where neutral atoms serve as physical qubits. This work demonstrated scalable improvements by increasing the
surface code distance from d = 3 to d = 7. Similarly, for superconducting processor achieved below-threshold
error correction, showing a logical error suppression factor of λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 by increasing the code distance [5].
These developments represent key steps toward scalable quantum computation.
Quaternion quantum mechanics (QQM) extends standard quantum mechanics by using quaternions instead
of complex numbers. Yang [6] showed that, in a generalized quantum framework, pure states can be uniquely
represented as rays in a vector space. This requires the Hilbert space H to be defined in one of the three number
fields [7]:

Quaternions were introduced as a natural extension of complex numbers into four dimensions. Quaternions,
introduced by Hamilton [8], extend complex numbers to four dimensions and are defined asq = w + xi + yj + zk,

operators [9]. Here q ∈H, w, x, y, z ∈R and xi + yj + zk is a vector.
Adler [10] developed a complete formulation of quantum mechanics in quaternionic Hilbert spaces, aiming
for a possible unification with gravity. Later, Danielewski and Sapa [7] derived QQM from a Cauchy elastic
continuum model, proposing it as a physically motivated alternative. Their work introduces quaternionic versions
of non-relativistic and relativistic wave equations, but does not address QEC. Although QQM is theoretically
well established, its application to QEC remains largely unexplored. Existing research on surface codes and color
codes [3], and on continuous-variable systems [11], does not consider quaternionic frameworks. In principle, QEC
methods such as logical encoding and syndrome measurement can be extended to quaternionic Hilbert spaces,
which satisfy the same core postulates as complex ones. However, Vlasov [12] showed that certain QEC schemes
fail in standard complex quantum mechanics but succeed in real and quaternionic cases. Adler also suggested
the feasibility of quaternionic quantum field theories [13]. Whether quaternions can offer practical advantages
for QEC, such as improved error detection or fault tolerance, remains an open question.

In standard QEC, the physical error rate p represents the probability of an error occurring on a physical qubit,
typically modeled by Pauli operators X, Y , and Z. The logical error rate pL is the probability that such errors

additional error types such as four-dimensional rotations and non-commutative transformations. These richer
dynamics like directional interference and 4D amplitude shifts require adapted decoding strategies and influence
both the error threshold pth and the scaling behavior of pL.

In Ref. [21], on the other hand, it was shown that if we are interested in the average time that it would take to purify

Introduction
Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires logical error rates far below those achievable with
physical qubits, necessitating quantum error correction (QEC) codes that encode logical infor-
mation redundantly across many physical qubits [1, 2]. The surface code [3, 4] is the leading
candidate for near-term implementation due to its high threshold error rate and local stabi-
lizer structure, and continues to see active research in code design [5] and decoder development.
However, the practical utility of any QEC code depends critically on the decoder—the classical
algorithm that infers logical errors from noisy stabilizer measurements.
An ideal decoder must satisfy three competing requirements simultaneously: accuracy (ap-
proaching the maximum-likelihood estimate), speed (keeping pace with the quantum hardware
cycle time, typically ∼1 µs for superconducting qubits [6]), and scalability (maintaining perfor-
mance as code distance increases). In practice, existing decoders make tradeoffs among these
three axes, and achieving all three simultaneously—particularly at the code distances required
for fault tolerance—remains an open challenge.

Conclusions
This work develops a quaternion-based formulation of quantum mechanics by extending standard quantum theory
to quaternionic Hilbert spaces. It defines quaternionic Pauli-like operators and introduces quantum-like gates
(e.g., HH, CNOTH). We examine how syndrome measurements in the quaternionic extension of the five-qubit
code correspond to quaternionic error components specifically the i, j, and k directions requiring auxiliary
measurements to detect these errors. The five-qubit quaternionic code achieves a threshold of approximately
pth ≈0.015, benefiting from improved error distinguishability in higher dimensions. This value is between the
thresholds reported in prior studies. For example, [20] reports a threshold of 0.0185 for depolarizing noise, nearing
the upper bound of 0.189 for surface codes when noise correlations are considered [21, 22]. In contrast, Takagi [23]
found the five-qubit code exhibits a lower threshold due to its round-robin structure and error accumulation,
similar to the Bacon-Shor code. The proposed framework opens new avenues for QEC by utilizing quaternionic
structures to improve noise resilience. While it departs from conventional quantum mechanics, it provides a
potential pathway toward more robust and fault-tolerant quantum architectures. Future work will extend this
analysis to quaternionic codes [[n, k, d]], with a focus on their syndrome-based error correction properties. The
quaternionic [[5, 1, 3]] code will serve as a baseline case, with generalizations aimed at evaluating feasibility and
performance in practical QEC scenarios.

5.2
Feature Design Rationale
The 13-dimensional defect representation encodes information analogous to what matching-based
decoders rely on, while remaining compatible with variable-length sequence processing.
The
spatial coordinates (xi, yi) and stabilizer type τi identify where and what kind of defect occurred—
the same information that anchors each node in MWPM’s matching graph.
The boundary
distances bZ, bX encode proximity to the logical operators, which directly determines whether
a chain of errors produces a logical failure; matching decoders encode this implicitly through
boundary nodes. The four spatial neighbor flags n1, . . . , n4 and two temporal neighbor flags
18

n5, n6 provide a local error fingerprint: an isolated defect (all flags zero) likely results from a
measurement error, while a defect with fired neighbors signals a data qubit error—a distinction
that matching decoders make through edge weights in the detector error model. Finally, the
reconstructed measurement mi,t via cumulative XOR provides the model with both a change
signal (the detection event itself) and a state signal (the current stabilizer value), following the
dual-input approach of AlphaQubit [10]. Together, these features make the geometric structure
of the surface code accessible to a purely sequential model, without requiring the learned 2D
convolutions that dense decoders rely on to recover spatial context.
5.3
Scalability and Limitations
The sparse approach offers several advantages. Computational cost scales with the number of
errors rather than the code size; geometry is encoded directly in the feature vector, eliminating
the need for 2D convolutions or spatial embedding; and training and inference run on commodity
GPUs without specialized hardware. The result is an ∼7.5–16M parameter decoder that achieves
competitive accuracy with O(k) scaling on a single RTX 4090 or H200 NVL.
Several extensions remain natural directions for future work. Our compute budget restricted
experimental evaluation to d ≤7 under SI1000 noise; with additional resources, the same training
protocol applies directly to d = 9, 11 and beyond. The present architecture also processes the full
R-round volume in one pass and is therefore optimized for batched throughput (Table 9) rather
than the ∼1 µs per-cycle budget required for real-time decoding on superconducting qubits.
Reaching that regime would combine SMD’s O(k) scaling with the streaming, hardware-specific
optimizations developed for AQ2-RT [11]—a complementary direction enabled by the small model
size and sparse input representation.
This work focuses specifically on the rotated surface code, evaluated on synthetic noise (depo-
larizing, uniform circuit-level, SI1000) and on Sycamore experimental data. Natural extensions
include applying the sparse representation to recent surface-code experiments such as Google’s
Willow distance-7 chip [23], where the same three-stage SI1000→DEM→experimental curricu-
lum should transfer directly; adapting the 13-dimensional features for color codes and quantum
LDPC codes, where structurally sparser syndromes should make the O(k) scaling advantage even
more pronounced; implementing a streaming variant for real-time decoding; and incorporating
soft information (I/Q readout data) for further accuracy gains.
6
Conclusion
We have introduced the Sparse Mamba Decoder, a neural decoder for quantum error correction
that processes only active detection events rather than the full dense syndrome array. By rep-
resenting each defect with 13 engineered features—including spatial coordinates, neighborhood
connectivity, boundary distances, and reconstructed measurements via cumulative XOR—and
processing the resulting variable-length sequences with a Mamba state-space model, our approach
achieves O(k) computational complexity where k is the number of defects.
Across four benchmarks spanning synthetic noise models and experimental data from Google’s
Sycamore quantum processor, SMD demonstrates competitive or superior accuracy compared to
existing decoders. Under depolarizing noise with perfect stabilizers, the dual-head variant out-
performs MWPM, Tesseract (near-MLD), and Belief Matching by 40–91% at d = 5–11 through
joint (λZ, λX) decoding that exploits Y -error correlations—a structural advantage over matching-
based decoders that decode each basis independently. Under uniform circuit-level noise, SMD
outperforms MWPM at all distances d = 3–9. On the SI1000 benchmark, it reduces the MWPM
logical error rate by up to 49%, and on the Sycamore experimental benchmark, the ensemble
matches or slightly surpasses the dense Mamba decoder of Lee et al. despite using a sparse input
representation.
19

A key practical advantage is the decoder’s favorable scaling: under uniform circuit-level
noise at p = 0.002, latency increases only 2.4× from d = 3 to d = 9 (24 µs to 57 µs on RTX
4090), compared to 773× for Belief Matching over the same range. At d = 9, SMD decodes
230× faster than Belief Matching, while achieving higher accuracy than MWPM. Under SI1000
noise, the speedup over near-MLD decoders grows to 95–467× (Tesseract) and 232–463× (Belief
Matching). With ∼7.5–16M parameters on commodity NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 4090 for smaller
models, H200 for the largest), SMD provides a practical alternative to approaches requiring
specialized accelerator hardware.
Our results suggest that the inherent sparsity of quantum error syndromes at physically rele-
vant error rates is a powerful structural prior that should be exploited by decoder architectures.
As quantum processors scale to larger code distances, the gap between dense and sparse pro-
cessing costs will only grow, making defect-centric approaches increasingly attractive. Future
work includes adapting the sparse representation for color codes and quantum LDPC codes,
implementing a streaming variant for real-time decoding, and combining the O(k) scaling with

## Paper type
Theory/review chapter (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.). No experiments, no superconducting hardware,
no numerical fault-tolerance thresholds. It provides the *framework* for thinking about continuous
error correction, not a surface-code threshold result.

## Core framework
- Discrete QEC formalism (CPTP noise map E + recovery R) idealizes both noise and correction as
  instantaneous discrete maps. In reality correction takes finite time, and with non-Markovian noise the
  system correlates with the environment, so effective maps between corrections need not even be CP.
- **CTQEC** = both noise and correction are continuous processes. Protected info lives in a *subsystem*
  (subsystem principle); the author works in an "encoded basis" where HA = logical factor, plus
  (n-r-1) syndrome qubit factors and r gauge qubits, for an [[n,1,r,d]] stabilizer code. This reduces
  multi-qubit QEC to the single-qubit problem of protecting a *known* state.
- **Paz-Zurek (PZ) quantum-jump model / direct feedback**: instantaneous full correction operations
  applied at random times with rate kappa. Master equation dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), with jump generator
  J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ. Physically: a stream of fresh ancillas weakly coupled and discarded, i.e. a
  *cooling* process that continuously pumps out entropy.
- **ADL scheme / indirect feedback**: continuous weak syndrome (stabilizer) measurement + feedback
  Hamiltonians whose strength λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ) is chosen to maximize instantaneous
  code-space fidelity. Weakened weak map: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) over time τc, giving κ = ε²/τc.
  Note in ADL, syndrome measurement is on the *code* stabilizers and correction acts back; in PZ the
  role of X and Z measurements/rotations is swapped relative to the intuitive picture.

## Why continuous can beat discrete ("freezing")
Correctable error weight grows as O(Δt) per step while uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²).
So as correction becomes continuous, uncorrectable weight never accumulates: in the limit of infinite
correction rate the state *freezes*. The whole point is to suppress the second-order term.

## Performance results (direct feedback, bit-flip codes, exactly solvable models)
- Markovian, 3-qubit bit-flip code, ratio r = κ/λ: weight outside code space → 3/(4+r) ~ 1/r.
  Encoded qubit then decays *inside* the code space like bare bit-flip noise at rate (6/r)γ, i.e.
  overall decoherence reduced by ~r/6. In the limit r -> ∞ protection is perfect for all times.
- Uncorrected weight scales roughly **linearly with the number of qubits** for fixed κ, and the κ needed
  to hold a given code-space overlap also scales ~linearly in n. Resource cost grows with code size.
- **Non-Markovian / Zeno regime (the headline result)**: for a system initially decoupled from its bath
  the fidelity is α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³). Balancing Zeno decay 2√C√(1-α)Δt against correction
  κ(1-α)Δt gives quasi-stationary equilibrium fidelity
      1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ²,   vs  1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ.
  So effective error rate reduction improves **quadratically (κ²)** in the non-Markovian case but only
  linearly (κ) in the Markovian case. Same 1/κ² scaling argued to hold for any code, since every
  syndrome qubit in the encoded basis undergoes Zeno-type evolution.
- Valid only in the regime γδt << 1 << κδt, i.e. the weak correction must be *faster than the Zeno
  time* to reveal the non-Markovian structure. Resource caveat: ε ∝ g²τc², so κ ∝ g²τc - shrinking
  τc to raise time resolution lowers κ. The paper notes the "paradoxical" possibility that a *lower*
  correction rate gives better performance because the quadratic κ² gain outweighs the linear loss.
- Error *prevention* (frequent syndrome measurement only, no correction) works only in the Zeno regime,
  fails under Markovian assumptions, but allows lower redundancy (4-qubit encoding of 1 qubit vs 3-qubit
  repetition for correction). Error correction therefore works in regimes where prevention fails, at the
  cost of higher redundancy and added correcting unitaries.

## Relevance to the topic question (surface codes + superconducting qubits, below-threshold operation)
- CTQEC is an **alternative paradigm to discrete syndrome-extraction cycles**, not a threshold theorem.
  It shifts the burden from "error rate per cycle < threshold" to "correction rate κ and time resolution
  τc vs bath correlation time".
- Superconducting qubits plausibly sit in the favourable regime: long T1/T2 and quasi-static
  (1/f, telegraph) noise mean bath memory is *not* negligible, i.e. evolution is non-Markovian at long
  times - exactly where the Zeno/quadratic argument applies. This is the paper's strongest link to the
  question, but it is a qualitative argument, not evidence.
- The paper contains **no** statement about surface codes specifically, no comparison of rotated vs
  unrotated layouts, and no threshold numbers. Its examples are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes.
- Direct/indirect feedback schemes are called "largely heuristic" and "not thoroughly understood" by the
  author; the theoretical analysis is done only for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model.
- Author's own open question, directly relevant to the review: "whether CTQEC can be made fault
  tolerant" - FT theory assumes discrete transversal logical operations; he proposes looking for
  fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak* operations. Also open: scalability with
  local (1-2 qubit) Hamiltonians only, and whether an equilibrium-fidelity analogue exists for
  indirect feedback.

## Key takeaways for the synthesis
1. CTQEC offers a second, independent route to below-threshold operation: continuous weak
   measurement + feedback, where protection comes from a Zeno/freezing argument instead of a
   threshold theorem. Nothing here contradicts threshold theory; it is a different resource assumption.
2. The single strongest quantitative claim: uncorrectable error weight 1/κ (Markovian) vs 1/κ²
   (non-Markovian/Zeno) - super-linear returns on correction rate, conditional on resolving the Zeno
   time scale.
3. Honest limitation: this paper is theory from 2013 with toy codes; any claim that "CTQEC enables
   below-threshold surface codes on superconducting qubits" would be an extrapolation beyond the paper.

**Theoretical / benchmark thresholds**
- Matching-based decoders (MWPM and correlated variants) reach a *circuit-level* threshold of

  all land on **identical** logical error rates at every d and p tested (Table 4). Interpretation
  offered by the authors: MWPM is already near-optimal *among factorized, independent-basis
  decoders* in that regime.

  (also restated in 2504.19833).

| Operation | Rate |
|---|---|
| two-qubit CZ | p |
| single-qubit gate | p/10 |
| measurement readout | 5p |
| reset | 2p |
| idle (per round) | 4.2p |

(5e-3) sits far below the ideal 0.5-1%.

  decoders are at or slightly past the tensor-network reference, and the experimental numbers

- The gap is not the matching *algorithm* per se, it is that matching decoders are
  **factorized into independent X- and Z-graph matchings**, so they structurally cannot use
  cross-basis correlations created by Y errors.

  and scalable *simultaneously*; the paper frames this as the open problem.
- MWPM: 9.3 / 27.7 / 54.1 us per shot (d=3/5/7) on one CPU core. Belief Matching 19-297 ms.

  **decoder engineering on the hardware interface**, not the code.

dense Mamba O(d^2 R) on RTX 4090; SMD O(k) on RTX 4090 / H200, 7.5-16M params.

constant across d, so O(k) grows much more slowly than O(d^2 R).

1. **Theoretical FT threshold for surface codes:** ~0.5-1% circuit-level for matching decoders;

   dominate). Perfect-stabilizer depolarizing comparison puts MWPM at parity with near-MLD.

   temperature, 5 GHz qubit resonance (2601.07522, IBM Kawasaki), feedforward latency several
   microseconds vs tens of ns for gates - a real handicap for feedforward-dependent schemes.
3. **Below-threshold experiments?** On synthetic SI1000, yes and cleanly. On Sycamore
   experimental data, neural decoders reach parity with the tensor-network reference, and the
   below-threshold demonstrations themselves (Acharya 2024, Willow d=7) are cited secondhand,
   not verifiable from this archive.

   decoder latency vs 1 us cycle, scarcity of experimental data, and un-modelled
   leakage/crosstalk physics.

  the same 4-bit syndrome table, with X->iX, Y->jY, Z->kZ relabelling. The extra "syndrome
  measurements" are measurements of the j and k amplitude components, and the paper itself
  says quaternionic errors produce the *trivial* syndrome (+1,+1,+1,+1) - i.e. the extra
  structure is orthogonal to the standard detection events. The improvement claim rests on
  numerical fits of p_L ~ p^2 vs p^2.2 to simulation, not on a decoding argument, and it is
  admitted to be a departure from conventional QM with no experimental basis. **Recommend
  treating this as a speculative outlier, not evidence about superconducting surface codes.**

  information can be done *below the Landauer limit* by recycling the athermal bath left over
  from resetting an algorithm's failure branch (demonstrated on IBM with HHL + 3-qubit QEC).

  superconducting hardware, latency and idle-time decoherence - not algorithmic elegance -

- 0909.5103 and 1401.0456 are background/framework and add nothing to the threshold question;
  0909.5103's useful line is that concatenation and stabilizer pasting are both special cases
  of nested codes, and that long-code search becomes a search over short codes.

- Standard discrete QEC represents noise and correction as discrete CPTP maps with correction applied
  after the noise; this is only an approximation, because a real correcting operation takes finite time and
  under non-Markovian dynamics the effective map between corrections need not be CP at all (L42-49).
- **CTQEC**: noise *and* correction are continuous. Protected information sits in a subsystem HA of
  HS = HA ⊗ HB ⊕ K; in the encoded basis for an [[n,1,r,d]] code, HS = HA ⊗(n-r-1 syndrome qubits)⊗(r gauge qubits)
  (L15, L195-206). Multi-qubit QEC then reduces to protecting a *known* single-qubit state.
- **PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback**: ρ -> (1-κdt)ρ + κdt R(ρ), master equation
  dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ (L60-73). Physical reading: coupling to a **stream of fresh
  ancillas** that continuously pump out accumulated entropy, i.e. a cooling process; also implementable by
  weak measurement + weak unitary (L103-108).
- **Weak map form**: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) acting over a small but finite time τc, with effective
  rate **κ = ε²/τc** (L96-101).
- **ADL indirect feedback**: stochastic master equation with continuous weak measurement of the stabilizer
  generators Ml (Wiener-process jumps) plus correcting Hamiltonians Hr switched on with strength
  λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ), chosen to maximize instantaneous code-space fidelity (L128-154).
  Weak X-measurement can be done with one ancilla: HX = -X ⊗ Y for time ~ε/2, then destructive ancilla
  measurement, outcome probabilities p± = ½(1 ± ε Tr(Xρ)) (L584-600).

## 2. The "freezing" / Zeno argument

- Correctable error weight in a short step Δt is ∝ Δt, uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²);
  therefore continuously applied correction stops accumulation, and in the limit Δt -> 0 the state
  **freezes** (L112-119).
- Encoded-basis bound: ||dρA/dt|| ≤ B(1-α) + C√(α(1-α)), so keeping (1-α) small suppresses the
  accumulation rate of uncorrectable errors; CTQEC is thus "the goal of keeping every syndrome qubit close
  to |0>" (L340-364).

## 3. Weak measurement + feedback, and the honest limitation (quoted)

- "All these schemes are to a large extent **heuristic**, and their workings are not thoroughly
  understood. The difficulty in rigorously motivating the construction of error-correction protocols based
  on weak measurements and feedback is that stochastic evolutions are generally too complicated to study
  analytically." (L155-162)
- Both schemes are related to known optimal single-qubit purification protocols: PZ ≈ fast average-fidelity
  protocol (measure X, rotate about Y), ADL ≈ fastest-average-time protocol (measure Z, rotate about X);
  optimality is claimed only w.r.t. these single-qubit criteria, not for their resource cost (L888-908).
- Retaining the measurement record would improve PZ only by O((1-α*_M)²) - i.e. PZ is "very close to
  optimal" in the regime where 1-α*_M is small, but only if the relation between measurement strength and
  correcting rotation (Eq. 36, L470-476) can be met (L910-925).

## 4. Numbers and performance (direct feedback, exactly solvable bit-flip models)

Single qubit, Markovian bit-flip (dα/dt = -(κ+2λ)α + (κ+λ)):
- quasi-stationary α* = 1 - 1/(2 + r), r = κ/λ (L554-560);
- general bound (1-α)_max = γmax/κ, |β|_max = 2γmax/κ (L570-578).

Three-qubit bit-flip code, Markovian, r = κ/λ:
- weight outside code space b(t)+c(t) = 3/(4+r)(1 - e^{-(4+r)γt}) -> **3/(4+r) ~ 1/r** (L1043-1050);
- residual: the encoded qubit decays like bare bit-flip noise at rate (6/r)γ, i.e. ~r/6 reduction,
  perfect protection in the limit r -> ∞ (L1057-1077);
- **cost scales with code size**: uncorrected weight scales "approximately linearly with the number of
  qubits" and the required r likewise scales linearly in n (L1051-1055).

Non-Markovian (single bath qubit, H = γ X⊗X, R = κ/γ):
- α*_NM = 1 - 2/(4 + R²) (L1170-1176);
- "A remarkable difference ... the asymptotic weight outside the code space (1 - α*_NM) decreases with
  κ as **1/κ²**, whereas in the Markovian case the same quantity decreases as **1/κ**" (L1208-1211);
- for the 3-qubit code under the same non-Markovian bath, the effective error-rate reduction "increases
  quadratically as κ² in the non-Markovian case, whereas it increases only linearly as κ in the Markovian
  case" (L1401-1402); perturbation validity requires **γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt** (L1289, L1405) - i.e. the weak
  correction must resolve the Zeno time;
- Zeno bookkeeping: α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³) (L1091), and balancing 2√C√(1-α)Δt against
  κ(1-α)Δt gives 1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ² vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ (L1414-1449); same 1/κ² conclusion argued
  for general codes because each syndrome qubit in the encoded basis is Zeno-driven (L1450-1454).
- **Resource caveat**: ε ∝ g²τc², hence **κ ∝ g²τc** (L1462-1466). Shrinking τc to gain time
  resolution lowers κ; the quadratic gain can outweigh the linear loss, giving a "seemingly paradoxical"
  better performance at lower κ (L1468-1474). **This is the failure condition the director asked for.**

## 5. Answers to the four questions

**Q: Does continuous-time correction beat discrete-cycle correction, and under what conditions?**
The paper never benchmarks against a discrete-cycle protocol. What it shows is that CTQEC reaches perfect
protection in the limit of infinite correction rate (freezing), whereas a Markovian discrete cycle always
leaves O(1/r) residual uncorrectable weight that then produces logical errors at rate ~6γ/r (L1057-1077).
So the honest statement is: CTQEC's *floor* is lower and it avoids the dead time of a real correcting
operation, but there is no head-to-head comparison. CTQEC's advantage is real only if the weak operation is
genuinely continuous and cheap; the paper's own resource relation κ ∝ g²τc (L1466) says you pay for
faster resolution with lower correction rate.

**Q: Is the Zeno/freezing result a threshold result or something weaker?**
Much weaker, and it is *not* the foundation of the threshold theorem - the author says so explicitly. The
freezing argument is asymptotic and qualitative: correctable O(Δt) vs uncorrectable O(Δt²) (L112-119).
It has no code-size scaling, no logical error rate per cycle, no threshold constant, and no requirement
that errors be correctable in the discrete sense - it works even below the code's usual error radius
(indeed that is the point). It is also weaker in that it protects *quantum memory*: "So far, CTQEC has been
considered only as a method of protecting quantum memory. ... An important question in this respect is
whether CTQEC can be made fault tolerant" (L1503-1505). Fault tolerance assumes discrete transversal
operations; the author proposes looking for fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak*
operations, which is an open research programme. Treat the freezing/Zeno result as **an alternative
route to below-threshold behaviour, not a threshold theorem**.

**Q: What would a superconducting surface-code cycle have to look like to realize this?**
The paper contains no surface-code, superconducting, or hardware numbers at all; it is the director's
framing that a ~1 µs surface-code cycle is "coarse, not continuous". Within the paper's own framework
the requirements are explicit and demanding:
  (i) τc ≪ the Zeno/bath correlation time, and γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt (L1405), i.e. weak, *fast*,
      continuously repeated operations at a rate κ well above the noise rate;
  (ii) a physically available weak syndrome measurement - the paper's own realization is an ancilla
      coupled by HX = -X ⊗ Y, i.e. a two-qubit XX/YY-type interaction plus fast readout (L584-600);
  (iii) enough control bandwidth to keep r = κ/λ large *and* linear in n (L1051-1055), since surface
      codes have large n and many syndromes;
  (iv) locality: the author flags scalability with 1-2 qubit Hamiltonians as an open problem (L1498-1502).
A 1 µs round with measurement/reset latencies of comparable size is in the regime where the
continuous-time description is a poor fit, and where the paper's freezing argument buys nothing beyond
what ordinary threshold analysis already gives.

**Q: What is irrelevant to surface codes, and why should the director not over-claim?**
- No surface code is mentioned anywhere; the only codes analysed are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes
  (L1218-1220, L1237-1238). No rotated/unrotated layout, no lattice, no decoder, no threshold value.
- Noise models are independent bit-flips (Markovian) or a single Ising-type bath spin H = γX⊗X
  (L70, L1240-1250). No amplitude damping, no leakage, no measurement error, no crosstalk, no cosmic-ray
  or quasi-static 1/f drift - the dominant superconducting failure modes. The weakly non-Markovian
  bath is modeled as a *single* spin qubit, which is the most favourable possible limit.
- The ADL/feedback family is explicitly labelled heuristic (L155-162); the rigorous analysis exists only
  for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model (L19-23).
- CTQEC is memory protection only; fault tolerance is an open question raised by the author himself
  (L1503-1505).
- So the defensible statement is: "continuous-time correction provides a Zeno/freezing mechanism and,
  in non-Markovian noise, a 1/κ² rather than 1/κ residual-error law, which is a *complementary* argument
  for suppressing logical errors; it is not evidence about surface codes or superconducting thresholds."
  Any phrasing like "CTQEC shows surface codes can operate below threshold" would be an extrapolation the
  paper does not support.

## Bottom line for the synthesis
Use 1311.2485 for definitional and conceptual framing only: it defines continuous-time correction, gives the
freezing mechanism, the Markovian 1/κ vs non-Markovian 1/κ² contrast, and the honest statement that
continuous-time protection is not yet fault tolerant. Let res_2/res_3/res_4 carry the surface-code and
superconducting evidence.

1: # Shift 24 Summary - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)
2: 
3: ## Paper type
4: Theory/review chapter (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.). No experiments, no superconducting hardware,
5: no numerical fault-tolerance thresholds. It provides the *framework* for thinking about continuous
6: error correction, not a surface-code threshold result.
7: 
8: ## Core framework
9: - Discrete QEC formalism (CPTP noise map E + recovery R) idealizes both noise and correction as
10:   instantaneous discrete maps. In reality correction takes finite time, and with non-Markovian noise the
11:   system correlates with the environment, so effective maps between corrections need not even be CP.
12: - **CTQEC** = both noise and correction are continuous processes. Protected info lives in a *subsystem*
13:   (subsystem principle); the author works in an "encoded basis" where HA = logical factor, plus
14:   (n-r-1) syndrome qubit factors and r gauge qubits, for an [[n,1,r,d]] stabilizer code. This reduces
15:   multi-qubit QEC to the single-qubit problem of protecting a *known* state.
16: - **Paz-Zurek (PZ) quantum-jump model / direct feedback**: instantaneous full correction operations
17:   applied at random times with rate kappa. Master equation dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), with jump generator
18:   J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ. Physically: a stream of fresh ancillas weakly coupled and discarded, i.e. a
19:   *cooling* process that continuously pumps out entropy.
20: - **ADL scheme / indirect feedback**: continuous weak syndrome (stabilizer) measurement + feedback
21:   Hamiltonians whose strength λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ) is chosen to maximize instantaneous
22:   code-space fidelity. Weakened weak map: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) over time τc, giving κ = ε²/τc.
23:   Note in ADL, syndrome measurement is on the *code* stabilizers and correction acts back; in PZ the
24:   role of X and Z measurements/rotations is swapped relative to the intuitive picture.
25: 
26: ## Why continuous can beat discrete ("freezing")
27: Correctable error weight grows as O(Δt) per step while uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²).
28: So as correction becomes continuous, uncorrectable weight never accumulates: in the limit of infinite
29: correction rate the state *freezes*. The whole point is to suppress the second-order term.
30: 
31: ## Performance results (direct feedback, bit-flip codes, exactly solvable models)
32: - Markovian, 3-qubit bit-flip code, ratio r = κ/λ: weight outside code space → 3/(4+r) ~ 1/r.
33:   Encoded qubit then decays *inside* the code space like bare bit-flip noise at rate (6/r)γ, i.e.
34:   overall decoherence reduced by ~r/6. In the limit r -> ∞ protection is perfect for all times.
35: - Uncorrected weight scales roughly **linearly with the number of qubits** for fixed κ, and the κ needed
36:   to hold a given code-space overlap also scales ~linearly in n. Resource cost grows with code size.
37: - **Non-Markovian / Zeno regime (the headline result)**: for a system initially decoupled from its bath
38:   the fidelity is α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³). Balancing Zeno decay 2√C√(1-α)Δt against correction
39:   κ(1-α)Δt gives quasi-stationary equilibrium fidelity
40:       1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ²,   vs  1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ.
41:   So effective error rate reduction improves **quadratically (κ²)** in the non-Markovian case but only
42:   linearly (κ) in the Markovian case. Same 1/κ² scaling argued to hold for any code, since every
43:   syndrome qubit in the encoded basis undergoes Zeno-type evolution.
44: - Valid only in the regime γδt << 1 << κδt, i.e. the weak correction must be *faster than the Zeno
45:   time* to reveal the non-Markovian structure. Resource caveat: ε ∝ g²τc², so κ ∝ g²τc - shrinking
46:   τc to raise time resolution lowers κ. The paper notes the "paradoxical" possibility that a *lower*
47:   correction rate gives better performance because the quadratic κ² gain outweighs the linear loss.
48: - Error *prevention* (frequent syndrome measurement only, no correction) works only in the Zeno regime,
49:   fails under Markovian assumptions, but allows lower redundancy (4-qubit encoding of 1 qubit vs 3-qubit
50:   repetition for correction). Error correction therefore works in regimes where prevention fails, at the
51:   cost of higher redundancy and added correcting unitaries.
52: 
53: ## Relevance to the topic question (surface codes + superconducting qubits, below-threshold operation)
54: - CTQEC is an **alternative paradigm to discrete syndrome-extraction cycles**, not a threshold theorem.
55:   It shifts the burden from "error rate per cycle < threshold" to "correction rate κ and time resolution
56:   τc vs bath correlation time".
57: - Superconducting qubits plausibly sit in the favourable regime: long T1/T2 and quasi-static
58:   (1/f, telegraph) noise mean bath memory is *not* negligible, i.e. evolution is non-Markovian at long
59:   times - exactly where the Zeno/quadratic argument applies. This is the paper's strongest link to the
60:   question, but it is a qualitative argument, not evidence.
61: - The paper contains **no** statement about surface codes specifically, no comparison of rotated vs
62:   unrotated layouts, and no threshold numbers. Its examples are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes.
63: - Direct/indirect feedback schemes are called "largely heuristic" and "not thoroughly understood" by the
64:   author; the theoretical analysis is done only for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model.
65: - Author's own open question, directly relevant to the review: "whether CTQEC can be made fault
66:   tolerant" - FT theory assumes discrete transversal logical operations; he proposes looking for
67:   fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak* operations. Also open: scalability with
68:   local (1-2 qubit) Hamiltonians only, and whether an equilibrium-fidelity analogue exists for
69:   indirect feedback.
70: 
71: ## Key takeaways for the synthesis
72: 1. CTQEC offers a second, independent route to below-threshold operation: continuous weak
73:    measurement + feedback, where protection comes from a Zeno/freezing argument instead of a
74:    threshold theorem. Nothing here contradicts threshold theory; it is a different resource assumption.
75: 2. The single strongest quantitative claim: uncorrectable error weight 1/κ (Markovian) vs 1/κ²
76:    (non-Markovian/Zeno) - super-linear returns on correction rate, conditional on resolving the Zeno
77:    time scale.
78: 3. Honest limitation: this paper is theory from 2013 with toy codes; any claim that "CTQEC enables
79:    below-threshold surface codes on superconducting qubits" would be an extrapolation beyond the paper.

1: # Shift 22 Report - res_1 - Paper 1311.2485 "Continuous-time quantum error correction" (Oreshkov, 2013)
2: 
3: File: archive/quantum_error_correction/papers/1311.2485.txt (book chapter, Lidar & Brun eds.; line numbers below refer to this file).
4: Topic question: *Are surface codes with superconducting qubits capable of operating below fault-tolerant error thresholds?*
5: 
6: ## 1. Model (as requested)
7: 
8: - Standard discrete QEC represents noise and correction as discrete CPTP maps with correction applied
9:   after the noise; this is only an approximation, because a real correcting operation takes finite time and
10:   under non-Markovian dynamics the effective map between corrections need not be CP at all (L42-49).
11: - **CTQEC**: noise *and* correction are continuous. Protected information sits in a subsystem HA of
12:   HS = HA ⊗ HB ⊕ K; in the encoded basis for an [[n,1,r,d]] code, HS = HA ⊗(n-r-1 syndrome qubits)⊗(r gauge qubits)
13:   (L15, L195-206). Multi-qubit QEC then reduces to protecting a *known* single-qubit state.
14: - **PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback**: ρ -> (1-κdt)ρ + κdt R(ρ), master equation
15:   dρ/dt = L(ρ) + κJ(ρ), J(ρ) = R(ρ) - ρ (L60-73). Physical reading: coupling to a **stream of fresh
16:   ancillas** that continuously pump out accumulated entropy, i.e. a cooling process; also implementable by
17:   weak measurement + weak unitary (L103-108).
18: - **Weak map form**: ρ -> (1-ε²)ρ + ε²R(ρ) acting over a small but finite time τc, with effective
19:   rate **κ = ε²/τc** (L96-101).
20: - **ADL indirect feedback**: stochastic master equation with continuous weak measurement of the stabilizer
21:   generators Ml (Wiener-process jumps) plus correcting Hamiltonians Hr switched on with strength
22:   λr(ρ) = λ sgn Tr([Πc, Hr]ρ), chosen to maximize instantaneous code-space fidelity (L128-154).
23:   Weak X-measurement can be done with one ancilla: HX = -X ⊗ Y for time ~ε/2, then destructive ancilla
24:   measurement, outcome probabilities p± = ½(1 ± ε Tr(Xρ)) (L584-600).
25: 
26: ## 2. The "freezing" / Zeno argument
27: 
28: - Correctable error weight in a short step Δt is ∝ Δt, uncorrectable (higher-order) weight is O(Δt²);
29:   therefore continuously applied correction stops accumulation, and in the limit Δt -> 0 the state
30:   **freezes** (L112-119).
31: - Encoded-basis bound: ||dρA/dt|| ≤ B(1-α) + C√(α(1-α)), so keeping (1-α) small suppresses the
32:   accumulation rate of uncorrectable errors; CTQEC is thus "the goal of keeping every syndrome qubit close
33:   to |0>" (L340-364).
34: 
35: ## 3. Weak measurement + feedback, and the honest limitation (quoted)
36: 
37: - "All these schemes are to a large extent **heuristic**, and their workings are not thoroughly
38:   understood. The difficulty in rigorously motivating the construction of error-correction protocols based
39:   on weak measurements and feedback is that stochastic evolutions are generally too complicated to study
40:   analytically." (L155-162)
41: - Both schemes are related to known optimal single-qubit purification protocols: PZ ≈ fast average-fidelity
42:   protocol (measure X, rotate about Y), ADL ≈ fastest-average-time protocol (measure Z, rotate about X);
43:   optimality is claimed only w.r.t. these single-qubit criteria, not for their resource cost (L888-908).
44: - Retaining the measurement record would improve PZ only by O((1-α*_M)²) - i.e. PZ is "very close to
45:   optimal" in the regime where 1-α*_M is small, but only if the relation between measurement strength and
46:   correcting rotation (Eq. 36, L470-476) can be met (L910-925).
47: 
48: ## 4. Numbers and performance (direct feedback, exactly solvable bit-flip models)
49: 
50: Single qubit, Markovian bit-flip (dα/dt = -(κ+2λ)α + (κ+λ)):
51: - quasi-stationary α* = 1 - 1/(2 + r), r = κ/λ (L554-560);
52: - general bound (1-α)_max = γmax/κ, |β|_max = 2γmax/κ (L570-578).
53: 
54: Three-qubit bit-flip code, Markovian, r = κ/λ:
55: - weight outside code space b(t)+c(t) = 3/(4+r)(1 - e^{-(4+r)γt}) -> **3/(4+r) ~ 1/r** (L1043-1050);
56: - residual: the encoded qubit decays like bare bit-flip noise at rate (6/r)γ, i.e. ~r/6 reduction,
57:   perfect protection in the limit r -> ∞ (L1057-1077);
58: - **cost scales with code size**: uncorrected weight scales "approximately linearly with the number of
59:   qubits" and the required r likewise scales linearly in n (L1051-1055).
60: 
61: Non-Markovian (single bath qubit, H = γ X⊗X, R = κ/γ):
62: - α*_NM = 1 - 2/(4 + R²) (L1170-1176);
63: - "A remarkable difference ... the asymptotic weight outside the code space (1 - α*_NM) decreases with
64:   κ as **1/κ²**, whereas in the Markovian case the same quantity decreases as **1/κ**" (L1208-1211);
65: - for the 3-qubit code under the same non-Markovian bath, the effective error-rate reduction "increases
66:   quadratically as κ² in the non-Markovian case, whereas it increases only linearly as κ in the Markovian
67:   case" (L1401-1402); perturbation validity requires **γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt** (L1289, L1405) - i.e. the weak
68:   correction must resolve the Zeno time;
69: - Zeno bookkeeping: α(t) = 1 - Ct² + O(t³) (L1091), and balancing 2√C√(1-α)Δt against
70:   κ(1-α)Δt gives 1 - α*_NM ≈ 4C/κ² vs 1 - α*_M ∝ 1/κ (L1414-1449); same 1/κ² conclusion argued
71:   for general codes because each syndrome qubit in the encoded basis is Zeno-driven (L1450-1454).
72: - **Resource caveat**: ε ∝ g²τc², hence **κ ∝ g²τc** (L1462-1466). Shrinking τc to gain time
73:   resolution lowers κ; the quadratic gain can outweigh the linear loss, giving a "seemingly paradoxical"
74:   better performance at lower κ (L1468-1474). **This is the failure condition the director asked for.**
75: 
76: ## 5. Answers to the four questions
77: 
78: **Q: Does continuous-time correction beat discrete-cycle correction, and under what conditions?**
79: The paper never benchmarks against a discrete-cycle protocol. What it shows is that CTQEC reaches perfect
80: protection in the limit of infinite correction rate (freezing), whereas a Markovian discrete cycle always
81: leaves O(1/r) residual uncorrectable weight that then produces logical errors at rate ~6γ/r (L1057-1077).
82: So the honest statement is: CTQEC's *floor* is lower and it avoids the dead time of a real correcting
83: operation, but there is no head-to-head comparison. CTQEC's advantage is real only if the weak operation is
84: genuinely continuous and cheap; the paper's own resource relation κ ∝ g²τc (L1466) says you pay for
85: faster resolution with lower correction rate.
86: 
87: **Q: Is the Zeno/freezing result a threshold result or something weaker?**
88: Much weaker, and it is *not* the foundation of the threshold theorem - the author says so explicitly. The
89: freezing argument is asymptotic and qualitative: correctable O(Δt) vs uncorrectable O(Δt²) (L112-119).
90: It has no code-size scaling, no logical error rate per cycle, no threshold constant, and no requirement
91: that errors be correctable in the discrete sense - it works even below the code's usual error radius
92: (indeed that is the point). It is also weaker in that it protects *quantum memory*: "So far, CTQEC has been
93: considered only as a method of protecting quantum memory. ... An important question in this respect is
94: whether CTQEC can be made fault tolerant" (L1503-1505). Fault tolerance assumes discrete transversal
95: operations; the author proposes looking for fault-tolerant implementations of a universal set of *weak*
96: operations, which is an open research programme. Treat the freezing/Zeno result as **an alternative
97: route to below-threshold behaviour, not a threshold theorem**.
98: 
99: **Q: What would a superconducting surface-code cycle have to look like to realize this?**
100: The paper contains no surface-code, superconducting, or hardware numbers at all; it is the director's
101: framing that a ~1 µs surface-code cycle is "coarse, not continuous". Within the paper's own framework
102: the requirements are explicit and demanding:
103:   (i) τc ≪ the Zeno/bath correlation time, and γδt ≪ 1 ≪ κδt (L1405), i.e. weak, *fast*,
104:       continuously repeated operations at a rate κ well above the noise rate;
105:   (ii) a physically available weak syndrome measurement - the paper's own realization is an ancilla
106:       coupled by HX = -X ⊗ Y, i.e. a two-qubit XX/YY-type interaction plus fast readout (L584-600);
107:   (iii) enough control bandwidth to keep r = κ/λ large *and* linear in n (L1051-1055), since surface
108:       codes have large n and many syndromes;
109:   (iv) locality: the author flags scalability with 1-2 qubit Hamiltonians as an open problem (L1498-1502).
110: A 1 µs round with measurement/reset latencies of comparable size is in the regime where the
111: continuous-time description is a poor fit, and where the paper's freezing argument buys nothing beyond
112: what ordinary threshold analysis already gives.
113: 
114: **Q: What is irrelevant to surface codes, and why should the director not over-claim?**
115: - No surface code is mentioned anywhere; the only codes analysed are 1- and 3-qubit bit-flip codes
116:   (L1218-1220, L1237-1238). No rotated/unrotated layout, no lattice, no decoder, no threshold value.
117: - Noise models are independent bit-flips (Markovian) or a single Ising-type bath spin H = γX⊗X
118:   (L70, L1240-1250). No amplitude damping, no leakage, no measurement error, no crosstalk, no cosmic-ray
119:   or quasi-static 1/f drift - the dominant superconducting failure modes. The weakly non-Markovian
120:   bath is modeled as a *single* spin qubit, which is the most favourable possible limit.
121: - The ADL/feedback family is explicitly labelled heuristic (L155-162); the rigorous analysis exists only
122:   for the quantum-jump (direct feedback) model (L19-23).
123: - CTQEC is memory protection only; fault tolerance is an open question raised by the author himself
124:   (L1503-1505).
125: - So the defensible statement is: "continuous-time correction provides a Zeno/freezing mechanism and,
126:   in non-Markovian noise, a 1/κ² rather than 1/κ residual-error law, which is a *complementary* argument
127:   for suppressing logical errors; it is not evidence about surface codes or superconducting thresholds."
128:   Any phrasing like "CTQEC shows surface codes can operate below threshold" would be an extrapolation the
129:   paper does not support.
130: 
131: ## Bottom line for the synthesis
132: Use 1311.2485 for definitional and conceptual framing only: it defines continuous-time correction, gives the
133: freezing mechanism, the Markovian 1/κ vs non-Markovian 1/κ² contrast, and the honest statement that
134: continuous-time protection is not yet fault tolerant. Let res_2/res_3/res_4 carry the surface-code and
135: superconducting evidence.

  x (n-r-1) syndrome qubits x r gauge qubits for [[n,1,r,d]] code -> reduces QEC to protecting a
  known single-qubit state.
- Two schemes: PZ quantum-jump / direct feedback (dρ/dt = L(ρ)+κ(R(ρ)-ρ), fresh-ancilla cooling
  picture) and ADL indirect feedback (continuous weak stabilizer measurement + fidelity-maximizing
  feedback, κ = ε²/τc).
- Freezing: correctable error weight O(Δt), uncorrectable O(Δt²) -> uncorrectable weight does not
  accumulate as correction becomes continuous.
- 3-qubit bit-flip, Markovian, r=κ/λ: weight outside code space 3/(4+r) ~ 1/r; residual decay inside
  code space like bare bit-flip at rate 6γ/r.
- Cost scales ~linearly in number of qubits for fixed κ.
- Headline: non-Markovian Zeno regime gives quasi-stationary 1-α* ≈ 4C/κ² (quadratic) vs ∝1/κ
  (linear) for Markovian. Valid only if γδt << 1 << κδt, i.e. weak correction must resolve the Zeno
  time; κ ∝ g²τc so higher time resolution costs correction rate (possible "paradox" of better
  performance at lower κ).
- Error *prevention* (measurement only) works only in the Zeno regime, fails for Markovian, needs less
  redundancy (4-qubit encoding).

### Bearing on the review question (surface codes + superconducting qubits below threshold)
- CTQEC is an alternative to discrete syndrome cycles, not a threshold result; the paper gives no
  surface-code numbers, no threshold values, no rotated/unrotated comparison. Codes studied are 1- and
  3-qubit bit-flip.
- Superconducting relevance is a qualitative argument: long T1/T2 and quasi-static 1/f noise mean the
  bath memory is non-negligible, i.e. the Zeno/non-Markovian regime where the κ² law applies.
- Author's own open question: can CTQEC be made fault tolerant (FT assumes discrete transversal
  ops)? Also open: local-Hamiltonian scalability, equilibrium fidelity for indirect feedback.
- Caution for synthesis: do not let the director claim CTQEC "proves" below-threshold surface-code

23:Abstract
24:We propose quaternion-based strategies for quantum error correction by extending quantum mechanics into
25:quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Building on the properties of quaternionic quantum states, we define quaternionic
26:analogues of Pauli operators and quantum gates, ensuring inner product preservation and Hilbert space condi-
27:tions. A simple encoding scheme maps logical qubits into quaternionic systems, introducing natural redundancy
28:and enhanced resilience against noise. We construct a quaternionic extension of the five-qubit code, introducing
29:a framework of 15 syndrome measurements to detect quaternionic errors, including quaternionically rotated error
30:components. Numerical estimates show that the quaternionic five-qubit code achieves a logical error threshold
31:of approximately pth ≈0.015, demonstrating improved performance compared to the standard complex-valued
32:code. These results suggest a new pathway for quantum error correction in high-noise environments, leveraging
33:the richer structure of quaternionic quantum mechanics to improve fault tolerance.

35:Introduction
36:Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computing, protecting fragile
37:quantum states from errors such as bit flips, phase flips, and amplitude damping [1, 2]. Logical qubits are typically
38:formed by entangling multiple physical qubits using codes such as the surface code [3] being a widely studied
39:example. Recent advances include the use of reconfigurable atom arrays to build logical quantum processors [4],
40:where neutral atoms serve as physical qubits. This work demonstrated scalable improvements by increasing the
41:surface code distance from d = 3 to d = 7. Similarly, for superconducting processor achieved below-threshold
42:error correction, showing a logical error suppression factor of λ = 2.14 ± 0.02 by increasing the code distance [5].
43:These developments represent key steps toward scalable quantum computation.
44:Quaternion quantum mechanics (QQM) extends standard quantum mechanics by using quaternions instead
45:of complex numbers. Yang [6] showed that, in a generalized quantum framework, pure states can be uniquely
46:represented as rays in a vector space. This requires the Hilbert space H to be defined in one of the three number
47:fields [7]:
48:• R: real numbers
49:1
50:arXiv:2504.19833v1  [quant-ph]  28 Apr 2025
51:
52:• C: complex numbers
53:• H: quaternions
54:Quaternions were introduced as a natural extension of complex numbers into four dimensions. Quaternions,
55:introduced by Hamilton [8], extend complex numbers to four dimensions and are defined asq = w + xi + yj + zk,
56:where imaginary units satisfy the relations: i2 = j2 = k2 = ijk = −1, to represent quantum states and
57:operators [9]. Here q ∈H, w, x, y, z ∈R and xi + yj + zk is a vector.
58:Adler [10] developed a complete formulation of quantum mechanics in quaternionic Hilbert spaces, aiming
59:for a possible unification with gravity. Later, Danielewski and Sapa [7] derived QQM from a Cauchy elastic
60:continuum model, proposing it as a physically motivated alternative. Their work introduces quaternionic versions
61:of non-relativistic and relativistic wave equations, but does not address QEC. Although QQM is theoretically
62:well established, its application to QEC remains largely unexplored. Existing research on surface codes and color
63:codes [3], and on continuous-variable systems [11], does not consider quaternionic frameworks. In principle, QEC
64:methods such as logical encoding and syndrome measurement can be extended to quaternionic Hilbert spaces,
65:which satisfy the same core postulates as complex ones. However, Vlasov [12] showed that certain QEC schemes
66:fail in standard complex quantum mechanics but succeed in real and quaternionic cases. Adler also suggested
67:the feasibility of quaternionic quantum field theories [13]. Whether quaternions can offer practical advantages
68:for QEC, such as improved error detection or fault tolerance, remains an open question.
69:In this work, we investigate the mathematical foundations and applications of quaternionic quantum mechan-
70:ics (QQM) for quantum error correction. By leveraging the richer algebraic structure of quaternions, we define
71:quaternionic analogues of quantum gates and Pauli operators, and construct new error correction schemes. In par-
72:ticular, we extend the five-qubit code into a quaternionic Hilbert space, introducing 15 syndrome measurements
73:to detect quaternionic errors. We also compare the logical error performance of the standard and quaternionic
74:codes, showing improved resilience against noise and decoherence. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2
75:introduces the mathematical foundations of QQM, emphasizing quaternion algebra in error detection. Section 3
76:presents quaternionic Pauli-like operators, error classification, and syndrome mapping. Section 4 compares the
77:logical error rates of the standard and quaternion-extended five-qubit codes. Section 5 concludes with a summary
78:and future directions.

Method: Sparse Mamba Decoder
A physical Pauli error on a data qubit persists until corrected; left in place, it would cause its
adjacent stabilizers to fire every subsequent round, producing a dense “always-on” syndrome. The
detection event di,t = si,t ⊕si,t−1 converts this persistent state into a sparse spacetime signal:
each error contributes detection events only at the endpoints of its trajectory in spacetime,
where it appears and where it is cancelled. This is the structural reason the syndrome volume is
overwhelmingly zero at physical error rates of interest.

contains (d2 −1) × R entries, but the expected number of active detection events is

20:    - Properties of retrieval heads:
21:      - Universal: all long-context capable models have them
22:      - Sparse: <5% of attention heads are retrieval heads
23:      - Intrinsic: exist in base models pretrained with short context; same heads used after context extension
24:      - Dynamically activated: strongest heads always active; weaker heads context-dependent
25:      - Causal: pruning retrieval heads → hallucination; pruning random heads → no effect
26:    - Retrieval heads critical for:
27:      - Needle-in-a-Haystack (factuality)
28:      - Extractive QA (document QA)

59: 1. **2503.03213: "Convergence Rates for Softmax Gating Mixture of Experts"** (arXiv 2025, Nguyen, Ho, Rinaldo)
60:    - Theoretical analysis of MoE convergence rates under softmax gating, dense-to-sparse gating, and hierarchical MoE
61:    - Key findings:
62:      - **Strong identifiability condition**: Expert functions must have linearly independent derivatives (satisfied by 2-layer FFNs with GELU/sigmoid/tanh; violated by linear experts)
63:      - **Convergence rates**: 
64:        - Strongly identifiable experts (FFNs): Polynomial rates Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ²) exactly-specified, Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ⁴) over-specified
65:        - Linear experts: Slower than any polynomial Oₚ(1/log^λ(n)) - requires exponential data O(exp(ε⁻¹ᐟˡ))
66:      - **Parameter interaction**: Linear experts create PDE coupling gating params ω and expert params (a,b): ∂²F/∂ω∂b = ∂F/∂a
67:      - **Dense-to-sparse gating**: Linear router induces temperature-gating interaction slowing convergence even for FFN experts; fix = algebraically independent router (MLP + non-linearity)
68:      - **HMoE**: Same pattern - strongly identifiable experts → polynomial rates; linear experts → exponential rates with cross-level contamination
69:      - **Practical implications**: (i) Use FFN experts (standard in Transformers), not linear; (ii) For dense-to-sparse gating, use non-linear router
70: 
71: ### Key Synthesis Points:
72: - **Theoretical foundation for compute efficiency**: Polynomial convergence rates justify that sparse MoE with proper architecture (FFN experts, softmax gating) can match dense models at matched training compute
73: - **Architecture is critical**: The standard Transformer MoE design (FFN experts + softmax gating) falls exactly in the "strongly identifiable" regime with fast polynomial rates
74: - **Explains empirical success**: Mixtral, DeepSeekMoE etc. work because they use architectures that satisfy the strong identifiability condition
75: - **Connects to res_1's paper (2402.14800)**: Theory explains why expert pruning/skipping works - experts are statistically identifiable and learnable, so some can be pruned without catastrophic loss

13: The theory of quantum error correction was established more than a decade ago as the primary
14: tool for ﬁghting decoherence in quantum information processing [1, 2, 3, 4]. Although great progress
15: has already been made in this ﬁeld, limited methods are available in constructing new quantum error
16: correction codes from old codes. Here we exhibit a simple and general method to construct new
17: quantum error correction codes by nesting certain quantum codes together. The problem of ﬁnding
18: long quantum error correction codes is reduced to that of searching several short length quantum
19: codes with certain properties. Our method works for all length and all distance codes, and is quite
20: eﬃcient to construct optimal or near optimal codes. Two main known methods in constructing new
21: codes from old codes in quantum error-correction theory, the concatenating and pasting, can be
22: understood in the framework of nested quantum error correction codes.

59: Introduction
60: Quantum error-correcting codes (QECCs) have turned out to have many applications; but their
61: primary purpose, of course, is to protect quantum information from noise. This need manifests
62: itself in two rather different situations. The ﬁrst is in quantum computing. The bits in a quantum
63: computer are subject to noise due both to imprecision in the operations (or gates) and to interac-
64: tions with the external environment. They undergo errors when they are acted upon, and when
65: they are just being stored (though hopefully not at the same rate). All the qubits in the computer
66: must be kept error-free long enough for the computation to be completed. This is the principle of
67: fault-tolerance.
68: A rather different situation occurs in quantum communication. Here, the sender and receiver
69: (Alice and Bob) are assumed to be physically separated, and the qubits travel from the sender
70: to the receiver over a (presumably noisy) channel. This channel is assumed to be the dominant
71: source of errors. While the qubits may undergo processing before and after transmission, errors
72: during this processing are considered negligible compared to the channel errors. This picture of
73: transmission through a channel is very close to the picture underlying classical information theory.
74: The types of codes that are of interest in quantum computation and quantum communication
75: may be quite different. In computation, reliability is key. Therefore, codes with a high distance
76: (such as concatenated codes) are used. Also, the choice of code may be highly constrained in
77: other ways: for instance, it is very important that the codes allow efﬁcient circuits for encoded
78: logic gates (such as the transversal gates allowed by the Steane code). The more efﬁcient these
79: circuits, the better the fault-tolerant threshold. (See [LB13, chapter 5] for a fuller discussion of
80: this.)
81: By contrast, in communication one often imagines sending a very large number of quantum
82: bits, perhaps even a continuous stream of qubits (as in the convolutional codes of [LB13, chapter
83: 9]). Here, one is generally trying to maximize the rate of transmission, often by encoding many
84: qubits into a large block, within the constraint of a low error probability for the block. In the
85: asymptotic limit, one would like to achieve the actual capacity of the channel—the maximum rate
86: of communication possible.
87: Because the sender and receiver are separated, joint unitary transformations are impossible.
88: However, they might be able to draw on other resources, such as extra classical communication,
89: pre-shared randomness, or pre-shared entanglement. In this chapter we study the use of pre-
90: shared entanglement in quantum communication, and how we can design QECCs that use entan-
91: glement to boost either the rate of communication or the number of errors that can be corrected.
92: Codes that use pre-shared entanglement are called entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting
93: codes (EAQECCs). We will study a large class of these codes that generalizes the usual stabilizer
94: formalism from [LB13, chapter 2]. We will also see how these codes can readily be constructed
95: from classical linear codes, and how they can be useful tools in building standard QECCs.
96: 1.1
97: Entanglement-assisted codes
98: In a standard QECC, the encoding operation proceeds in two steps. First, to the quantum state |ψ⟩
99: of k qubits that one wishes to encode, one appends some number of ancilla qubits in a standard
100: state (usually |0⟩), and then applies an encoding unitary Uenc:
101: |ψ⟩→|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k →|ΨL⟩= Uenc|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k,
102: (1)
103: where |ΨL⟩is the encoded or logical state. The systems in states |ψ⟩and |0⟩are initially in the
104: possession of Alice, the sender. The encoding unitary acts on the space of the input qubits and
105: 1
106: 
107: ancillas together.
108: In an EAQECC, one can append not only ancillas, but also ebits, before doing the encoding
109: unitary:
110: |ψ⟩→|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k−c ⊗|Φ+⟩⊗c
111: AB →(Uenc ⊗ˆIB)|ψ⟩⊗|0⟩⊗n−k ⊗|Φ+⟩⊗c
112: AB.
113: (2)
114: The states |Φ+⟩AB are EPR pairs shared between the sender (Alice) and the receiver (Bob). The
115: encoding operation Uenc acts on the qubits in Alice’s possession; we write (Uenc ⊗ˆIB) above to
116: indicate that the encoding acts as the identity on Bob’s halves of the ebits. Obviously, in order to
117: append c ebits to the information qubits, Alice and Bob must have c ebits of pre-shared entangle-
118: ment. After Alice does the encoding, all of her qubits are sent through the channel, including the
119: c halves of ebits. So this procedure consumes c ebits of preshared entanglement.
120: Figure 1: Schematic structure of an entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting code. Alice
121: and Bob share ebits that Alice uses in encoding her quantum information; these qubits all pass
122: through the noisy channel, but Bob’s halves of the initial ebits do not.
123: However, note that Bob’s halves of the c ebits do not pass through the channel. These ebits
124: were prepared ahead of time, by entanglement distillation or a similar procedure (see [BBP+96,
125: BDSW96] and [LB13, chapter 22]). Because Bob’s qubits do not pass through the channel, they are
126: assumed to be error-free.
127: Why should we wish to use shared entanglement in our encoding? There are two ways to see
128: how this could enhance the power of the code. First, we can compare EAQECCs to teleportation. In
129: teleportation, an ebit can be used (in combination with classical communication) to transmit one
130: qubit perfectly from the sender to the receiver. We might therefore expect that making use of ebits
131: in error-correction could boost the rate of transmission.
132: Second, we can compare EAQECCs to superdense coding. In superdense coding, by using an
133: ebit the sender can send two classical bits of information to the receiver by means of a single
134: qubit. Each ancilla bit in a standard QECC can be thought of as holding one classical bit of infor-
135: mation about any errors that have occurred. Replacing an ancilla with one half of an ebit could,
136: in principle, allow the receiver to extract two bits of classical information about the errors; with
137: more information, more errors can be corrected. We shall see, in the constructions that follow,
138: that we can think of the enhanced power of EAQECCs in both of these ways, but the superdense
139: coding interpretation is more often the best ﬁt. EAQECCs can achieve some communication tasks
140: with fewer resources (or less chance of error) than would be needed by a standard QECC plus
141: teleportation [HW10b].
142: The possibility of constructing entanglement-assisted codes was suggested in [BDSW96], though
143: no practical codes were constructed. From asymptotic results in quantum information theory, we
144: know that having pre-shared entanglement allows an enhanced rate of quantum communication
145: 2
146: 
147: between a sender and receiver [DHW04, DHW08]. EAQECCs are the ﬁnite-length realization
148: of this idea. By constructing larger and larger code blocks, in principle one can approach the
149: entanglement-assisted quantum capacity of the channel. An example of such a code was con-
150: structed by Bowen in [Bow02], starting from a standard stabilizer QECC (see [LB13, chapter 2]). In
151: [BDH06, BDH14, HDB07] an essentially complete theory of stabilizer EAQECCs was constructed.
152: That is the theory presented in this chapter.
153: Note, however, that in general shared entanglement does not come for free: entanglement
154: must be established between the sender and receiver, and this in general requires the use of quan-
155: tum channels, and perhaps additional entanglement puriﬁcation. Therefore, EAQECCs do not
156: outperform standard quantum codes under all circumstances. The enhanced communication rates
157: that come from the use of entanglement must be paid for in establishing the entanglement in the
158: ﬁrst place. For many purposes, what is important is the net rate of the code: the number of qubits
159: transmitted minus the number of ebits consumed. With this measure, EAQECCs tend to perform
160: about the same as standard codes. Even in this case, though, EAQECCs sometimes have advan-
161: tages: as we shall see, there are many fewer restrictions on the construction of EAQECCs than
162: standard codes.

917: General codes and code parameters
918: The canonical code described above is not very useful for actual error correction. It corrects a
919: set of highly nonlocal errors, of a type that are not likely to occur in reality. However, it is very
920: helpful in clarifying how the process of error correction works, and the role of the resources used
921: in encoding. Each added ancilla can contain, in principle, one bit of information about any errors
922: that occur. Each shared ebit between the sender and receiver can contain two bits of information
923: about errors. This information about the errors is retrieved by measuring the stabilizer generators.
924: After Alice’s qubits have passed through the channel, Bob has all the qubits and can perform these
925: measurements.
926: A general EAQECC has exactly the same algebraic structure as the canonical code. The en-
927: coded state, before going through the channel, has c ebits of entanglement with the c qubits on
928: 12
