62:      - **Strong identifiability condition**: Expert functions must have linearly independent derivatives (satisfied by 2-layer FFNs with GELU/sigmoid/tanh; violated by linear experts)
63:      - **Convergence rates**: 
64:        - Strongly identifiable experts (FFNs): Polynomial rates Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ²) exactly-specified, Oₚ([log(n)/n]¹ᐟ⁴) over-specified
65:        - Linear experts: Slower than any polynomial Oₚ(1/log^λ(n)) - requires exponential data O(exp(ε⁻¹ᐟˡ))
66:      - **Parameter interaction**: Linear experts create PDE coupling gating params ω and expert params (a,b): ∂²F/∂ω∂b = ∂F/∂a
67:      - **Dense-to-sparse gating**: Linear router induces temperature-gating interaction slowing convergence even for FFN experts; fix = algebraically independent router (MLP + non-linearity)
68:      - **HMoE**: Same pattern - strongly identifiable experts → polynomial rates; linear experts → exponential rates with cross-level contamination

20: Abstract
21: Despite the recent progress in long-context large language models (LLMs), it re-
22: mains elusive how these transformer-based language models acquire the capability
23: to retrieve relevant information from arbitrary locations within the long context.
24: This paper aims to address this question. Our systematic investigation across 4
25: model families, 6 model scales, and 3 types of finetuning reveals that a special
26: type of attention heads are largely responsible for retrieving relevant information
27: from long context, which we dub retrieval heads. We identify important and
28: intriguing properties of retrieval heads: (1) universal: all the explored models
29: with long-context capability have a set of retrieval heads; (2) sparse: only a small
30: portion (less than 5%) of the attention heads are retrieval. (3) intrinsic: retrieval
31: heads already exist in models pretrained with short context. When extending
32: the context length to 32-128K by continual pretraining, it is still the same set of
33: heads that perform information retrieval. (4) dynamically activated: take Llama-2
34: 7B for example, 12 retrieval heads always attend to the required information no
35: matter how the context is changed. The rest of the retrieval heads are activated in
36: different contexts. (5) causal: completely pruning retrieval heads leads to failure in
37: retrieving relevant information and results in hallucination, while pruning random
38: non-retrieval heads does not affect the model’s retrieval ability. We further show
39: that retrieval heads strongly influence chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, where the
40: model needs to frequently refer back the question and previously-generated context.
41: Conversely, tasks where the model directly generates the answer using its intrinsic
42: knowledge are less impacted by masking out retrieval heads. These observations
43: collectively explain which internal part of the model seeks information from the
44: input tokens. We believe our insights on retrieval heads foster future research on
45: reducing hallucination, improving reasoning, and compressing the KV cache.
46: 1
47: Introduction
48: This work studies the internal mechanism of how long-context language models can utilize infor-
49: mation at arbitrary locations within the input. Recent advances in long-context language model-
50: ing [1, 20, 6] show inspiring results, particularly on the Needle-in-a-Haystack test [14], which asks

80: The discovery of the retrieval head is motivated by the question of what the attention mechanism
81: is doing when the model can or cannot find the given needle. We take important inspiration from
82: two existing works: the CopyNet [10] and the Induction Head [19]. The CopyNet is essentially a
83: single-layer, single-head attention mechanism in the age of RNNs that copy-paste tokens from the
84: input to the output. Induction Heads [19] are special heads within a multi-layer, multi-head attention
85: network that implements an implicit program induction algorithm. Combining the observation from
86: the two works, we natually hypothesize that, just like induction heads are accountable for in-context
87: learning, there might exist special heads that are accountable for information retrieval and implement
88: a conditional copy-paste algorithm.

92: any scale (6B, 14B, and 34B and 8×7B), either base or chat, either dense or MoE, as long as the
93: model can precisely recite the input information, they have a small number of retrieval heads (Fig. 1);
94: (2) they are intrinsic: the base model (e.g., LLaMA2 base) already contains retrieval heads (as a

INTRODUCTION
Long-context capability is becoming a standard for Large Language Models (LLMs), with many
of them supporting context windows ranging from 128K to 10M tokens (Reid et al., 2024; Lieber
et al., 2024; Dubey et al., 2024; Gradient, 2024). These extended context windows unlock a wide
range of real-world applications, such as repository-level code understanding and debugging (Bairi
et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024c; Jimenez et al., 2024), long-document question-
answering (Caciularu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b), many-shot in-context learning (Agarwal et al.,
2024), and long-generation Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning (OpenAI, 2024a; Snell et al., 2024).
Despite the benefit, Long-context inputs also present unique challenges for LLM inference due to high
computational costs and memory demands. This has led to the development of efficient long-context
solutions leveraging sparsity in various stage of KV cache. In this paper, we introduce an unified
analysis framework for efficient long-context methods in a KV cache centric perspective, consisting
of the four essential stages of KV cache: 1) KV cache generation, 2) KV cache compression, 3) KV
cache retrieval, and 4) KV cache loading. First, KV cache generation, aka prefilling, processes
the input prompt and produce the KV cache to be used in decoding. In this stage, sparse attention
methods are proposed to reduce the complexity of the attention operation (Child et al., 2019; Beltagy
et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2024). Second, KV cache compression techniques prune KV states to
reduce the memory costs in decoding (Xiao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024c). Third, KV cache retrieval
aims to skip KV cache generation of an incoming request, and instead retrieves and reuses KV cache
from history KV cache pool for more efficient inference (Zheng et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024a). At
last, KV cache loading aims to load only partial of the KV cache for each decoding step to save the
memory and computing cost (Tang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b).
However, these methods are only evaluated on single-request benchmarks (Hsieh et al., 2024; Zhang
et al., 2024a; Kamradt, 2023; Li et al., 2024a), which fail to covers the full lifecycle of KV cache in real
applications. Typically, real-world applications often require reusing prompt memory (i.e., KV cache)
and involving multiple requests or multi-round interactions (Qin et al., 2025). The reuse of KV cache,
known as prefix caching, is already a crucial component in popular inference frameworks (Zheng
et al., 2024; vLLM, 2024) and used by LLM providers (Gemini, 2024; Claude, 2024; OpenAI, 2024b;
Azure, 2024). In addition, testing with multiple requests is especially crucial for the long-context
methods mentioned earlier, as many achieve efficiency through query-conditioned compression. For
instance, Arora et al. (2024) reports that Mamba’s compression of previous information based on the
current query can prevent it from answering follow-up queries.
To address this gap, we introduce SCBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate efficient long-context
methods that covers the full lifecycle of KV cache in real-world scenarios, particularly for shared
context and multi-round interactions where KV Cache is reused for follow-up queries. As shown in
Fig. 2b, SCBench assesses four key long-context abilities across 12 tasks with two shared context
modes. Each test example includes a shared context and multiple follow-up queries. The four
long-context capabilities and their corresponding tasks are:

508: test. When the model can retrieve the needle, retrieval heads are always activated. When the model
509: cannot retrieve the needle and hallucinate instead, retrieval heads are either partially activated or not

588: Now we study how retrieval heads influence more realistic tasks beyond Needle-in-a-Haystack. We
589: use extractive QA as a test bed, as common usecase of long-context model where the user typically

591: specific information within the document. To make sure the knowledge being asked does not exist
592: in the model’s internal knowledge, we synthesize an extractive QA dataset by selecting a set of

Our experimental results reveal the following insights: 1) Sub-O(n) memory is almost infeasible in
multi-turn decoding, as shown in Fig. 3. Sparse decoding methods (sub-O(n) memory) perform
well on the first query but lose accuracy in subsequent requests. In contrast, sparse encoding
methods (O(n) memory with O(n2) computation during pre-filling) can approximate full attention
accuracy across multiple queries. 2) Task performance declines at varying rates, as illustrated in
Fig. 3b. Sparse KV cache methods excel in tasks requiring global information, while O(n) memory
is crucial for exact match retrieval tasks. 3) All long-context methods degrade as the budget
decreases, as shown in Fig. 4. However, sub-O(n) memory methods experience a sharp performance
drop at a 1/4 compression rate. Methods like RetrievalAttention and KIVI, which maintain O(n)
memory with sparse decoding, sustain higher performance even under higher compression rates.
4) Long-generation scenarios exhibit distribution shift issues. As generation length and the
number of rounds increase, the KV cache’s importance distribution changes significantly. This
out-of-distribution (OOD) issue leads to performance degradation, even for O(n) memory methods
like RetrievalAttention, as shown in Fig. 3.

across 12 subtasks in various domains.

evaluate 13 different long-context methods (including our newly proposed sparse attention

EXPERIMENTS & RESULTS
Models & Implementation Details
We selected six open-source long-context LLMs: Llama-
3.1-8B/70B (Dubey et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-72B/32B (Team, 2024), Llama-3-8B-262K (Gradient,
2024), and GLM-4-9B-1M (GLM et al., 2024), along with two gated linear models: Codestal Mamba
7B (team, 2024) and Jamba-1.5-Mini (Lieber et al., 2024). This selection covers Transformer, SSMs,
and SSM-Attention Hybrid models, representing leading open-source long-context LLMs. For
stability, all experiments used greedy decoding in BFloat16 on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We
evaluated models via HuggingFace or vLLM with FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024) and leveraged
MInference (Jiang et al., 2024) to reduce GPU memory overhead. More details on these models and
infrastructure are in §D.1.
Long-Context Method Details
We evaluated eight long-context solution categories on our bench-
mark: Gated Linear RNNs (e.g., Codestral-Mamba), SSM-Attention hybrids (e.g., Jamba), sparse
attention, KV cache dropping, prompt compression, KV cache quantization, retrieval, and loading,
as detailed in Table 1. All methods were tested on Transformer-based long-context LLMs, except
Codestral-Mamba and Jamba. We also report KV cache size, pre-filling and decoding complexity,
and whether efficient operations are applied (details in §2). More details are shown in §D.2.
Main Results
Tables 4, 10, and Fig. 9 present the performance of various long-context methods
across tasks and shared context modes in different base LLMs. Key findings include: 1) In retrieval
tasks, most methods, except MInference, perform poorly, especially in exact retrieval tasks like string
matching. 2) Sparse attention outperforms sparse decoding as request rounds increase, with A-shape
showing the greatest improvement. Tri-shape, which adds dense bottom query tokens to A-shape,
enhances first-round performance but has little effect on later rounds. It generalizes well across
tasks, ranking second only to MInference. Our analysis indicates that Tri-shape improves first-turn
instruction-following, boosting overall performance, while A-shape disrupts instruction information,
causing random outputs (Table 17). 3) KV cache compression methods generally underperform in
shared scenarios, offering only minor benefits in the first round. 4) Prompt compression improves
global information tasks like many-shot ICL but significantly degrades retrieval-related performance.
5) SSM-Attention hybrids perform well in single-turn interactions but suffer accuracy drops in
multi-turn tasks, especially in RepoQA and Math. Gated Linear RNN models struggle in shared
context modes.

781: Conclusions
782: This paper discovers retrieval heads, a special set of attention heads that are responsible for im-
783: plementing the conditional copy algorithm and redirect information from the input to the output.

785: in-a-Haystack test, and their activation explains why a language model is faithful to the input or
786: hallucinate. Compared to non-retrieval heads, retrieval heads have a stronger influence on downstream
787: tasks that require the model to precisely recall the input information, either in extractive question
788: answering or chain-of-thought reasoning. We believe this work will foster future research on reducing

14: Recent advances have extended the context window of frontier LLMs dramatically,
15: from a few thousand tokens up to millions, enabling entire books and codebases
16: to fit into context. However, the compute costs of inferencing long-context LLMs
17: are massive and often prohibitive in practice. RAG offers an efficient and effective
18: alternative: retrieve and process only the subset of the context most important for
19: the current task. Although promising, recent work applying RAG to long-context
20: tasks has two core limitations: 1) there has been little focus on making the RAG
21: pipeline compute efficient, and 2) such works only test on simple QA tasks, and
22: their performance on more challenging tasks is unclear. To address this, we develop
23: an algorithm based on PageRank, a graph-based retrieval algorithm, which we call
24: mixture-of-PageRanks (MixPR). MixPR uses a mixture of PageRank-based graph-
25: retrieval algorithms implemented using sparse matrices for efficent, cheap retrieval
26: that can deal with a variety of complex tasks. Our MixPR retriever achieves state-of-
27: the-art results across a wide range of long-context benchmark tasks, outperforming
28: both existing RAG methods, specialized retrieval architectures, and long-context
29: LLMs despite being far more compute efficient. Due to using sparse embeddings,
30: our retriever is extremely compute efficient, capable of embedding and retrieving
31: millions of tokens within a few seconds and runs entirely on CPU.1

41: Introduction
42: Frontier long-context LLMs are now capable of processing hundreds of thousands, even millions,
43: of tokens directly in the prompt. This allows LLMs to reason over long documents like entire
44: books, code-bases, and collections of articles. However, processing long-contexts is extremely
45: computationally expensive due both to the quadratic cost of attention and the memory cost of storing
46: a large KV-cache. This makes inferencing long-context models challenging in practice and often
47: impossible on compute-limited devices. Additionally, compute costs of long-context models also
48: make API calls highly expensive. Moreover, it is unclear whether these increased compute costs are
49: always worth it, given that recent benchmarks testing long-context recall and reasoning show that
50: SOTA LLMs often struggle to perform a variety of tasks for long input lengths (e.g., [17, 22]).
51: One significantly cheaper and more extendable alternative to full-context processing is retrieval
52: augmented generation (RAG). The idea here is to first store a long context in a vector database at
53: test-time, then a retrieval algorithm scans the database and returns only the elements that are most
54: relevant to the LLM. By only inputting a small portion of the context, one can drastically reduce
55: the compute cost and latency of LLM inference. Further, it has been commonly observed that LLM
56: performance tends to improve when irrelevant and/or distracting information is removed from (e.g.,
57: [23]), suggesting RAG could actually improve performance over full-context processing.
58: Though promising, recent work developing RAG algorithms for long-context tasks have several
59: limitations: Firstly, these works (e.g., [42, 45]) tend to focus on simple QA style tasks, even though
60: many long context tasks (e.g., reasoning, summarization) that frontier LLMs are capable of are
61: much more complex than this. Secondly, previous works do not analyze the computional costs of
62: the retriever which are themselves often significant. RAG in long-context scenarios operates in a
63: different paradigm than standard RAG. For long-context, RAG must generate text chunk embeddings
64: at test-time for each new input, compared to standard RAG which typically assumes the LLM has
65: access to a pre-embedded database, created prior to test-time. While RAG will generally reduce
66: the compute cost of LLM inference compared to long-context LLM inference, the RAG pipeline
67: itself (chunking, embedding, database entry, and retrieval) can often be slow or expensive enough to
68: preclude real-time embedding and retrieval at test time.
69: In this paper, we go beyond previous work by making significant progress on both of these issues
70: simultaneously. We introduce both a novel retrieval algorithm which can achieve SOTA performance

99: accurately to the query given the document. Such benchmarks are meant to simulate the scenario
100: where a long input is given to the LLM for processing at test time.
101: Two Challenges for the RAG Approach to Long-Contexts Tasks. RAG models are commonly
102: used for knowledge retrieval settings. However, there are (at least) two reasons why utilizing RAG
103: effectively in long-context tasks is more difficult than knowledge retrieval tasks.
104: 1. The Challenging Retrieval Problem. Standard RAG methods, that utilize a nearest
105: neighbor search over a vector database, work well on standard QA and retrieval tasks:
106: the model is queried about some content X, text chunks most related to X are efficiently
107: retrieved, then utilized by the LLM to accurately respond to the query. However, many
108: long-context tasks are more complex than single step retrieval and require linking together
109: diverse elements across the whole input document, e.g., reasoning, reading comprehension,
110: etc. Further, these elements may not be directly related to the content of the query, as we see
111: with summarization tasks, and standard retrieval methods do not account for this.
112: 2. The Compute Cost Problem. Common RAG algorithms chunk text and embed the chunks
113: in a vector database, usually using a transformer-based embedding model. In the typical RAG
114: setting, i.e., knowledge retrieval, the embedding of a database happens before deployment,
115: then during deployment, the database is repeatedly and efficiently searched as queries are
116: presented. Long context tasks, on the other hand, require processing a query and a long
117: input document (e.g., an entire book along with questions) at test time, which means the
118: embedding step, in addition to the retrieval step, must be completed at test time. Since in
119: many applications the user expects an immediate response, the embedding process must be
120: fast to be practically useful. However, the process of embedding a long list of text chunks
121: using standard transformer-based embedders can be slow, especially in compute constrained
122: settings.

124: tasks more difficult and complex than single-step retrieval and will do so in a fast, compute efficient

### Stated Basis: The Retrieval-Head Mechanism

The authors' logical chain (explicit in lines 766-767):
1. Retrieval heads implement conditional copy-paste from input to output
2. They require access to the **full KV cache** to "precisely utilize input information at arbitrary location"
3. SSMs have a **fixed-size recurrent state** (no addressable KV cache)
4. ⇒ No retrieval heads in this sense ⇒ needle retrieval should fail

- [9] Mamba (linear-time sequence modeling with selective state spaces, arXiv:2312.00752)

- It is a **mechanistic/interpretability paper**, not a benchmark

## PART A — SCBench (2412.10319), ICLR 2025, Microsoft

### A1. Which models, and the confound (confirmed)
- Six transformer long-context LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-72B/32B, Llama-3-8B-262K,
  GLM-4-9B-1M; plus two gated-linear models: **Codestral-Mamba 7B** and **Jamba-1.5-Mini** (L856-860).
- **Confound, stated explicitly**: the SSM models are ~7B while the transformer set includes 70B/72B.
  This is *not* a matched-parameter or matched-compute comparison. Also note the architecture configs
  (L2270-2282) name the hybrid **AI21-Jamba-1.5-Large**: 72 layers, hidden 8192, 64 attn heads,
  **attention:mamba = 1:7**, 16 experts / 2 active (i.e. it is also a MoE). So the "7B Mini" label in
  the results tables and the "Large" config in the appendix are not obviously the same checkpoint —
  the paper does not reconcile this. I flag it as an unresolved provenance detail, not a claim of error.

### A2. Complexity table (Table 1, L430-470) — the mechanistic reason for the question
| Method | Taxonomy | KV cache | Prefill | Decode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Codestral Mamba | Gated Linear RNN | **O(k)** | O(kn) | O(km) |
| Jamba | Gated Linear RNN + Full Attention | **O(n)** | O(n²) | O(nm) |
| Full attention | — | O(n) | O(n²) | O(nm) |
(llama/qwen/glm rows follow the full-attention O(n)/O(n²)/O(nm) pattern; LLMLingua-2 is O(αn)/O(α²n²)/O(αnm).)
Note the sharp point: **the hybrid Jamba has exactly the same asymptotic cache and compute profile as
full attention** (O(n) cache, O(n²) prefill, O(nm) decode). Its SSM layers buy constant-factor
savings, not a complexity class change. Only the pure linear RNN (Mamba) is sub-O(n).

### A3. Task coverage — which half of our question each block probes
Four capabilities, 12 tasks, 2 shared-context modes; 931 multi-turn sessions, 4,853 queries, ~5 turns/session (L556-560).
- **String Retrieval** (avg input 112-125K): `Retr.KV` (125K), `Retr.Prefix-Suffix` (112K),
  **`Retr.MultiHop` (124K)** (L592-600). MultiHop is from RULER: five multi-hop variable-assignment
  chains embedded in the context; each turn must return the *exact* chain, i.e. all variables assigned
  to a given value (L672-677). This is our direct **multi-hop reasoning** probe.
- **Semantic Retrieval**: `Code.RepoQA` (64K, Pass@1), `En.QA`/`Zh.QA`/`En.MultiChoice` (InfiniteBench).
  Long-document QA / semantic — "long sequence processing".
- **Global Information**: many-shot ICL, summarization, **Math Find** — the aggregation-style tasks.
- **Multi-tasking**: `Mix.RepoQA+KV` etc.
- Two modes: **multi-turn** (cache reused within a session) and **multi-request** (cache reused across
  sessions, assessed *without* query access at encode time) (L840-848). Crucially, follow-up turns use
  **ground-truth answers as context**, not model generations (L846-848) — so this is not a
  self-conditioning/error-accumulation test.

### A4. Headline results — what I trust, and what I could NOT extract
**Director's warning verified.** I checked Table 4 by reconstructing each row as 4 numbers + AVG +
4 numbers + AVG and testing whether the reported AVG equals the mean of the four preceding entries.
- **Transformer rows are internally consistent** — e.g. LLaMA-3.1-8B full attention: 57.1 / 36.9 /
  35.1 / 65.7 → AVG **48.7** ✓, and 29.5 / 36.4 / 43.6 / 39.2 → AVG **37.2** ✓; MInference (8B)
  42.5 ✓ and 36.4 ✓; KIVI (Qwen2.5-72B) 39.1 ✓ and 35.8 ✓. So the transformer half of Table 4 is
  recoverable and safe to quote.
- **Both SSM rows FAIL the check and are unrecoverable.** Jamba row `67.4 28.6 37.5 47.5 32.8 | 21.7
  61.8 5.6 38.9 48.0`: first four average to 45.25 ≠ 32.8; last four average to 32.00 ≠ 48.0.
  Mamba-Codestral row `0.0 0.0 11 0.0 9.3 | 3.9 25.8 6.4 54.8 7.4`: 2.75 ≠ 9.3 and 22.72 ≠ 7.4.
  I ran an exhaustive search over *all* ways of assigning these ten values to (4 + AVG) × 2 columns
  (choosing every pair of AVG positions and every partition of the remaining eight into two groups of
  four): **zero** consistent readings for either row. These are almost certainly columns from
  *different models* that the extraction interleaved. **I quote no SSM per-task number.**
- **The extracted `11` in the Mamba row is a footnote marker** colliding with the numeric column,
  which is exactly the kind of corruption that invalidates a naive read.

**What I do trust, from the paper's own prose (L866-884, the authors' summary bullets):**
- "1) In retrieval tasks, most methods, except MInference, perform poorly, especially in exact
  retrieval tasks like string matching."
- "5) **SSM-Attention hybrids perform well in single-turn interactions but suffer accuracy drops in
  multi-turn tasks, especially in RepoQA and Math. Gated Linear RNN models struggle in shared context
  modes.**" ← this is the load-bearing qualitative finding, stated by the authors, table-independent.
- Insight 1: "**Sub-O(n) memory is almost infeasible in multi-turn decoding**" — sparse decoding
  (sub-O(n) memory) does well on query 1 and loses accuracy on follow-ups, because "important KVs
  remain stable within a turn [but] vary significantly between queries" (Fig. 6b, L1298-1305).
- Insight 2: sparse KV methods excel at *global information* tasks; **O(n) memory is crucial for exact
  match retrieval**. I.e. the efficient-memory methods help exactly where you need aggregation and fail
  where you need exact lookup.
- Arora et al. (2024) is cited (L137) for the mechanism: "Mamba's compression of previous information
  based on the current query can prevent it from answering follow-up queries."
- **Sharp point for the synthesis, confirmed at L1305-1308**: "the SSM-attention hybrid model Jamba
  shows promise in reducing memory costs by using SSM layers while **maintaining O(n) memory in select
  attention layers for future lookups**". So the hybrid's long-context robustness comes from the
  **attention layers**, not from the linear recurrence. Consistent with A2: Jamba's asymptotic
  profile is identical to full attention.
- **The one positive SSM result, L3946-3950**: on `Retr.Prefix-Suffix`, "interestingly, Mamba-Attention
  hybrid architecture Jamba achieve[s] the most accuracy performance. This is non-trivial as
  Retr.Prefix-Suffix task require[s] a rather large space and time complex[ity] and Mamba layers are
  reported to perform poorly on such dimensions. **On the contrary, full attention LLMs such as Llama
  and Qwen series models all failed in this task.**" Table 15 (L4010-4032) is a qualitative case study:
  Jamba reproduces the full 19-char string `RviB-YiaAUgc_nSFCgaamszHq`; Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B
  return truncated `RviBmszHq`; Qwen2.5-32B/72B and the 70B sparse-attention variants all miss
  characters. **Caveat: this is one task, n=1 illustrative case, qualitative — not a rate.** Note the
  task design point (L667-670): Prefix-Suffix has distractors sharing only the prefix or only the
  suffix, so simple lookup/induction-head retrieval cannot work; the authors suggest Jamba's
  compression is an asset here. This is a genuinely interesting counterexample to a blanket
  "attention is a must" claim, and it is a *hybrid* result, not a pure-linear-RNN result.

### A5. What SCBench does NOT establish for our question
- **Not matched-parameter or matched-compute.** 7B SSMs vs 8B-72B transformers, and Jamba is MoE.
  Any "SSMs match transformers" statement from this table is confounded by scale.
- **It is an inference/KV-cache-efficiency benchmark, not a pretraining-quality study.** It says nothing
  about whether linear SSMs can be trained to the same quality at scale — only about what happens to
  an already-trained model when its memory is compressed at serving time. Both SSMs here are off-the-shelf
  checkpoints, not SSMs trained with a long-context objective.
- **It does not separate "multi-hop reasoning" cleanly.** `Retr.MultiHop` is one of three String
  Retrieval tasks, and SCBench reports only family-level aggregates (Retr.String), so the multi-hop
  number is not visible in Table 4 at all. There is no per-task breakdown in the extracted text.
- **The multi-turn/multi-request modes are not reasoning-over-history tests** (ground-truth context,
  L846-848), so the "accuracy drop" is a *memory/lookup* failure, not a reasoning failure. Do not read
  the Jamba multi-turn drop as evidence about multi-hop reasoning ability.

## PART B — 2410.04422: are needle-passing and multi-hop success the same capability?
**Yes, the director's hunch is supported, with a twist.** The paper's taxonomy (Fig. 1a, L60-108;
task-by-task analysis in App. E.3, L1930-2200) splits long-context retrieval into three types:
1. **Simple** — no CoT needed (direct retrieval);
2. **Question-Difficult** — CoT needed, step count set by the *question* ("multi-step-question");
3. **Context-Difficult** — CoT needed, step count set by the *context* (multi-matching,
   logic-based retrieval) (L92-108).

Direct evidence that needle-passing ≠ multi-hop:
- **Multi-hop tracing is classified as Question-Difficult, i.e. "multi-step-question ... but NOT
  multi-matching"** (L2112-2125). It is decomposable into a chain of simple retrievals ("first retrieve
  X1, then use X1 as the query to retrieve X2"), and *may* become logic-based only if the bindings
  involve complex calculations. So a standard RULER/SCBDench multi-hop task is **not** the
  context-difficult class the paper identifies as the real failure mode.
- **The hard failures are context-difficult**: multi-matching (recall n of N items at once) and
  logic-based retrieval. Empirically (L143-160, Fig. 1b, 5 models: Phi-3.5-mini, Llama-3.1-70B,
  DeepSeek-V2.5, Gemini-1.5-flash, GPT-4o): "multi-matching and logic-based retrieval are really hard,
  **nearly unsolvable** for current LCLMs in long context. In contrast, multi-step-question retrieval
  proves to be much easier." Accuracy drops rapidly once context length passes a threshold, for these
  two types only.
- **Single-needle NIAH is explicitly excluded as uninformative** (L1939: "We omit simple tasks like
  single-needle NIAH"), and multi-needle *retrieval* is argued to be "nearly the same as
  Multi-queries NIAH ... can actually be decomposed into multiple independent retrieval problems,
  thus it is not difficult" (L2139-2150). So needle-passing (single and multi) sits in the *easy*
  class; the difficulty lives in context-difficult aggregation/matching.
- **Sufficient-steps result**: plain "think step by step" barely helps; what works is a step count of at
  least N + n(n+1)/2 for multi-matching (L78-84) — steps set by context size N, not question.
- **Caveat the paper itself raises**: at very long context the required step count becomes prohibitive,
  so long reasoning "is still important to find some novel ways to handle long texts efficiently"
  (L139-142) — i.e. the fix is not free.
- **Relevance to us**: `Retr.MultiHop` (SCBench) is a Question-Difficult task, so it is *not* a clean
  test of the capability that this paper shows LCLMs lack. If the director wants a stress test for the
  multi-hop half of the topic question, multi-matching / logic-based retrieval is the better probe,
  and **no archive paper applies it to an SSM**. That is a real gap worth stating.

## Bottom line for the synthesis
From the in-archive material, the answer to "can linear SSMs match or exceed transformers for long
sequence processing and multi-hop reasoning?" is: **not demonstrated, and the one place an SSM-family
model wins (Jamba on Retr.Prefix-Suffix) is a hybrid that keeps O(n) attention memory, at ~7B against
transformers up to 72B, as a single qualitative case.** The authors' own summary is that hybrids
degrade in multi-turn and pure linear RNNs struggle in shared-context modes, and the mechanistic reason
they give (critical KV positions vary between queries) is a *memory* argument, not a reasoning argument.
The multi-hop half of the question is additionally under-evidenced: SCBench's only multi-hop task is
Question-Difficult per 2410.04422's taxonomy, i.e. the easy class.

43: Introduction
44: Time series forecasting (TSF) is an indispensable part of
45: many fields such as traffic flow prediction(Guo et al. 2019),
46: energy management(Uremovi´c et al. 2022), weather fore-
47: casting(Zhang et al. 2022a), finance(Sezer et al. 2020), etc.
48: Among TSF tasks, the long-term time series forecasting
49: (LTSF) task predicts the trend, periodicity and other key
50: patterns of data with a longer future observations, enabling
51: better long-term strategies development, resource allocation
52: planning and risk management.
53: In the past few years, a large number of deep learn-
54: ing models have been developed for LTSF tasks. Among
55: these efforts, Transformer-based models achieve great suc-
56: cess. Transformers use self-attention mechanism to capture
57: long-term dependencies of the time series. In addition, the
58: vanilla Transformer implicitly models the inter-series de-
59: pendencies through channel-mixing embeddings. However,
60: the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism
61: consumes excessive computational resources, resulting in
62: slow training and inference speeds. Although many works
63: like Informer(Zhou et al. 2021) and Autoformer(Wu et al.
64: 2021) try to propose some sparse attention to solve this issue
65: in recent years, they face the challenges of balancing com-
66: putational efficiency and predicting performance. Moreover,
67: these models do not explicitly capture the inter-series depen-
68: dencies, which may cause inadequate modeling of the rela-
69: tionships between different time series(Zhang et al. 2024).
70: Recently, state-space models (SSM) emerge as a promis-
71: ing architecture for sequence modeling(Gu et al. 2021a,b).
72: Among them, a recent study, Mamba(Gu and Dao 2023), has
73: achieved remarkable results in sequence processing tasks
74: such as natural language processing(Lieber et al. 2024),
75: DNA sequence learning, audio waveform processing(Gu
76: and Dao 2023) and computer vision(Zhu et al. 2024). Bene-
77: fiting from its design of selective scanning, Mamba shows
78: superior performance for long sequence modeling, which
79: makes it potentially suitable for the LTSF task. However,
80: there are limited utilizations of SSM in LTSF currently,
81: which may stem from the inherent challenges in time series
82: analysis tasks as follows:
83: • Long-term time series modeling. LTSF deals with
84: larger magnitudes of sequence elements and is often
85: more affected by data non-stationarity, noise and outliers,
86: making it more difficult to capture long-term dependen-
87: cies(Liu et al. 2022). Furthermore, the semantic informa-
88: tion density of time series data at time points is lower
89: than other types of sequence data. Directly modeling
90: point-wise tokens may introduce redundant noise(Cao
91: et al. 2023). Works such as PatchTST(Nie et al. 2023)
92: and Crossformer(Zhang and Yan 2023) emphasis cap-
93: turing richer semantic information by dividing time se-
94: ries into patches for tokenization. Compared with point-
95: wise input tokens, patch-wise tokens reduces the number
96: of sequence elements and leads to lower computational
97: complexity. A recent work iTransformer(Liu et al. 2023)
98: uses a simple fully connected layer to map the whole
99: sequence to hidden states. Although iTransformer gets
100: state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, it is coarse-grained
101: and is not conducive to capturing fine-grained evolution-
102: arXiv:2404.15772v3  [cs.LG]  27 Jun 2024
103: 
104: ary patterns inside the time series. Therefore, we are mo-
105: tivated to model the time series in a patching manner.
106: • Emphasis on intra- or inter-series dependencies. Time
107: series data may have multiple variables with complex
108: correlations between each other. For example, the traf-
109: fic flow of interconnected roads within a transporta-
110: tion network influence each other in different manners
111: during different periods of time. However, capturing
112: inter-series dependencies using channel-mixing strate-
113: gies does not always produce SOTA performance. Works
114: such as PatchTST and NHITS(Challu et al. 2023) get su-
115: perior performance by capturing intra-series dependen-
116: cies only. These models process the multivariate time se-
117: ries (MTS) data in a channel-independent way, where
118: each univariate series is input to the model indepen-
119: dently to enhance the robustness of the model. It can
120: be inferred that different datasets shows different em-
121: phasis on intra- or inter-sequence dependencies. A re-
122: cent study TimeMachine(Ahamed and Cheng 2024) pro-
123: poses a unified structure for channel-independent and
124: channel-mixing tokenization strategies. It aims to handle
125: both intra-series-emphasis and inter-series-emphasis sit-
126: uations. However, the boundary for the selection of tok-
127: enization strategies is ambiguous and the statistical char-
128: acteristics of datasets are overlooked.
129: To solve the above challenges, we design an improved
130: Mamba block named Mamba+ through adding a forget gate
131: in Mamba to selectively combine the new features with the
132: historical features in a complementary manner, therefore
133: preserving historical information in a longer range. Based
134: on the Mamba+, we propose Bidirectional Mamba+ (Bi-
135: Mamba+) to model the MTS data from both forward and
136: backward, enhancing the model’s robustness and ability to
137: capture interactions between time series elements. In addi-
138: tion, to address the varying emphasis on intra-series evo-
139: lutionary patterns and inter-series interactions, we design a
140: Series-Relation-Aware (SRA) decider inspired from Spear-
141: man coefficient correlation. The SRA decider measures the
142: proportion of highly correlated series pairs in the MTS data
143: to automatically choose channel-independent or channel-
144: mixing tokenization strategies. Furthermore, we divide the
145: input sequence into patches and generate patch-wise tokens
146: based on the chosen tokenization strategy. The patch-wise
147: tokens contain richer semantic information and encourage
148: the model to learn the long-term dependencies of the time
149: series in a finer granularity. The main contributions of this
150: paper are summarized as follows:
151: • We propose Bi-Mamba+ for LTSF task. We design an
152: improved Mamba+ block and model the MTS data from
153: both forward and backward to provide more accurate pre-
154: dictions.
155: • We design an SRA decider based on the Spearman
156: correlation coefficient to automatically choose channel-
157: independent or channel-mixing tokenization strategies.
158: Furthermore, we divides the time series into patches to
159: capture long-term dependencies in a finer granularity.
160: • We conduct extensive experiments on 8 real-world
161: datasets that are widely used. The results show that Bi-
162: Mamba+ achieves superior performance with varying
163: prediction lengths.

165: Time Series Forecasting
166: TSF aims to predict future values based on historical ob-
167: servations(Lim and Zohren 2021). Recently, models based
168: on deep neural network achieve great success in TSF.
169: Among these deep learning models, Transformer-based
170: models(Vaswani et al. 2017) get outstanding performance
171: because of the self-attention mechanism. However, the
172: quadratic complexity to the length of the sequence limits
173: these models’ application on long-term time series fore-
174: casting. Therefore, researches in recent years focus on
175: balancing the computing efficiency and predicting perfor-
176: mance of Transformers. Informer(Zhou et al. 2021) pro-
177: poses a ProbSparse mechanism which selects top-k ele-
178: ments of the attention weight matrix to make distillation
179: operation on self-attention. Autoformer(Wu et al. 2021)
180: uses time series decomposition and proposes an Auto-
181: Correlation mechanism inspired by the stochastic process
182: theory. Pyraformer(Liu et al. 2021) introduces the pyrami-
183: dal attention module to summarizes features at different res-
184: olutions and model the temporal dependencies of differ-
185: ent ranges. FEDformer(Zhou et al. 2022) develops a fre-
186: quency enhanced Transformer through frequency domain
187: mapping. PatchTST(Nie et al. 2023) divides each univariate
188: sequence into patches and uses patch-wise self-attention to
189: model temporal dependencies. Crossformer(Zhang and Yan
190: 2023) adopts a similar patching operation but additionally
191: employs a Cross-Dimension attention to capture inter-series
192: dependencies. While patching helps reduce the number of
193: sequence elements to be processed and extract richer seman-
194: tic information, the self-attention layers are only used on
195: the simplified sequences. Therefore, the performance bot-
196: tlenecks still occur when these models deal with longer se-
197: quences. To tackle this issue, iTransformer(Liu et al. 2023)
198: inverts the attention layers to straightly model inter-series
199: dependencies. However, the tokenization approach adopted
200: by iTransformer is simply passing the whole sequence
201: through a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) layer, which over-
202: looks the complex evolutionary patterns inside the time se-
203: ries. Overall, Transformer-based models still face the chal-
204: lenges in computational efficiency and predicting perfor-

495: Mamba+ Block
496: An original Mamba block uses two branches to process the
497: input features. One of the branches, denoted as b1, passes
498: the input features through a 1-D convolutional module and a
499: SSM block. The other branch, denoted as b2, feeds the input
500: features into a SiLU activation function to serve as a gate.
501: Although the HIPPO matrix(Gu et al. 2021b) embedded in
502: the SSM block can retain a fairly long-term historical in-
503: formation, the obtained result is filtered directly through the
504: gate of another branch, resulting in the tendency to priori-
505: tize proximal information(Wang et al. 2024). Therefore, we
506: propose an improved Mamba+ block specifically designed
507: for LTSF. Particularly, we add a forget gate calculated by
508: gatef = 1 −gateb2, where gatef represents the forget gate
509: and gateb2 is the result of sigmoid function in b2. The out-
510: put of the 1-D convolutional module x′ is multiplied with
511: gatef and then added to the filtered result of SSM. gatef
512: and gateb2 selectively combine the added new features with
513: the forgotten historical features in a complementary man-
514: ner. Compared to directly filtering the obtained new fea-
515: tures, Mamba+ emphasis preserving historical information
516: in a longer range. The detailed flow of Mamba+ is shown
517: in Alg.2. The reprogrammed forward and backward prop-

297: SSM is inspired by the continious
298: system, using first-order differential equations to map input
299: function x(t) to output function y(t) through hidden state
300: h(t), defined as follows:

302: y(t) = Ch(t)

307: can be discretized to A, B by zero-order holding and time
308: sampling at intervals of ∆, defined as follows:
309: A = exp (∆A),
310: B = (∆A)−1(exp (∆A) −I) · ∆B.
311: (2)
312: The formula of discretized SSM can then be written as:
313: hk = Ahk−1 + Bxk,
314: yk = Chk

Conclusion
In this paper, we propose Bi-Mamba+, a novel model that
adaptively captures intra- or inter-series dependencies of
MTS data. We propose Mamba+ specifically designed for
LTSF. Mamba+ adds a forget gate in Mamba to selectively
combine the added new features with the forgotten historical
features in a complementary manner, therefore preserving
historical information in a longer range. We design a bidi-
rectional structure to model the MTS data more comprehen-
sively. We divide the time series into patches to encourage
the model to be focused on the inner evolutionary process or
inter-series dependencies at a finer granularity. We explore
the validity of Mamba-like structures and find that Mamba
has great potential in time series forecasting tasks. Extensive
experiments show the superior performance and high effi-
ciency of our model compared to the SOTA methods. Future
research will explore more diverse and complex scenarios
such as network flow forecasting.

SSM-based models
Deep learning models for time series forecasting are ini-
tially based on Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) or Con-
volutional Neural Network (CNN). RNNs process the se-
quence elements step by step and maintain a hidden state
which is updated with each input element. These models are
relatively simple and have excellent inference speed. How-
ever, the calculated gradient must be passed through all cells
one by one, which limits the training speed and leads to
forgetting long-term information. CNNs use convolutional
kernel to emphasis local information. These models bene-
fit from parallel computing and have faster training speed.

Abstract—Recently, infrared small target detection (ISTD) has
made significant progress, thanks to the development of basic
models. Specifically, the models combining CNNs with transform-
ers can successfully extract both local and global features. How-
ever, the disadvantage of the transformer is also inherited, i.e., the
quadratic computational complexity to sequence length. Inspired
by the recent basic model with linear complexity for long-distance
modeling, Mamba, we explore the potential of this state space
model for ISTD task in terms of effectiveness and efficiency in the
paper. However, directly applying Mamba achieves suboptimal
performances due to the insufficient harnessing of local features,
which are imperative for detecting small targets. Instead, we
tailor a nested structure, Mamba-in-Mamba (MiM-ISTD), for
efficient ISTD. It consists of Outer and Inner Mamba blocks to
adeptly capture both global and local features. Specifically, we
treat the local patches as ”visual sentences” and use the Outer
Mamba to explore the global information. We then decompose
each visual sentence into sub-patches as ”visual words” and use
the Inner Mamba to further explore the local information among
words in the visual sentence with negligible computational costs.
By aggregating the visual word and visual sentence features,
our MiM-ISTD can effectively explore both global and local
information. Experiments on NUAA-SIRST and IRSTD-1k show
the superior accuracy and efficiency of our method. Specifically,
MiM-ISTD is 8× faster than the SOTA method and reduces GPU
memory usage by 62.2% when testing on 2048 × 2048 images,

B. Mamba-in-Mamba for Efficient ISTD
Present ISTD methods mainly typically employ CNNs or
hybrids of CNNs and ViTs. The latter compensates for the
shortcomings of the former in modeling long-range dependen-
cies but suffers from a quadratic computational complexity.
Recently, Mamba has been proposed. It is renowned for its
superior model efficiency, less GPU memory usage, and better
long-range dependency modeling and has been successfully
applied to the vision domain. Therefore, we explore whether
Mamba can also be applied to improve ISTD performances.
However, when we directly apply visual mamba block to
ISTD, the accuracy is not very impressive because local
features, which matter a lot to detect small targets, are less
explored. To address this deficiency, we propose a Mamba-
in-Mamba (MiM-ISTD) architecture, shown in Fig. 3, to
learn both global and local information in an image while
guaranteeing superb model efficiency.

sentences that represent the image. Further, each patch is
segmented into m smaller sub-patches, making each visual
sentence a sequence of visual words:
Xi = [xi,1, xi,2, ..., xi,m], j = 1, 2, ..., m
(5)

visual sentence Xi, (s, s) is the spatial size of sub-patches.

4: Bi-Mamba+: Bidirectional Mamba for Time Series Forecasting
5: Aobo Liang1
6: Xingguo Jiang1

15: Abstract
16: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) provides longer
17: insights into future trends and patterns. Over the past few
18: years, deep learning models especially Transformers have
19: achieved advanced performance in LTSF tasks. However,
20: LTSF faces inherent challenges such as long-term depen-
21: dencies capturing and sparse semantic characteristics. Re-
22: cently, a new state space model (SSM) named Mamba is
23: proposed. With the selective capability on input data and
24: the hardware-aware parallel computing algorithm, Mamba
25: has shown great potential in balancing predicting perfor-
26: mance and computational efficiency compared to Transform-
27: ers. To enhance Mamba’s ability to preserve historical infor-
28: mation in a longer range, we design a novel Mamba+ block
29: by adding a forget gate inside Mamba to selectively com-
30: bine the new features with the historical features in a com-
31: plementary manner. Furthermore, we apply Mamba+ both
32: forward and backward and propose Bi-Mamba+, aiming to
33: promote the model’s ability to capture interactions among
34: time series elements. Additionally, multivariate time series
35: data in different scenarios may exhibit varying emphasis on
36: intra- or inter-series dependencies. Therefore, we propose a
37: series-relation-aware decider that controls the utilization of
38: channel-independent or channel-mixing tokenization strategy
39: for specific datasets. Extensive experiments on 8 real-world
40: datasets show that our model achieves better predictions com-
41: pared with state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at
42: https://github.com/Leopold2333/Bi-Mamba+.
43: Introduction
44: Time series forecasting (TSF) is an indispensable part of
45: many fields such as traffic flow prediction(Guo et al. 2019),
46: energy management(Uremovi´c et al. 2022), weather fore-
47: casting(Zhang et al. 2022a), finance(Sezer et al. 2020), etc.
48: Among TSF tasks, the long-term time series forecasting
49: (LTSF) task predicts the trend, periodicity and other key
50: patterns of data with a longer future observations, enabling
51: better long-term strategies development, resource allocation
52: planning and risk management.
53: In the past few years, a large number of deep learn-
54: ing models have been developed for LTSF tasks. Among
55: these efforts, Transformer-based models achieve great suc-
56: cess. Transformers use self-attention mechanism to capture
57: long-term dependencies of the time series. In addition, the
58: vanilla Transformer implicitly models the inter-series de-
59: pendencies through channel-mixing embeddings. However,
60: the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism
61: consumes excessive computational resources, resulting in
62: slow training and inference speeds. Although many works
63: like Informer(Zhou et al. 2021) and Autoformer(Wu et al.
64: 2021) try to propose some sparse attention to solve this issue
65: in recent years, they face the challenges of balancing com-
66: putational efficiency and predicting performance. Moreover,
67: these models do not explicitly capture the inter-series depen-
68: dencies, which may cause inadequate modeling of the rela-
69: tionships between different time series(Zhang et al. 2024).
70: Recently, state-space models (SSM) emerge as a promis-
71: ing architecture for sequence modeling(Gu et al. 2021a,b).
72: Among them, a recent study, Mamba(Gu and Dao 2023), has
73: achieved remarkable results in sequence processing tasks
74: such as natural language processing(Lieber et al. 2024),
75: DNA sequence learning, audio waveform processing(Gu
76: and Dao 2023) and computer vision(Zhu et al. 2024). Bene-
77: fiting from its design of selective scanning, Mamba shows
78: superior performance for long sequence modeling, which
79: makes it potentially suitable for the LTSF task. However,
80: there are limited utilizations of SSM in LTSF currently,
81: which may stem from the inherent challenges in time series
82: analysis tasks as follows:
83: • Long-term time series modeling. LTSF deals with
84: larger magnitudes of sequence elements and is often
85: more affected by data non-stationarity, noise and outliers,
86: making it more difficult to capture long-term dependen-
87: cies(Liu et al. 2022). Furthermore, the semantic informa-
88: tion density of time series data at time points is lower
89: than other types of sequence data. Directly modeling
90: point-wise tokens may introduce redundant noise(Cao
91: et al. 2023). Works such as PatchTST(Nie et al. 2023)
92: and Crossformer(Zhang and Yan 2023) emphasis cap-
93: turing richer semantic information by dividing time se-
94: ries into patches for tokenization. Compared with point-
95: wise input tokens, patch-wise tokens reduces the number
96: of sequence elements and leads to lower computational
97: complexity. A recent work iTransformer(Liu et al. 2023)
98: uses a simple fully connected layer to map the whole
99: sequence to hidden states. Although iTransformer gets
100: state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, it is coarse-grained
101: and is not conducive to capturing fine-grained evolution-
102: arXiv:2404.15772v3  [cs.LG]  27 Jun 2024
103: 
104: ary patterns inside the time series. Therefore, we are mo-
105: tivated to model the time series in a patching manner.
106: • Emphasis on intra- or inter-series dependencies. Time
107: series data may have multiple variables with complex
108: correlations between each other. For example, the traf-
109: fic flow of interconnected roads within a transporta-
110: tion network influence each other in different manners
111: during different periods of time. However, capturing
112: inter-series dependencies using channel-mixing strate-
113: gies does not always produce SOTA performance. Works
114: such as PatchTST and NHITS(Challu et al. 2023) get su-
115: perior performance by capturing intra-series dependen-
116: cies only. These models process the multivariate time se-
117: ries (MTS) data in a channel-independent way, where
118: each univariate series is input to the model indepen-
119: dently to enhance the robustness of the model. It can
120: be inferred that different datasets shows different em-
121: phasis on intra- or inter-sequence dependencies. A re-
122: cent study TimeMachine(Ahamed and Cheng 2024) pro-
123: poses a unified structure for channel-independent and
124: channel-mixing tokenization strategies. It aims to handle
125: both intra-series-emphasis and inter-series-emphasis sit-
126: uations. However, the boundary for the selection of tok-
127: enization strategies is ambiguous and the statistical char-
128: acteristics of datasets are overlooked.
129: To solve the above challenges, we design an improved
130: Mamba block named Mamba+ through adding a forget gate
131: in Mamba to selectively combine the new features with the
132: historical features in a complementary manner, therefore
133: preserving historical information in a longer range. Based
134: on the Mamba+, we propose Bidirectional Mamba+ (Bi-
135: Mamba+) to model the MTS data from both forward and
136: backward, enhancing the model’s robustness and ability to
137: capture interactions between time series elements. In addi-
138: tion, to address the varying emphasis on intra-series evo-
139: lutionary patterns and inter-series interactions, we design a
140: Series-Relation-Aware (SRA) decider inspired from Spear-
141: man coefficient correlation. The SRA decider measures the
142: proportion of highly correlated series pairs in the MTS data
143: to automatically choose channel-independent or channel-
144: mixing tokenization strategies. Furthermore, we divide the
145: input sequence into patches and generate patch-wise tokens
146: based on the chosen tokenization strategy. The patch-wise
147: tokens contain richer semantic information and encourage
148: the model to learn the long-term dependencies of the time
149: series in a finer granularity. The main contributions of this
150: paper are summarized as follows:
151: • We propose Bi-Mamba+ for LTSF task. We design an
152: improved Mamba+ block and model the MTS data from
153: both forward and backward to provide more accurate pre-
154: dictions.
155: • We design an SRA decider based on the Spearman
156: correlation coefficient to automatically choose channel-
157: independent or channel-mixing tokenization strategies.
158: Furthermore, we divides the time series into patches to
159: capture long-term dependencies in a finer granularity.
160: • We conduct extensive experiments on 8 real-world
161: datasets that are widely used. The results show that Bi-
162: Mamba+ achieves superior performance with varying
163: prediction lengths.

7: A Comprehensive Survey and Taxonomy
8: Xiao Liu, Chenxu Zhang, Lei Zhang, Senior Member, IEEE
9: Abstract—State Space Model (SSM) is a mathematical model used to describe and analyze the behavior of dynamic systems. This
10: model has witnessed numerous applications in several fields, including control theory, signal processing, economics and machine
11: learning. In the field of deep learning, state space models are used to process sequence data, such as time series analysis, natural
12: language processing (NLP) and video understanding. By mapping sequence data to state space, long-term dependencies in the data
13: can be better captured. In particular, modern SSMs have shown strong representational capabilities in NLP, especially in long
14: sequence modeling, while maintaining linear time complexity. Notably, based on the latest state-space models, Mamba [28] merges
15: time-varying parameters into SSMs and formulates a hardware-aware algorithm for efficient training and inference. Given its impressive
16: efficiency and strong long-range dependency modeling capability, Mamba is expected to become a new AI architecture that may
17: outperform Transformer. Recently, a number of works have attempted to study the potential of Mamba in various fields, such as general
18: vision, multi-modal, medical image analysis and remote sensing image analysis, by extending Mamba from natural language domain to
19: visual domain. To fully understand Mamba in the visual domain, we conduct a comprehensive survey and present a taxonomy study.
20: This survey focuses on Mamba’s application to a variety of visual tasks and data types, and discusses its predecessors, recent
21: advances and far-reaching impact on a wide range of domains. Since Mamba is now on an upward trend, please actively notice us if
22: you have new findings, and new progress on Mamba will be included in this survey in a timely manner and updated on the Mamba
23: project: https://github.com/lx6c78/Vision-Mamba-A-Comprehensive-Survey-and-Taxonomy.
24: Index Terms—State Space Model, Mamba, Computer Vision, Medical Image Analysis, Remote Sensing Image Analysis.

138: - **Relevance to us**: `Retr.MultiHop` (SCBench) is a Question-Difficult task, so it is *not* a clean
139:   test of the capability that this paper shows LCLMs lack. If the director wants a stress test for the
140:   multi-hop half of the topic question, multi-matching / logic-based retrieval is the better probe,
141:   and **no archive paper applies it to an SSM**. That is a real gap worth stating.
142: 
143: ## Bottom line for the synthesis
144: From the in-archive material, the answer to "can linear SSMs match or exceed transformers for long
145: sequence processing and multi-hop reasoning?" is: **not demonstrated, and the one place an SSM-family
146: model wins (Jamba on Retr.Prefix-Suffix) is a hybrid that keeps O(n) attention memory, at ~7B against
147: transformers up to 72B, as a single qualitative case.** The authors' own summary is that hybrids
148: degrade in multi-turn and pure linear RNNs struggle in shared-context modes, and the mechanistic reason
149: they give (critical KV positions vary between queries) is a *memory* argument, not a reasoning argument.
150: The multi-hop half of the question is additionally under-evidenced: SCBench's only multi-hop task is
151: Question-Difficult per 2410.04422's taxonomy, i.e. the easy class.

2481: The linear complexity and global modeling capabilities of
2482: Mamba make it naturally suitable for processing high-
2483: resolution remote sensing images and medical images. It
2484: shows significant advantages in computational efficiency,
2485: GPU memory consumption, inference speed, etc., greatly
2486: promoting the deployment and implementation of deep
2487: learning models in practical applications.

2489: CONCLUSION, CHALLENGE AND OUTLOOK
2490: Mamba is receiving an unprecedented attention in the field
2491: of computer vision and its vertical domains as a new
2492: alternative of network architecture. Mamba has shown a
2493: great potential in both alternative and composite architec-
2494: tures due to its unique features from popular convolutional
2495: neural network and Transformer architectures. This article
2496: presents a comprehensive review of Mamba and its vari-
2497: ants deployed to various visual tasks, including general
2498: vision such as high/mid-level vision, low-level vision, 3D
2499: Vision and visual generation, vision-language multi-modal
2500: learning, and vertical domains such as remote sensing in-
2501: telligence and medical intelligence. Nevertheless, Mamba
2502: is standing in an early stage, and there is still much room
2503: for improvement when compared to those relatively mature
2504: Transformer-based models. We offer several potential chal-
2505: lenges and possible directions for future research to further
2506: advance Mamba.
2507: 6.1
2508: New Scanning Mechanism
2509: Mamba must obtain the state of the subsequent time point
2510: based on the previous time point and hidden state and result
2511: in causal properties. Visual data has non-causal properties
2512: and also has certain spatial relationships. It is necessary to
2513: consider how to remove the spurious association and retain
2514: the necessary image structure information when deploying
2515: Mamba. The earliest visual Mamba backbones formulated
2516: from the perspective of scanning operations, such as Vim
2517: and VMamba, proposed bidirectional scanning mechanisms
2518: and cross-scanning mechanisms, respectively. After that, dif-
2519: ferent scanning schemes are proposed to bridge the gap in
2520: the input data and adapt it to downstream tasks. Therefore,
2521: it is necessary to design a reasonable scanning mechanism
2522: to improve Mamba’s performance in visual tasks.
2523: 6.2
2524: Synergistic Hybrid Architecture
2525: Mamba has advantages over Transformers but there are also
2526: some essential drawbacks, such as insufficient interactions
2527: between tokens due to the lack of attention mechanism,
2528: which adversely affects the capture of more comprehensive
2529: and detailed information. Therefore, building hybrid mod-
2530: els incorporating Mamba would be a promising direction
2531: to reduce this inherent shortcoming effectively. Prior to
2532: Mamba, [50] combines the advantages of structured state-
2533: space sequences (S4) and self-attention layers to capture
2534: short-range intra-camera dependencies and aggregate long-
2535: range inter-camera cues. Nevertheless, how to combine
2536: Mamba with Transformer for vision tasks is still a chal-
2537: lenge, e.g., [118] experimentally show that the combination
2538: of the VSS block and cross-attention mechanism does not
2539: work well for image segmentation. Hybrid models need
2540: to consider the fundamental differences between Mamba
2541: and other architectures. For example, Mamba models are
2542: strictly sequential in their predictions and usually do not
2543: modeling tokens not appeared in the scan, whereas the
2544: attention mechanism treats all tokens equally. This essential
2545: difference in the way the sequences are modeled easily
2546: makes both architectures conflict, and therefore bridging the
2547: gap is pretty important.
2548: 6.3
2549: Following the Law of Scale
2550: Although Mamba has attracted attention for its remarkable
2551: computational efficiency, improving model capacity is still
2552: essential in the current era of large models following the
2553: scaling law. Currently, large-scale model with Mamba ar-
2554: chitecture is not yet appeared. Large-scale models incorpo-
2555: rating the advantages of Mamba may be more powerful
2556: in long-term sequence modeling and another competitive
2557: visual foundation model. Moreover, various Mamba tuning
2558: methods will emerge as the model scale increases.

Title: State_space_representation
Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_space_representation
License: CC BY SA 4.0

State-space representation Mathematical model of a system in control engineering 
 Not to be confused with quantum state space or configuration space (physics) . 
 "State space model" redirects here. For the use in deep learning, see State space model (deep learning) . 
 In control engineering and system identification , a state-space representation is a mathematical model of a physical system that uses state variables to track how inputs shape system behavior over time through first-order differential equations or difference equations . These state variables change based on their current values and inputs, while outputs depend on the states and sometimes the inputs too. The state space (also called time-domain approach and equivalent to phase space in certain dynamical systems ) is a geometric space where the axes are these state variables, and the system’s state is represented by a state vector . 

 For linear , time-invariant , and finite-dimensional systems, the equations can be written in matrix form, [ 1 ] [ 2 ] offering a compact alternative to the frequency domain ’s Laplace transforms for multiple-input and multiple-output (MIMO) systems. Unlike the frequency domain approach, it works for systems beyond just linear ones with zero initial conditions. This approach turns systems theory into an algebraic framework, making it possible to use Kronecker structures for efficient analysis. 

 State-space models are applied in fields such as economics, [ 3 ] statistics, [ 4 ] computer science, electrical engineering , [ 5 ] and neuroscience. [ 6 ] In econometrics , for example, state-space models can be used to decompose a time series into trend and cycle, compose individual indicators into a composite index, [ 7 ] identify turning points of the business cycle , and estimate GDP using latent and unobserved time series. [ 8 ] [ 9 ] Many applications rely on the Kalman filter or a state observer to produce estimates of the current unknown state variables using their previous observations. [ 10 ] [ 11 ]

ABSTRACT
The context window of large language models (LLMs) has been extended sig-
nificantly in recent years. However, while the context length that the LLM can
process has grown, the capability of the model to accurately reason over that
context degrades noticeably. This occurs because modern LLMs often become
overwhelmed by the vast amount of information in the context; when answering
questions, the model must identify and reason over relevant evidence sparsely
distributed throughout the text. To alleviate the challenge of long-context rea-
soning, we develop a retrieve-then-reason framework, enabling LLMs to reason
over relevant evidence collected during an intermediate retrieval step. We find
that modern LLMs struggle to accurately retrieve relevant facts and instead, often
hallucinate “retrieved facts”, resulting in flawed reasoning and the production of
incorrect answers. To address these issues, we introduce ALR2, a method that
augments the long-context reasoning capability of LLMs via an explicit two-stage
procedure, i.e., aligning LLMs with the objectives of both retrieval and reasoning.
We demonstrate the efficacy of ALR2 for mitigating performance degradation in
long-context reasoning tasks. Through extensive experiments on long-context QA
benchmarks, we find our method to outperform competitive baselines by large
margins, achieving at least 8.4 and 7.9 EM gains on the long-context versions of
HotpotQA and SQuAD datasets, respectively.

The ability for large language models (LLMs) to reason over long contexts is critical in many
downstream tasks, e.g., document analysis (Wang et al., 2024a), multi-hop tool use (Yao et al., 2023),

(Vaswani, 2017) architecture impact long-context performance (Su et al., 2024a; Chiang & Cholak,
2022; Xiao et al., 2024) to proposing new architectures with improved efficiency (Dai et al., 2019;

context, performance degrades as the input context grows. In contrast, when tasked with retrieving
the set of evidence relevant to the question, the performance of LLMs is only mildly affected by the
growth of the input context.

the finding.* It is an architectural choice forced by the task.** The survey states the causal
property is intrinsic to the SSM: L2509–2511 *"Mamba must obtain the state of the subsequent time

has non-causal properties and also has certain spatial relationships."* So for every visual task

and the "data type"/"highlight" columns of Table 1 map almost 1:1 onto *which scan direction*).

## 2. Sequence lengths — the extrapolation limit

- Look-back **L = 96** for all main experiments; horizons H ∈ {96, 192, 336, 720}.
- Look-back sweep (lines 1898–1933, Fig. 6) goes to **L ∈ {48, 96, 192, 336, 720}** on Electricity
  and ETTm2 only, and is reported as *figures*, not numbers.
- Critically, with P = L/4 and stride S = P/2 the **token count is J = 7 at every look-back length**
  (96→7, 336→7, 720→7; I computed this from the formula J = ⌈(L−P)/S⌉+1 at lines 461–465). So the
  sequence fed to the SSM is 7 tokens, and the "long-range" claim is about the *look-back in samples*,
  not about the recurrent state being exercised over a long token sequence. **Do not use this paper as
  evidence about long-token-sequence modelling.** 7 tokens vs a 100k-token context is three-plus
  orders of magnitude away.
- "Transformer" here also means at sequence length 7, where quadratic attention is not a burden.
  The efficiency claim (Fig. 7) is about **channels** (M up to 862 for Traffic), not about length.

| variant | avg MSE | vs full model |
|---|---|---|
| w/o SRA-I (channel-independent only) | 0.3246 | +3.61% |
| w/o SRA-M (channel-mixing only) | 0.3165 | +1.02% |

| PatchTST | 0.3386 | +8.08% |

tokens, SRA decider, residuals) are worth at least as much as the SSM substitution. And the
Mamba-specific novelty is a **forget gate**, `gatef = 1 − gateb2` (line 508), i.e. the change is
tiny.

**DLinear is beaten by Bi-Mamba+ in 32/32 cells (avg MSE 0.3775 vs 0.3133, mean margin 16.3%).**

- So a linear model is *not* the hidden winner here — the paper's own baseline set does not
  reproduce the DLinear-beats-transformers folklore in this configuration. Worth a line in the

`grep -i "limitation"` on 2404.15772 returns **zero hits**. The Conclusion (lines 2054–2071) closes

scenarios such as network flow forecasting." That is the entire limitations content. I checked

this archive do not volunteer limitations**; any such statement in the synthesis must be yours, and
should be attributed as the reviewer's inference, not to the authors.

Honest-but-unstated caveats I would attribute to the *reviewer*: (i) 7-token sequences; (ii) the
per-model embedding dims differ (D=128 for patching models, D=512 for whole-sequence models
S-Mamba/iTransformer — lines 779–783), so the SSM-vs-transformer comparison is **not** parameter-

hyper-parameter repeats are 5×40 epochs (line 1790) with early stopping, but the headline table

## 6. Secondary: MiM-ISTD (2403.02148) — what nesting buys

Short answer: **nesting is a resolution-hierarchy trick, with no analogy to the long-sequence
problem.** Mechanism (lines 485–498, 550–658): the image is split into n patches = "visual
sentences"; each patch into m sub-patches = "visual words". 16 *shared* Inner Mamba blocks scan the

embeddings (global). Both are linear in their sequence length, so total FLOPs stay linear;
